News.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla enjoy Braemar Gathering ahead of Andy Burnham meeting
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla enjoy Braemar Gathering ahead of Andy Burnham meeting

The King and Queen were greeted by thousands of spectators at the famous Highland Games event before travelling to Balmoral to meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham

View 2 Images King Charles and Queen Camilla during the Braemar Gathering (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

The King and Queen basked in Highland sunshine at the annual Braemar Gathering before hosting a meeting with the Prime Minister.

‌



Charles and Camilla received a warm welcome from thousands of onlookers at the celebrated Highland Games event prior to heading to Balmoral to meet Andy Burnham.

‌



Sunshine pierced through the clouds and the countryside burst into life as masses descended upon the venue in the heart of the Cairngorms National Park, famed for its royal connections.

‌



A variety of competitions were on display, from cross country racing and tug of war to caber tossing, the high jump and Highland dancing. Spectators stood to welcome the royal pair before the national anthem rang out.

Pipers and drummers received thunderous applause from attendees as they paraded around the games arena.

‌



View 2 Images Charles and Camilla enjoyed the games before a meeting at Balmoral with Andy Burnham (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Meghan Markle may not appear in public for weeks after moving back to UK with Prince Harry READ MORE :

The Queen received a heather posy from 11 year old Highland dancer Ally Dey.

Master of ceremonies Robert Lovie declared during the royal entrance: "We are greatly honoured that your majesties have graced us with your presence today, which enriches this gathering and all that Highland Games and culture represents, and I know I speak for everyone – both in your beloved Royal Deeside and from the family of Highland Games officials and competitors – in sending you both our warmest and most loyal good wishes.

Article continues below

"Today, in the fine autumnal splendour of this Highland village, we present the finest of athletes, sportsmen and women, dancers, pipers and drummers and a proud showcase of talent from your majesty's armed forces."

News.title: Nigel Farage claims he 'wasn't listening' in donor drama meeting as Reform's disaster conference closes
News.content:
Nigel Farage claims he 'wasn't listening' in donor drama meeting as Reform's disaster conference closes

There were hundreds of empty seats in the hall as Farage gave his closing address at the event in Birmingham., which had been overshadowed by revelations in a Channel 4 sting

Nigel Farage dodges Mirror journalist's questions

Nigel Farage claimed he "wasn't listening" during the meeting that sparked the party's donor drama and derailed the party's conference.

‌



There were hundreds of empty seats in the hall as Farage gave his closing address at the event in Birmingham.

‌



It had been overshadowed by revelations in a Channel 4 sting, which showed senior Reform figures discussing how to disguise donations from foreign sources.

‌



Accepting donations from a foreign company could constitute a criminal offence, and the party has been reported to the police.

Farage told ITV he was certain Reform had accepted no illicit donations and dismissed claims in the documentary by one of his long-term aides, Dan Jukes, that the party had previously concealed the origin of some donations as "loose pub talk".

Two senior aides - including Dan Jukes, Farage's former Chief of Staff - stepped down on Friday.

‌



8 weird and sinister moments from Reform conference - from free speech to flags READ MORE :

View 3 Images The conference was overshadowed by the donations scandal (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Jukes, who denies any wrongdoing, and James Orr, the party's head of policy, have stood down pending an internal investigation of their appearance in the footage.

Farage has said Mr Jukes and Mr Orr were "injudicious at best", while denying any wrongdoing and saying he was told that any arrangements were "above board".

‌



Speaking to the BBC on Saturday, he claimed to "know donation law better than anybody" and said the two men "should have done basic checks" before bringing potential donors to meet him.

He said he "frankly wasn't even listening" during a meeting with the undercover reporters in Clacton, adding: "I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London."

‌



Farage, who is already facing scrutiny over his failure to declare a £5 million gift from a party donor, said investigations "will go on".

But the row has sparked speculation that Farage might not lead the party into the next general election.

He was tight-lipped when confronted about his future by the Mirror on the conference floor.

‌



View 3 Images Suella Braverman insisted there wasn't a leadership contest (Image: Getty Images)

In his speech on the main stage, Mr Jenrick, who was privately educated, told Reform delegates: "People like my Dad who drove a white van, built a small business at our kitchen table down the road in Wolverhampton, and toiled for his family.

"Because I know who I'm in politics for, where I’m from, and who my people are."

‌



He told Reform fans he was proud to "take my place amongst the ranks of the people’s army.

"To stand and fight by your side. And to do so as Westminster went to war against us."

Mr Jenrick told the final day of the Reform conference in Birmingham that he would increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days of taking office.

‌



The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.

Meanwhile there was mounting fury over peaceful protesters being manhandled out of Farage's keynote speech on Friday - and assaulted by party members.

West Midlands Police yesterday(SAT) said officers want to speak to a female protester who was assaulted by Reform members after she heckled Nigel Farage.

‌



View 3 Images Zia Yusuf has faced criticism for his social media outbursts (Image: James Manning/PA Wire)

A sickening clip shared online showed her being hit around the head with a crutch before her hair was pulled and a hand put over her mouth.

The grey haired man seen assaulting her was not a member of the event's security team.

‌



Another woman was shown pulling her hair as she was escorted from Birmingham's NEC.

Reform's Nadine Dorries yesterday(SAT) responded to a question by The Mirror by saying protesters should not expect to be treated gently.

And chairman Lee Anderson made light of the incident in his speech, telling cheering supporters: "I did see an old chap, a pensioner, somewhere with a walking stick... Look I don't condone any of that type of behaviour, but if anyone wants to have a quick whip around later we are collecting for a new walking stick."

‌



Ms Dorries said: “If you’re going to come into a conference like this (to cause disruption) of course you’re not going to get gentle treatment.”

A West Midlands Police spokesman told The Mirror: “We’re aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK Conference showing an incident with a protester.

“We haven’t received a complaint but would ask the woman involved to come forward and contact us so we can carry out enquiries."

‌



Asked if she thought Mr Jenrick and Home Affairs Spokesman Zia Yusuf were "on manoeuvres, ex-Tory Suella Braverman said: "The simple answer is no.

"Listen, I've seen a lot of skulduggery, let's say, within the Conservative Party. And it's another reason why I left."

She added: "I know we're all behind 100% Nigel. I want him to be Prime Minister. So does Robert, so does Zia. And we're not going to stop working and fighting until we achieve that goal.

‌



Closing the conference on Saturday, Farage told delegates: "There will be times in this journey when there are good days and times when there are difficult days.

"More often than not, things will be put upon us that are unfair.

"But sometimes we will make mistakes, sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking for it.

Article continues below

"But what this conference has shown is whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever they throw at you, the people's army, we immediately pick ourselves up, dust ourselves down and start all over again."

Responding, Bridget Phillipson MP, Chair of the Labour Party, said: "Farage finishes conference as he started: with desperate excuses and pathetic deflection tactics to try to distract from his and his Party's shady finances. The sleaze and scandals engulfing Reform aren't going away. Farage needs to wake up, take responsibility and realise the buck stops with him.

"While Reform's chaos and scandals roll on, Andy Burnham is bringing back hope to Britain: through decisive action to give vital breathing space on the cost of living, and with key changes to drive growth in every postcode of our country."

News.title: Alex Ferguson in stitches as wife Cathy fell for prank that he would be TV detective Taggart
News.content:
Alex Ferguson in stitches as wife Cathy fell for prank that he would be TV detective Taggart

EXCLUSIVE: Lady Cathy, who hated the detective series, stormed off saying she would not let him take the job

View 2 Images Sir Alex Ferguson and wife Cathy after he was knighted in 1999 (Image: PA)

Sir Alex Ferguson pranked his wife Cathy by getting an ITV executive to tell her he’d been asked to star as the new Taggart.

‌



The series, which starred Mark McManus as hard-nosed Glaswegian detective Jim Taggart, first aired in 1985.

‌



Despite McManus dying in 1994, the series continued under the same name until 2010.

‌



Fergie let slip the prank to The Script pop singer Danny O’Donoghue when the pair were at a golf do.

Speaking about meeting Sir Alex at the bash just before the manchester-united-fc>Manchester United legend retired in 2013, the 45-year-old singer said Sir Alex quizzed him about the TV show.

View 2 Images Mark McManus played TV detective Taggart

‌



Cruz Beckham takes fresh dig at brother Brooklyn amid feud with telling social media post READ MORE :

Danny said: “Me and Sir Alex were stood in the foyer.

“He said ‘Do you know Taggart?’…I’m about to retire and my wife was asking what I was going to do’.”

He said that Sir Alex continued, saying: “We were having dinner with a friend who worked for ITV and I got him to say that ITV wanted me as the new Taggart.”

‌



Danny said that Sir Alex told him that Lady Cathy - who died aged 84 in 2023 - ‘absolutely hated Taggart’ and stormed off saying there was no way she’d let him take the job

Danny said that Sir Alex and his ITV pal were ‘rolling around laughing’ after Cathy fell for the prank.

TV and radio presenter Edith Bowman, 52, previously revealed how her nickname for Sir Alex was ‘Taggart’, as he looks similar to Mark McManus - and has the same broad Scottish accent.

Article continues below

Edith, whose family have known Sir Alex for more than 30 years, said: “He (Sir Alex) is in my phone as Taggart because of the detective show.

“We kind of take the p**s out of him that that’s who he is in real life.”

Sir Alex never entered the acting world - but his former star man Eric Cantona has appeared in a string of movies.

News.title: 8 weird and sinister moments from Reform conference - from free speech to flags
News.content:
8 weird and sinister moments from Reform conference - from free speech to flags

Explosive allegation on foreign donations dominated the news during Reform conference. But The Mirror also wanted to ensure no gaffes, or strange moments were missed

View 7 Images Nigel Farage was caught out by his own backdrop at Labour conference (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

Reform UK's annual conference went off the rails in spectacular fashion after the party was plunged into a dodgy donations scandal.

‌



Nigel Farage's plans to get voters talking about his hardline policies were dashed, as two of his top aides were forced to go after being caught in undercover filming allegedly seeking to evade the rules on donations.

‌



The report, aired by Channel 4, completely dominated the news agenda during the gathering of Reform party faithful in Birmingham. But The Mirror was on hand to ensure no gaffes, weird moments and sinister exchanges were missed.

‌



Reform conference sees woman hit on head with crutch and hair pulled in sickening clip READ MORE :

Reform plunged into chaos by donations row as Nigel Farage heckled during major speech READ MORE :

Nadine Dorries defends banning journalists - during free speech debate

View 7 Images Reform's Nadine Dorries doesn't appear to like free speech... (Image: Will Colebourne/PA Wire)

Nadine Dorries defended Reform's decision to bar critical journalists - during a debate about free speech.

The ironic exchange saw her label one of those refused entry - award-winning broadcaster and writer Michael Crick - a "pain in the bum". Ms Dorries, a former Tory cabinet minister who defected to Reform - said Mr Crick should be barred from all conferences as he makes a nuisance of himself.

‌



She said: "He’s only there to cause trouble and to try derail what’s taking place at the time. I don’t think Michael Crick should be able to attend any conference because he’s there to cause trouble."

Also barred was Guardian journalist Anna Isaac, who exposed the £5million gift received by Mr Farage, and investigative reporter Peter Geoghegan.

Made in China blunder after deputy goes on attack

Nigel Farage's number two opened Reform's conference by having a dig at China - while standing yards away from a Reform UK merch stand selling items manufactured there.

‌



Richard Tice vowed his party would be championing British business, and pointing at a bus on display at Birmingham's NEC, he said: "I don't want any Chinese buses in here please."

But a quick glance over the nearby conference shop reveals Farage fans can purchase caps, pendants and water bottles manufactured in China.

View 7 Images A lot of Chinese-made merch was on sale at the conference (Image: David Burke/ ReachPLC)

‌



The merch sits alongside caps made in Bangladesh, hoodies from Pakistan and tote bags made in India. Max Wilkinson, the Lib Dem home affairs spokesman, quipped: "I hear the Reform gift shop is quickly selling out of hypocrisy. But luckily for conference-goers, they have plenty of snake oil left over.”

Click here for the full story

Lee Anderson slags off Mirror journalist’s suit

Reform chairman Lee Anderson wasn’t in a mood to answer questions about the donations scandal gripping the party.

‌



We confronted him in the conference hall, to ask if Reform will take cash from just about anyone. The tetchy politician retorted: “By the looks of your suit, you could do with some money, mate.”

He then refused to answer whether oysters - as Nigel Farage was filmed enjoying - was the breakfast of a man of the people. Funny that.

View 7 Images Tetchy Lee Anderson lashed out at the Mirror over donations row (Image: Getty Images)

‌



... as another Mirror journalist kicked out of Farage speech

Things got very fraught during Nigel Farage’s speech, as spooked security began throwing journalists out of the hall.

One of our team had been filming - and doing nothing wrong - when security escorted her out.

Her pass was confiscated but no proper explanation was given. She was eventually allowed back into the conference after other Mirror journalists intervened.

‌



Farage looks like a ‘laughing stock’ with 'boring' backdrop

Reform staffers were accused of making Nigel Farage look like a “complete laughing stock” during his speech after they flashed up a sign saying “boring, boring, boring” behind him.

When the Reform UK leader faced hecklers during his main stage speech on Friday, he shouted back “boring, boring, boring". It’s a line he’s used when his speeches have been interrupted before and has become a meme on social media.

View 7 Images Nigel Farage was mocked by his own backdrop (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

‌



Anticipating hecklers, Reform UK staff had organised for the quote to flash up behind their boss when they disrupted the speech. But what they hadn’t thought through… was that this would mean their beloved leader Mr Farage would inadvertently be labelled as “boring” during his own speech.

A Labour source told The Mirror: "Reform have made Farage look a complete laughing stock - gaffes like this just prove how unfit they are for high office." And on social media, Labour’s press team responded to a photo of Mr Farage on stage, saying: “For once, we couldn't agree more.” Lib Dem deputy leader also said: “At last! Farage saying something we can all agree with.”

Reform member calls for people who push 'wokeism' to be 'made to hang'

A Reform member has called for people who have pushed “wokeism” in the UK to be “made to hang”.

‌



Harry, from Romsey and Southampton North, was given a platform to speak in the main conference hall during a segment chaired by TV host and Reform supporter Jeremy Kyle.

Standing at a mic next to a platformed stage, where Mr Kyle sat, Harry told the host he wanted to speak about "wokeism”. He continued: “We are seeing if I'm not mistaken, the first signs of wokeism being excluded or disowned by the progressive left in America. I name for example (Zohran) Mamdami, the NYC Mayor, and AOC (US Democrat politician Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez).

“If I'm reading this correctly, this may come across to the UK and those in the UK politically who have pushed wokeism for 20+ years, they must be made to hang. Is that a fair comment?”

‌



Mr Kyle replies: “I don't think the hang thing is a fair comment, to be fair." The host then went on to rant about diversity, equity and inclusion, while other panellists engaged in a conversation on "wokeism".

Reform finance boss 'talking nonsense' over Boris Johnson by-election claim

Reform’s finance chief was accused of talking nonsense after he sensationally claimed Kemi Badenoch tried to get Boris Johnson to stand in the Clacton by-election.

Billionaire Nick Candy, a former Tory bankroller, told the Daily T podcast: "She [Badenoch] asked Boris to run in the Clacton by-election against Nigel, that is what I'm told.

‌



View 7 Images The Tories slapped down claims Boris Johnson was asked to run in the Clacton by-election (Image: AP)

"I don't know first hand. I actually haven't picked up the phone to Boris on it." He continued: "Boris decided not to do it, or chose not to do it."

But a Tory source told The Mirror: "This is another nonsense story made up by Reform. No one has spoken to Boris about standing in any seat."

‌



Jeremy Kyle and Nigel Farage go flags crazy

Not long before his closing speech on the main stage, Nigel Farage managed to find some time to spend with his mate Jeremy Kyle.

The pair sat in armchairs for a cosy chat on a platformed stage in the main conference hall. The crowd wooed as a grinning Mr Farage did some unsightly acrobatics to show off his Union Jack socks.

View 7 Images Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage reacts with host Jeremy Kyle following a panel discussion (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Mr Kyle told him to be careful as he could be "arrested" for wearing those in Birmingham. A conference delegate, who set up a grassroots campaign backing the flag, told Mr Farage he was fighting court battles against authorities who told him not to raise flags.

Mr Farage said he would give the man’s proposals to his lawyers and ranted about the “anti-flag” campaign. In a typically long-winded rant, he made a jibe about Dame Emily Thornberry and questions Labour being the “party of working people” because she accepted a damehood.

Isn’t this coming from the man who accepted a £5million gift?

News.title: United Nations votes to adopt new world map which will shrink the US and supersize Africa
News.content:
United Nations votes to adopt new world map which will shrink the US and supersize Africa

For over 450 years we have been misled about what the world actually looks like. . . . until now. And one notable nation is less than impressed.

View 5 Images UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small (Image: Getty Images)

The world as we know it is about to change.

‌



The United Nations has voted to retire the world map. Yep, the commonly used world map used in classrooms, government buildings, and on globes worldwide. Instead, a new map will be endorsed which will see the United States shrink and Africa increase in size.

‌



So why has the UN chosen to ditch our centuries-old, beloved world map? It all comes down to design, with a 2018 design called the Equal Earth projection now found to be a more accurate representation of what our world actually looks like.

‌



It corrects scale and layout issues that have distorted our world view for more than 450 years thanks to geographical and geometrical warping caused by Mercator, the original world map designer.

View 5 Images A vintage map of the UK (Image: Getty)

Mercator's map artificially stretches land masses as they get further away from the equator. Basically, it has been distorting some nations and shrinking others for centuries. Take the United States and Greenland as an example. On a Mercator map, the two nations look to be the same size. But, in reality, Greenland is about 14 times larger in landmass compared to America.

‌



It is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart, so whenever a map of the world gets drawn up, sacrifices have to be made. Mercator aimed to preserve direction in order to help explorers fan out in ships to explore the world. So, at the expense of area, land masses must become enlarged the further they are from the equator to account for the Earth's curvature.

View 5 Images Those curves have brought nothing but trouble as far as cartography goes (Image: Getty Images)

As the new design corrects these spatial exaggerations, the US will be shrunken down on new maps going forward, while continents like Africa and Australia will look vastly larger.

‌



At the UN General Assembly, a resolution was put forward by a coalition of African nations calling for our world maps to stop minimising their continent. It proposed the UN endorse the updated map designs, with a total of 164 countries voting in agreement on Friday (September 4).

The resolution was passed, and the UN will now recommend the new world map design to ensure maps "more accurately reflect the true size" of our world.

Six countries – Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine – abstained from voting at the UN General Assembly, while one lone dissenting voice opposed the new map design: the United States of America.

‌



View 5 Images A depiction of Earth, as seen from space (Image: Getty Images)

With the US set to shrink under new map designs, it would seem that perhaps size does matter. But if that were the motivation behind America's 'no' vote, they weren't letting it on. Instead, Washington's representative accused the UN-approved map resolution of being about much more than just correcting map proportions.

“This resolution mocks the work and purpose of this institution,” US representative to the UN Yaryna Ferencevych, dubbing the "Correct the Map" vote as part of a wider “radical ideological project“ that undermines "common sense" global policies.

‌



In a statement explaining its reason to vote no, the US slammed the UN for "debating map projects from the 16th century" instead of real-world issues like "international peace, prosperity, or good relations".

Diplomats from Togo led the campaign to get the new map vote before the broader UN General Assembly. The nation's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, pointed out that maps are far more symbolic than people give them credit for.

“A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world,” he said.

Article continues below

View 5 Images France will see itself shrunk down to scale, as per the new maps (Image: Getty Images)

France, another nation set to shrink on the new proposed map designs, issued a statement of its own prior to the UN vote. French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Paris will nix the Mercator chart in favour of the Equal Earth projection.

As for Mercator, his maps won't just vanish from circulation, as the UN resolution is non-binding. Governments can choose to use either design, but the power of choice creates a new cartographic culture more focused on fairness and equality for all.

News.title: Woman, 38, dies after car crashes into brick wall in Liverpool
News.content:
Woman, 38, dies after car crashes into brick wall in Liverpool

The woman was sadly declared dead at the scene as emergency services said a car smashed into a brick wall late on Friday night

View 3 Images The scene of the crash shows a garden wall was completely destroyed (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A woman has tragically died after a car smashed into a brick wall late last night.

Emergency services scrambled to Allerton Road in Woolton, Liverpool, at around 11.30pm on Friday (September 4) to reports of a serious car crash.

A white Vauxhall Astra was seen with damage to its rear while a red Nissan Juke is said to have left the road and crashed into the brick wall at the junction of High Street.

Sadly, a 38-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene, Liverpool Echo reports. Her next of kin have been informed and will be supported by specially trained officers, Merseyside Police said in a statement.

Photographs of the scene show the extent of the damage, with the wall and a post box among the crumbled debris in the road.

View 3 Images A woman has sadly died in the crash (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Sergeant Phil Everett, of Merseyside Police Matrix Roads Policing department, said: “Our thoughts are with the family members of the woman who sadly died following the collision late last night and they are being supported by a specially trained family liaison officer.

“We are in the early stages of an investigation into this incident and it is now our priority to confirm exactly how the collision occurred.

“We know this happened late last night when many residents may have been inside their homes but if anyone saw what happened or were driving through the area just before the incident occurred then please get in touch.

"Similarly, if you live in the area and have doorbell footage of the incident, please contact us. You may have information or footage that could be vital to our investigation.”

Today (September 5), the area remained cordoned off as Merseyside Police's serious collision investigation unit attended the scene. A white Vauxhall Astra car could be seen on the green in the middle of the east and westbound carriageways of High Street while the garden wall appears completely destroyed.

View 3 Images A huge cordon has remained in place today (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Further debris, including what appeared to be a car engine, was scattered across the road.

One Woolton Village resident, who witnessed the incident, said it was the second time a car had crashed into the wall at the Allerton Road junction in less than one year.

He told the ECHO: "The car was a Nissan Juke, just crushed. It came up the road, clipped another car, and it just rolled and hit the wall. The wall was damaged anyway at this end. But this just took it down a bit more."

One woman, who lives on Allerton Road, said she was alerted at around 11pm last night to police vehicles and fire engines on the street, and a helicopter hovering overhead.

Multiple residents said they had been unable to leave the area today due to their cars being contained within the widespread cordon, which spanned the whole High Street from Speke Road to Allerton Road, and Allerton Road itself.

The westbound carriageway of High Street was reopened at around 9.40am. The eastbound carriageway remained closed until 10.30am as the white car was removed by Recovery North West roadside assistance.

Article continues below

The debris was cleared and the damaged wall fenced off by Highways Maintenance.

Anyone who witnessed the crash at the junction of Allerton Road and High Street last night, who has any information, CCTV or dashcam, is asked to contact @MerPolCC, 101 or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111 with the reference 26000727021.

News.title: Ukraine 'ready' for limited ceasefire as Moscow and US officials begin negotiations
News.content:
Ukraine 'ready' for limited ceasefire as Moscow and US officials begin negotiations

The Ukrainian president said he had spoken with Donald Trump's team and that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were preparing for diplomatic engagements with Ukrainian officials.

View 4 Images (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

Ukraine is ready to observe a limited ceasefire in airstrikes on Kyiv and Moscow as US officials begin negotiations with Russia over a potential end to the war, has said.

‌



The Ukrainian president said he had spoken with Donald Trump's team and that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were preparing for diplomatic engagements with Ukrainian officials.

‌



Zelenskyy said the discussions marked the point at which Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Moscow while negotiations were under way, with Kyiv expecting Russia to take the same approach.

‌



"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv," he said.

View 4 Images (Image: AP Photo/Francisco Seco)

Earlier on Saturday, Russian state officials confirmed that Vladimir Putin had ordered a 72-hour pause in attacks on Kyiv.

‌



Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Russian forces would stop strikes on the Ukrainian capital for three days from midnight on Saturday.

"Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today (Saturday)," Peskov said.

He said the decision was linked to preparations for the arrival of US envoys Witkoff and Kushner, who are due to hold talks with Ukrainian officials as Washington continues efforts to broker a peace deal.

‌



The pair landed in Moscow on Saturday ahead of the weekend's diplomatic discussions. Trump told reporters on Friday that the envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war".

Their visit comes after months of stalled attempts by the US and its allies to bring an end to the conflict, which has now entered its fifth year.

The US delegation was met at the airport by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, according to Tass. Dmitriev shared photographs of himself meeting the officials as they arrived, alongside the caption: "Welcome to Moscow Peacemakers."

‌



View 4 Images (Image: SERGEY BOBYLEV/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Witkoff and Kushner last visited Moscow in January, when they met Putin at the Kremlin. They have not previously visited Kyiv, but Zelenskyy said he was expecting them in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

He said plans for diplomatic engagements with US officials in Kyiv had been approved.

‌



"We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," Zelenskyy said.

The proposed pause comes amid an escalation in aerial attacks by both sides.

Russia has intensified its bombardment of Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, with attacks increasingly stretching into daylight hours. The strikes have put further pressure on Ukraine's air defence capabilities.

‌



View 4 Images (Image: X / @kadmitriev/AFP via Getty Images)

On Friday, a Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service, known as the SBU, in Kyiv.

The agency is among those involved in carrying out long-range operations inside Russia.

Article continues below

Ukraine has also stepped up long-range attacks on Russian territory, targeting military facilities, oil refineries and other infrastructure in an effort to disrupt Moscow's war effort and put pressure on the Russian economy.

The latest diplomatic push comes as Washington's efforts to secure a wider peace agreement have lost momentum, with US attention also focused in recent months on its conflict with Iran.

The 72-hour pause ordered by Putin, alongside Ukraine's offer to refrain from strikes on Moscow, could provide a limited window for the US-backed talks to take place without further escalation from either side.

News.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked 'stop the boats' protesters block roads
News.content:
There has been major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting "stop the boats".

Traffic was stopped from going in and out of the port, with the government saying it condemned "the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused".

Kent Police, which made no arrests, described it as a "spontaneous" protest, while Mike Tapp MP said questions need to be asked around why it appeared the police "didn't know about it".

Officers moved the crowd from the port to Dover Priory railway station at about 11:30 BST and said "all involved had dispersed by 12:00".

Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told it was a "stop the boats protest".

Kent Police has not yet commented on who was behind the demo.

Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.

Thomas is believed to be the founder of the Patriot Platform network.

Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claims that Patriot Platform arranged the protest, saying the group began meeting in July and has brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.

Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Chris Mason: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
News.content:
Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year â not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.

But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.

In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.

Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.

Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.

Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.

Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.

And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.

Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.

But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."

There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.

Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.

Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.

Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.

Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.

Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.

Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.

Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.

The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms planned job cuts
News.content:
Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The firm said it needed to save about Â£1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".

It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first."

Unite general secretary. Sharon Graham. said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week.

"This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."

News.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
News.content:
Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.

With two energy companies â the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK â due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.

On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.

In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally.

The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.

Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.

Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

News.title: King and Queen join Highland games fans at Braemar Gathering
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla have joined cheering crowds watching Highland games events at the annual Braemar Gathering in Royal Deeside.

The event, which draws spectators from around the world, is held on the first Saturday of September every year and coincides with the monarch's annual summer holiday at nearby Balmoral.

Among the events watched by the spectators were tug-of-war, caber tossing, hammer throwing, Highland dancing and a parade of pipe bands.

This is the third Games that the King has attended since his coronation.

News.title: Counterfeit weight-loss jabs are booming - and doctors are worried
News.content:
Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.

But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.

The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.

But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.

Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.

Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street.

"The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe.

"It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."

One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.

Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.

The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy.

Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.

And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.

News.title: Why the USS Lincoln turned up in Thailand looking so rusty
News.content:
When the USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand this week some people were quick to criticise the condition it was in.

The US aircraft carrier has been at sea for about nine months where it's been supporting the US-Israel war with Iran.

BBC Verify has spoken to military experts who say, although the length of its deployment is unusual, the wear and tear isn't. Jake Horton reports.

News.title: New police team to crack down on illegal number plates across England
News.content:
A centralised crackdown on illegal number plates will target organised crime groups and drivers who dodge fines by bringing together data and information from police forces across England, the government has said.

The newly-created National Roads Policing Coordination Centre (NRPCC) will see improved collaboration across forces as well as new technology, such as specialist goggles that can detect number plates that have been made unreadable to cameras.

Illegal number plates are often used by organised crime groups to move stolen goods and to evade speeding, parking and clean air zone penalties, the Department for Transport (DfT) said.

Drivers with incorrectly displayed or missing number plates can be fined up to Â£1,000.

Illegal number plates can come in many forms including cloned plates - which copy the registration of a legitimate vehicle - and ghost plates - where a transparent film is used to make them undetectable to cameras.

Vehicles that hide from number plate recognition cameras are harder for police to track down when they are stolen or linked to crimes.

Policing and crime minister Sarah Jones said: "Illegal number plates are not a victimless offence.

"They are used by criminals to avoid detection, move illegal goods and stay one step ahead of law enforcement."

She said by bringing forces together and making better use of technology the new team would track down offenders faster and disrupt gangs.

Ch Supt Marc Clothier, deputy national co-ordinator for the NRPCC, said: "The police forces involved in our ghost plates operation have shown how effective a targeted and intelligence-led approach is in tackling offenders as well as educating and supporting drivers in ensuring their number plates are compliant."

News.title: Lauryn Hill, Wyclef and Giggs among surprise guests at Jay-Z's long-awaited UK show
News.content:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife BeyoncÃ© had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

News.title: Police probe after child dies in woodland
News.content:
A police investigation has been launched following the unexplained death of a child in woodland.

Emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest on land near Strawberry Lane, Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at about 08:45 BST on Saturday.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

The force, which has not confirmed the age of the child or any other details, is currently treating the death as unexplained.

Roads in the area were closed throughout the day while investigations took place and officers were expected to remain at the scene throughout the evening.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
News.content:
Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000, if it wins the next general election.

Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".

It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.

Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended.

In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled Â£500,000.

Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.

Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity, and responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".

Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.

News.title: Tonnes of rubble including 'bits of old toilets' being dumped in village, residents claim
News.content:
Wrexham Council has also issued a temporary stop notice after a "significant amount" of material was deposited "without planning permission".

The council said it would also be serving enforcement and stop notices "to remedy the situation and have the land restored".

Tom Lawson, from Coedpoeth, said he was frustrated that the activity was not stopped by NRW when it was first spotted.

He estimated there were thousands of tonnes of material, which he said looked like "low-grade demolition waste", saying that he had seen tar and lead batteries in amongst the rubble.

He said he also feared the people responsible would "just walk away from it".

"It'll be left for the public to pay... it's just wrong," he said.

Wrexham-based company SOS Aggregates said it owned the land in Coedpoeth and had been depositing "grade 1A fill material" on the site to make a plateau on which to create the equine arena which would then be "landscaped".

A spokesman for the firm denied it had continued depositing on the site when the temporary stop order was in place, but said it had continued work once the order expired.

He said that they had told the council they would be submitting a planning application this week and that they were also seeking legal advice.

He said the company would also be providing evidence to NRW of the materials being used on the site.

The investigations in Coedpoeth come as another field on the edge of the nearby village of Minera has seen dozens of lorries depositing materials, which one local councillor described as "reeking of diesel".

Caravans have also been placed on the site opposite a cul-de-sac of bungalows on Nantlais.

The farmland was sold approximately two months ago, but according to the council no planning application has been submitted for development there.

SOS Aggregates said it had delivered recycled construction material to the site in Minera, but that it was not involved in work taking place there and did not own the land.

Wrexham Council has served a temporary stop notice due to "a breach of planning control and the change of use of the land to a gypsy and traveller site with associated engineering operations".

NRW said it was investigating the materials on the site and would take action if appropriate.

News.title: Natalie Portman gives birth to third child, her first with boyfriend Tanguy Destable
News.content:

Natalie Portman has welcomed her third child, her first with her boyfriend, the French musician Tanguy Destable, according to multiple outlets.

The Black Swan actor, 45, gave birth to the child in Paris last month, according to People.

In photos published by Page Six, Portman was seen beaming while on a stroll in Paris, with Destable holding the baby in a carrier on his chest. The Independent has contacted Portman’s representatives for comment.

Portman has two older children, son Aleph, 15, and daughter Amalia, nine, with her ex-husband, the choreographer and director Benjamin Millepied.

The actor revealed her pregnancy in April during an interview with Harper’s Bazaar, calling it a “privilege and a miracle.”

Portman’s father is a fertility specialist, so she said she grew up “hearing about how hard it is to get pregnant,” adding that she’s had “so many people I love who’ve had such a hard time with it that I want to be respectful around that as well.”

open image in gallery Natalie Portman has welcomed her third child, her first with her boyfriend, the French musician Tanguy Destable, according to multiple outlets ( AFP/Getty )

She added that while fertility journeys are “such a beautiful, joyous thing,” they’re also “not an easy thing.”

“Tanguy and I are very excited,” she told the publication.

“And there’s a calm and knowing myself: who I want to spend time with, what kind of energy I want around me that makes the experience so beautiful every day. And knowing it’s probably the last time, I cherish every moment,” she added.

Portman, who lives in Paris, said she was spending the early stages of her pregnancy swimming and doing gyrotonics to keep strong and spending lots of time with her kids.

“I try and do some kind of physical activity every day,” Portman recently Elle. “I either swim or walk, and do gyrotonics. I’m still vegan. I take lots of vitamins. I try and sleep as much as possible.”

“There’s been beautiful spring weather,” she said, adding, “so it’s been pretty amazing to just walk in the incredible parks here and go see art. Just the usual things you do when you’re not working!”

She added: “In France, they consider full-term to be 41 weeks rather than 40, so I guess I get an extra week to be pregnant this time around.”

In July, Portman shared an Instagram post of her cradling her bump on a Paris balcony, writing in the caption: “Counting the days until we meet you.”

open image in gallery Natalie Portman and her ex-husband Benjamin Millepied were together for 11 years before their 2023 split ( AFP/Getty )

Portman has kept her relationship with Destable out of the spotlight since they were first linked in March 2025.

Destable, a music producer who goes by the moniker Tepr, was previously married to French actor Louise Bourgoin, who has appeared in the 2010 adventure movie The Extraordinary Adventures of Adèle Blanc-Sec and the medical drama Interns. They have two sons.

Portman moved to Paris in 2014 with her ex-husband and has resided there since she split from Millepied and filed for divorce in July 2023.

News.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili LIVE: Croke Park fight start time, undercard, updates and results tonight
News.content:
Barry Keoghan stars in Katie Taylor video before boxing icon retires

Katie Taylor will bring down the curtain on her staggering boxing career tonight, as she fights one last time.

The Irish icon – an Olympic gold medalist and two-weight undisputed champion – will finally realise her dream of boxing at Dublin’s iconic Croke Park, as she faces the unbeaten Flora Pili.

Yet tonight’s main event is less about the result, which will crown an undisputed super-lightweight queen, and more about celebrating Taylor.

The 40-year-old is widely seen as the greatest women’s boxer in history, having played a pivotal role in bringing the sport to the Olympics, after getting her own start by pretending to be a boy.

Whatever happens tonight, Taylor’s legacy is secure, but this evening’s action will be must-watch regardless. Follow live updates and results from Taylor vs Pili and the undercard, below.

When Killing Eve ended, many fans expressed their frustration with how the series concluded – and Jodie Comer has now reflected on this, revealing that she instead “reverts to the memory” of making the show.

The US drama, in which British actor Comer played Russian assassin Villanelle, received huge acclaim for its debut season. But the final episode received a backlash from dedicated fans, with some calling it “the worst finale since Game of Thrones”.

Much of the anger surrounded the fact that Villanelle was killed off in the closing moments, despite a happy romantic ending being teased for her and Sandra Oh’s character, Eve Polastri, throughout the final season.

open image in gallery Jodie Comer in 'Killing Eve' ( BBC America Original )

Comer acknowledged the fan outcry in The Independent series Life in Pictures, stating: “I think as an actor you just have to have your blinkers on in a sense. Of course, you want people to be fulfilled or happy – they’ve spent such a long time with your story and your character, you know?

“You want them to feel satisfied in some way, but it’s always ultimately out of your control, so it’s tricky really.”

However, Comer, who won an Emmy for the series, said that she chooses to look back at her time making the show when thinking about its legacy.

“I always revert back to the memory of being on the set and working with the crew, and people worked so tirelessly to honour that moment,” she commented.

When the series finale aired in 2022, writer Laura Neal said killing off Villanelle had been “really difficult to find the best ending”, and claimed the show’s team “talked about it loads”.

open image in gallery Jodie Comer reflects on career in new 'Independent' interview 'Life in Pictures' ( The Independent )

Comer herself told Elle at the time “It would have been easy for it to feel very maudlin, I think, or to go completely the other direction and make it feel too funny. So striking the right balance between the two of them felt really important.”

Comer said her character’s death was “inevitable”, adding: “She’s like a cat with nine lives. What I loved about the moment [she gets shot] was that was a really selfless act that she did that caused it.

“It felt right that in that moment she protected Eve. There was something about that shielding, I think, that signified how much she had changed.

“She was trying so desperately to change at the beginning and I don’t think she ever realised how much she had, which is so sad. That moment really shows how Eve changed her life.”

open image in gallery 'Killing Eve' fans were hoping the lead characters would have a happy ending ( BBC )

The following year, Comer told interviewer Josh Horowitz that she anticipated “a mixed reaction” and admitted that she doesn’t like to think of Villanelle “floating around the River Thames”, joking: “Perhaps she crawled out.”

Watch The Independent’s full interview with Comer here. The actor can currently be seen in Hugh Jackman film The Death of Robin Hood, which is in cinemas now.

News.title: Anger over immigration cannot justify intimidation
News.content:

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Let us be clear that The Independent is in favour of a sustainable level of immigration. It adds to the prosperity, dynamism and cultural richness of the nation. Furthermore, we believe that the United Kingdom should offer sanctuary to those fleeing persecution, so we should welcome our fair share of refugees.

Because we are not in favour of open borders, we support fair rules to determine who is and who is not allowed to enter the country, whether temporarily or to settle here.

The arrival of uninvited migrants by dinghy across the Channel offends against that principle, and we share the dismay of those who expect the government to end the dangerous traffic. At the same time, we want to open up safe and legal routes for genuine refugees, including the remaining Afghans who worked with our armed forces and who are at risk of Taliban retribution, who are still stranded in Afghanistan or neighbouring countries.

Demanding that the government “stop the boats”, therefore, is legitimate. Even if we disagreed, people would be entitled to demonstrate in support of that demand. What is not acceptable, however, is the gathering of large numbers of masked men on the streets of Dover. That they were briefly obstructing access to the port is also unacceptable.

The protesters, who chanted “England ’til I die”, “Whose streets? Our streets!” and “Stop the boats”, were wearing black, which was plainly intended to make them look like a paramilitary force. Their protest was intimidatory, ugly and un-British. It was no surprise that it was supported by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, otherwise known as Tommy Robinson, who wrote on social media: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover, patriots have mobilised to close down the port.”

There is nothing patriotic about intimidation and obstruction. The police had the power to require the protesters to remove their face-coverings, but chose not to exercise it. No arrests were made and the mob had dispersed by midday, according to Kent force.

We cannot gainsay the operational decisions made by police officers in Dover, and should be relieved that the protest passed off without violence, but it should be made clear that any attempt to repeat such threatening behaviour will not be tolerated.

Fortunately, there seems to be a broad consensus against the protest. Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, described it as “disgusting” and said: “Nobody in any political protest, whether they're on the left or the right, should appear in balaclavas. It is wrong.”

The Independent holds no torch for Mr Farage. He has stoked xenophobia and anti-immigrant feeling. His policies – including those intended to stop the boats – are mostly simplistic and unworkable. His admiration for Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and crypto billionaires shows how out of touch he is with the British people. His party appears to have attempted to solicit illegal foreign donations and the extent of his knowledge of the attempt is unclear – today he said “I frankly wasn’t even listening” when his aides were discussing it. Reform denies any wrongdoing.

However, even Mr Farage has drawn the line at working with Mr Yaxley-Lennon, and he has condemned the balaclava-wearing protesters unequivocally.

Let the protesters march, if they show their faces and dress in civilian clothes. Let the government tackle the legitimate concerns of the majority of the British people. But let us have no thuggish paramilitaries on our streets. Whose streets? Our streets, indeed.

News.title: Kennedy Center renews call for Trump-backed shutdown after part of a ceiling collapses
News.content:
