World.title: Whatever happened to the floating schools of Bangladesh?
World.content:
Whatever happened to the floating schools of Bangladesh?

toggle caption Ali Asif Shawon for NPR

In September 2018, we posted a story from flood-prone Bangladesh, 'Floating Schools' Make Sure Kids Get To Class When The Water Rises . Did the floating schools actually work, and what happened to the children who attended them? This story is part of our annual series, Whatever happened to …

About This Series We're revisiting some of our past global health and development stories to see "Whatever happened to ..."

Eight years ago, NPR correspondent Jason Beaubien visited a riverside village in the northwest of Bangladesh and found a small beige boat tied up in tall grass beside the Atrai River.

Sponsor Message

The boat was packed with narrow benches, which in turn were jammed with children. About 29 third-grade students sat shoulder to shoulder in front of a blackboard on this very first floating school of Bangladesh, which started its journey 24 years ago.

The floating schools were a response to a longstanding local problem of seasonal floods and impassable, muddy roads that kept children from reaching conventional schools. Now, as we come back in 2026, climate-related disruptions are affecting schooling on a much larger scale, and that practical local solution has become more necessary and more relevant beyond Bangladesh.

toggle caption Ali Asif Shawon for NPR



The schools were designed for one flood-prone region, but they now offer a model for how communities can preserve essential services as the environment changes. International recognition highlights the project's growing relevance.

Poetry on board

On a visit to one of the boat schools this summer, 27 students sat on benches and recited Bangla poetry with their teacher.

"This school picks me up from my house in the morning and, after class, drops me off beside my house," says Mahiya Khatun, a 12-year-old fourth grader. "Other schools are not too close; it is tough to reach there during the rainy season because of floods and mud. The teacher teaches us with care in this school, and I love to learn the rhymes."

Sponsor Message

Then she recites a Bangla rhyme written by the famous poet and author Farrukh Ahmad.

Another fourth grader, Himel Hasan, says he doesn't like the government-run primary school because it is too far from his house, so he loves coming to the boat school.

"I have five friends here in this class, and we enjoyed learning together," says Himel.

Mosammat Hosne Ara Khatun has been teaching in the boat school for the last 10 years.

"My house is near this school. Like me, most of the students are from nearby villages.. I enjoyed this job because the workplace is easy to commute to, and I think I am doing a noble job teaching underprivileged students," says Hosne Ara.

Suman Mia, who drives the boat, says "I didn't get the chance to study in my childhood, and now I am earning my livelihood by operating this engine boat. I dream that someday my son and daughter will be educated in those boat schools, and they will do a good job after growing up."

Student success stories

Rabbi Hossain started his schooling at the floating school, studying there from 2005 to 2010.

After completing grade five, Rabbi later went to a local high school and college. He now studies engineering at Dhaka University of Engineering & Technology, located in Gazipur.

"My life started from the boat school. I want to be an engineer after completing my studies," says Rabbi, whose father is a farmer and mother is a school teacher.

He credits the boat school for an important step in his schooling: "Just imagine, in 2005 we got the opportunity to learn computers."

Rabbi has many schoolmates who are in established positions after starting their education at the boat school.

Nahid Hossain, a classmate, received his education at the same floating school and is now a soldier in the Bangladesh Army.

Sponsor Message

For him, the boat school was more than just an educational institution.

"Boat school was an emotional place for me. I learned my basic education from that floating school," says Nahid. Without the floating school, he says, he would never have moved ahead in life.

To collect students, the boat school goes from one ghat — one docking place — to another, enabling children in difficult-to-reach areas to attend classes.

Even when there are storms and heavy rain, he says, classes generally went on.

"Flooding was a serious issue for conventional schools in that area because roads and communication lines would become unusable and muddy, school grounds might be flooded, and students' education would be disrupted. In contrast, the floating school could keep going and reach the children where they were," says Nahid.

Another successful student is Surovi Khatun, an undergrad student currently studying at Nawab Siraj-Ud-Dowla Government College of Natore, a neighboring district of Pabna.

Surovi was raised in a small village named Bolighati in Singra Upazila, Natore, and started her first schooling at a floating school.

She studied at the boat school at the primary level from 2012 to 2016; later, she was admitted to a local high school and college, and is now working toward a degree in English.

"The foundation that I achieved from the boat school advanced me in the English language, as teachers were so caring about teaching a second language in our early schooling days," she says.

She wishes the floating schools would go beyond grade 5.

"The education was free at boat schools. In addition, they provided us with textbooks, notebooks and even a pen. But after completing primary level, it required coaching tuition fees, school fees and educational material fees at the higher secondary level, which parents often cannot bear, and they sent their female children to marry at an early age."

Sponsor Message

Apart from formal education, the boat schools also taught tailoring skills to Surovi and her mother, and now the mother and daughter can make their own clothes and sometimes make clothes for neighbors to earn extra income.

Plans for the future

The floating boat school initiatives are run by Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha , a local nonprofit group.

The initiative received the UNESCO Confucius Literacy Prize 2025, in recognition of its efforts to deliver education to children in the flood-prone Chalan Beel wetlands.

"Bangladesh has had a remarkable journey from the lowest literacy rate globally in 1971 at only 17.6% to around 76% in 2026. The work of groups like Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha have made this possible," says Susan Vize, UNESCO representative to Bangladesh. "Their outreach to women and rural communities, the remaining pockets where literacy is lowest, is striving to ensure this journey continues."

Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha hopes to reach additional parts of the country with floating schools.

The founder of the group, Mohammed Rezwan, is designing a larger boat that could serve as a floating community hub, hosting classes as well as health care and other services and also serving as a shelter for up to 150 people during flood seasons.

He also hopes to build a global network of people working with this floating school model. Other flood-prone countries, including Cambodia, Vietnam, India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Brazil, have started similar floating school programs.

Ali Asif Shawon is the chief reporter at Dhaka Tribune in Bangladesh, where he covers politics, security, climate change, migration and global health. He can be reached on LinkedIn.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: U.S. envoys in Moscow in new push for peace between Russia and Ukraine
World.content:
U.S. envoys in Moscow in new push for peace between Russia and Ukraine

toggle caption Francisco Seco/AP

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday to try to revive a stalled push to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian state news outlets reported.

The visit came as both sides escalated their aerial attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the envoys' trip and urged Moscow to do the same. Moscow did not publicly respond to the proposal.

Washington's push to end the fighting, now in its fifth year, has lost momentum as U.S. attention has been focused for the last six months on its war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

The envoys were met at the airport by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Russia's state news agency Tass said.

The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin. They have never visited Kyiv, but Zelenskyy said he was expecting them in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

With peace efforts stalled, Russia intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with relentless bombardments recently stretching into daylight hours, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of air defensive systems.

On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv — the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service, known as the SBU, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.

The long-range strikes by Ukraine have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs, seeking to undermine the Kremlin's war effort and economy, as well as make ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.

Zelenskyy links Russian strikes to envoys' visit

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

Sponsor Message

In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy said that Russia had carried out overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports, and linked the attack to the planned U.S. visit.

"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," he said.

"We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side."

Strikes kill 5 at Ukrainian industrial site

Russian attacks killed five people and wounded five more at an industrial facility in Ukraine's southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. He described those killed as employees at the site. "A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives," he said.

A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region's Nikopol district, Hanzha said.

In a statement Saturday, Russia's Ministry of Defense said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as "major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine's military production."

A further two people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on Ukraine's Kyiv region, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. In the Boryspil district, a fire sparked by a strike partially destroyed a nine-story residential building.

Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping center in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine's state emergency services said. A 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were hurt.

Sponsor Message

Emergency crews responding to the incident were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency services said.

Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine's air force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft — around half of them jet-powered — as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the air force.

Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks wounded three people, including a 14-year-old girl, in Russia's border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

In a statement, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

World.title: Voters are fed up with data centers. Both parties are trying to cash in for midterms
World.content:
Voters are fed up with data centers. Both parties are trying to cash in for midterms

toggle caption Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images

In campaign ads airing everywhere from Georgia to Iowa, Republicans and Democrats are confronting the same enemy: data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom.

An NPR analysis of political advertising data from the firm AdImpact found that since January, campaigns and outside groups have spent more than $45 million on ads mentioning data centers in this year's gubernatorial, House and Senate races.

The two major parties driving that spending are largely making the same argument: the sprawling facilities get too many tax breaks, drive up electricity bills and need reining in.

From January to August, spending was nearly identical: over $22 million supported Republican candidates and more than $21 million for Democratic candidates, with independents driving the rest. Still, Democrats ran almost twice as many ads as Republicans — 127 compared to 67 — and spread their messaging across more states and races. The ads are clustered in states with competitive races, like Wisconsin and Michigan.

Sponsor Message

Mentions of data centers have grown from just a handful in ads from January, to 62 in June, more than 110 in July and about 164 in August, as the election draws nearer and the issue continues to heat up.

A June Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 77% of Americans are concerned about data centers raising electricity costs and two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans said they'd oppose a data center in their community.

This bipartisan anxiety helps explain why candidates in both parties are talking about the issue. Michael Franz, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising, said data centers give each side the talking points it wants.

Apart from a chance to talk about affordability, "Democrats can latch on to environmental concerns," Franz said, adding that for Republicans, criticizing data centers is a way "to go in opposition to big corporations, in opposition to a system that doesn't care about you."

Data centers are a unique issue where "MAGA Republicans and liberal Democrats" land in the same place, he said.

The convergence around affordability

Ads from both parties are tying data centers to rising energy costs.

A Believe in Wisconsin PAC ad for Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley, which the group spent $634,795 to air in August, promises that Crowley "will lower costs, make housing affordable, stop AI data centers from making your energy bills skyrocket."

Sponsor Message

Byron Donalds, Florida's Republican gubernatorial nominee, casts himself as a check on data centers, by vowing to "protect Florida families and communities from data centers that jack up utility rates and make everything else more expensive," and "fight for a ratepayer protection plan." The Friends of Byron Donalds PAC paid over $2.5 million to air the ad.

Similar ads have run in support of Democrat Rob Sand in Iowa and Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas.

A Republican Party operative spoke to NPR about this on condition of anonymity, and said the party is not commenting publicly on data centers because the views within the party vary. They said "The most popular answer that we've seen is: We could potentially have data centers as long as they pay for their own energy," adding that data centers are necessary to win the race against China "and increase jobs in local communities."

Similarly, Olivia Davis, a spokeswoman for the Democratic Governors Association said data centers are creating deep concerns around affordability and utility costs.

"That's why it's being included in paid media," she said.

Georgia and Ohio: where data centers take center stage

According to data from AdImpact, more than half of the GOP's spending on ads mentioning data centers has been in Georgia and the state has captured about 30% of total spending on data center ads.

Georgia's contest for governor is the race that has spent the most on ads mentioning data centers — $12.8 million across nine ads.

Six ads discouraged voters from backing Republican Lt. Gov. Burt Jones who lost the June runoff to healthcare billionaire Rick Jackson. The ads, some of which were run by Georgians for Integrity, a group that has dropped millions attacking Jones since 2025, used data centers as a bogeyman for Jones' alleged corruption.

In Ohio's U.S. Senate race, supporters of Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown have spent millions to describe his opponent, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, as the "the face of data centers," and accuse him of "giving corporations over $2.5 billion in out of control tax breaks and causing electric bills to spike by thousands of dollars."

Sponsor Message

Republicans are aware of the shifting tide. In an internal memo obtained by NPR and first reported by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee singled out the Ohio race, called data centers a "sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," and warned the tech industry that a Husted loss would make politicians nationwide wary of them.

Husted isn't airing ads on the topic. He championed data centers as Ohio's lieutenant governor but has since introduced congressional legislation to protect ratepayers from the higher electric rates that data centers can cause.

In an interview with Spectrum News, Husted addressed a seeming shift in his position.

"It's not really a shift. I was always trying to hold these companies accountable by making them pay local property taxes," he said, also highlighting his push to require the companies to hire locally. "So this is very consistent for me, holding them accountable."

A local issue with national attention

The Ohio contest is a rare Senate race with heavy spending on ads mentioning data centers.

According to AdImpact data, gubernatorial races spent the most on such ads, about $32 million, with House races in second place, spending $8 million and Senate races coming in third at roughly $5.3 million.

"The federal government doesn't really play a role in permitting the construction of new data centers," said Darrell M. West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation and co-editor in chief of TechTank. "Governors are under a lot of pressure to slow the construction of new data centers just based on public opposition to them."

The issue, however, has spilled beyond gubernatorial races. In some of the country's marquee Senate contests, candidates such as Texas's Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico have said that Washington should step in.

The Republican turn against data centers is more striking because experts say that the party has positioned itself as pro-business. West said Republican incumbents and nominees "want to slow down the movement towards data centers because they can see so many of their own voters are opposed."

Sponsor Message

That leaves the party at odds with President Trump who has urged states to keep building data centers while admitting that they could "use a little public relations help."

"Trump seems oblivious to public opinion on a number of fronts," said West. "Typically, when the public shifts, politicians shift with them. Trump is not doing that on data centers."

World.title: Flock cameras draw opposition from across the political spectrum
World.content:
Flock cameras draw opposition from across the political spectrum

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

There are plenty of issues Republicans and Democrats disagree on, but increasingly, they're aligned on this: they want Flock surveillance cameras gone.

The widespread backlash against AI-powered license plate readers, which allow police to track people over time, is becoming more of a political issue as the midterm elections approach in races from Florida to Ohio and Wisconsin .

At a press conference late last month, Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro said he believes law enforcement needs public safety tools, but Flock cameras are not among them.

"I would welcome bipartisan legislation to ban these across the state," Shapiro said. "This is not something in the public interest."

Sponsor Message

Earlier this week, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis announced plans to revoke permits for license plate readers on state highways.

"I'm all about having law enforcement have tools," DeSantis said. "But I don't want to have this become a surveillance state."

Every month, Flock cameras capture billions of license plates, along with other vehicle data. Police say this tool helps them find stolen vehicles and missing people. But the technology has been abused. Officers have used it to stalk ex-partners , for instance.

Flock recently changed some of its features to prevent abuse.

But the concerns are proving sticky, and largely bipartisan. Last week, Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott froze state spending for the cameras. And Senate Republicans are investigating concerns over police misuse.

Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the ACLU, says a wide swath of people across the political spectrum opposes Flock cameras. Americans have a strong distaste for government surveillance, Stanley said.

"Now you have to live your life with what sociologists call the third eye that is watching you," he said, "and I think a lot of Americans don't want to live that way."

The reasons people on the left and right oppose Flock are different.

Sponsor Message

Progressives have pointed out that the technology has been used to track immigrants and people seeking abortions .

Conservatives have warned that the cameras could be used to create a national gun registry .

Others, such as conservative commentator Glenn Beck, say it's a form of government overreach .

"You cannot allow this to happen. We are creating a panopticon," he said, referring to a circular prison design that allows a single guard to see all the inmates at once.

World.title: Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest
World.content:
Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posts bail after arrest

toggle caption Aaron Favila/AP

MANILA, Philippines — Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail Saturday after an order was issued for her arrest the previous day on charges that she publicly threatened to arrange the assassination of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and two other people.

Emerging in a black outfit from Quezon City Regional Trial Court in Metro Manila, Duterte consoled her supporters, hugging a woman who was sobbing as supporters chanted "Duterte! Duterte!"

The vice president, who has denied the allegations, showed a court order lifting the arrest warrant issued by the court Friday and said her lawyers instructed her to keep a copy on hand. She urged journalists to surround her on the way to her car because she did not feel safe.

Sponsor Message

"If possible please go with me, because I do not feel safe with all these police personnel who are harassing those at my home, harassing me since 2023," Duterte said. "What does this administration really want to do with me?"

Paul Lawrence Lim, one of her attorneys, said court staff took Duterte's fingerprints and she posted 360,000 pesos bail ($5,740) for three counts of grave threats.

After the arrest order was issued Friday, he said Duterte would fight the charges.

"She has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies," he said in a statement.

Case based on comments during online news conference

The case is seen as part of a high-stakes political showdown pitting Duterte against Marcos. A conviction may permanently disqualify her from holding public office and prohibit her from seeking the presidency in 2028, when Marcos's six-year term ends.

The charges stem from an alleged threat Duterte, 48, made during a 2024 online news conference. She said she would have Marcos, his wife and then-House of Representatives Speaker Martin Romualdez killed by an assassin if she herself was killed as their political disputes escalated.

The vice president warned during the event that her threat was not a joke.

Sponsor Message

Duterte later said she was expressing concern for her own safety and not threatening Marcos as the remarks set off a criminal investigation and national security concerns.

The House of Representatives, which is dominated by Marcos' allies, voted overwhelmingly in May to impeach Duterte over allegations of unexplained wealth, misuse of confidential state funds and the online news conference threats. The Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened her televised trial in July.

Former political partners turned rivals

Marcos and Duterte were running mates in the 2022 elections in an alliance that combined two of the country's most formidable political dynasties.

Marcos is the son of former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., who held the office from the 1960s to the 1980s, including a period of repression and martial law. The vice president is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the predecessor to the current President Marcos.

Rodrigo Duterte was arrested in 2025 on orders of the International Criminal Court and detained in The Hague, where he is scheduled to face a trial beginning in late November over alleged crimes against humanity connected to a brutal anti-drugs crackdowns that left thousands of mostly poor suspects dead. He has denied authorizing extrajudicial killings but repeatedly threatened suspects with death while in office.

Sara Duterte previously criticized the Marcos administration for surrendering her father to a foreign court, which currently has no jurisdiction over the Philippines.

Marcos and Sara Duterte also have contrasting geopolitical leanings.

Marcos has expanded defense engagements with the United States, a treaty ally of the Philippines, as his administration stood up to China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea.

The vice president has come under fire for not condemning China's assaults, including with the use of powerful water cannons, against Filipino forces and fishermen in the disputed waters.

World.title: As Canada-U.S. relations sour, border towns of upstate New York fear damage will be permanent
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At his marina in Sackets Harbor, N.Y., on a cloudy Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Alex Morgia looks toward the water and paints a vivid picture of the beauty he often sees, even on an overcast day.

"Sometimes those are the best sunsets because the sun will peek through underneath and then you get all of the cascading colours on the underside of the clouds," Morgia says, looking out over what has recently become North America's most controversial lake.

"We get sunsets over the lake year-round," Morgia says, before clarifying: "Over Lake Ontario, not to be vague."

Sackets Harbor, located on the lake's eastern shore around a 40-minute drive from the Canadian border, finds itself caught up in a war of words and wares, as the United States and Canada feud over tariffs and U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

The harbour, Morgia points out, was even mentioned in Trump's executive order.

It's not the first time the quaint village has been at the front lines of a fight between these two nations: Sackets Harbor was the site of two major battles during the War of 1812, Morgia says.

"People find cannonballs in their yard all the time," he said. "People use them as doorstops."

Alex Morgia, mayor of Sackets Harbor, N.Y., says there was a brief period when U.S. President Donald Trump was distracted with other issues, and he hoped it would take his attention off Canada so the two countries could be friends again. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

While Morgia downplayed how much support Trump has for renaming the lake, he — along with other U.S. residents and officials living near the border in upstate New York — is concerned this heightened fight could spell the end of close Canadian ties, to the detriment of their communities.

"We had a brief period of time where I thought he was distracted with other problems and was going to leave the Canadians alone and we could be friends again. Obviously, that ship has sailed," Morgia said.

'It hits in the heart'

About a half-hour drive north of Sackets Harbor, on the U.S. side of the Thousand Islands Bridge over the St. Lawrence River, Corey Fram is fretting that the already difficult situation he faces is about to get much worse.

As director of the Thousand Islands Regional Tourism Development Corporation, Fram is responsible for marketing on both sides of the border. But after Trump got elected for a second time, there was a substantial decline in Canadian spending and border crossing, he said.

"It hurts to lose that economic impact of Canadian visitors on the New York side. But in a border community, it hits in the heart," Fram added.

WATCH | Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues: Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues | Duration 1:56 The last long weekend of the summer is here. CBC’s Troy Charles looks at cross-border travel and, perhaps unsurprisingly, Canadians continue to avoid the United States.

While he understands there may be a strategy Washington and Ottawa are each pursuing that buoys their countries' economic standpoints, those efforts have the opposite effect on border communities, he said.

"There's almost a sense that those of us along the border are having to pay the price for what is a supposed economic benefit for the greater good of each of the respective countries," Fram said.

Anthony Adamczyk is facing the same issue in Ogdensburg, N.Y., about 45-minute drive northeast. He's the executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, which owns and manages the local bridge spanning the St. Lawrence.

Despite a slight uptick in border crossings from Canada in January 2025 compared to the previous year, they declined the following month and have never recovered, Adamczyk said.

Anthony Adamczyk, executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, says the volume of traffic from Canada at the border crossing decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

Overall, traffic volume decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024, equating to about 136,000 vehicles. The bridge's toll revenue went down 35 per cent, representing about $536,000 in lost revenue.

Fram's longer-term concern is that the number of Canadian tourists will permanently remain lower. He told CBC's The House that each time a major crisis affects border crossings — like the COVID-19 pandemic or the 9/11 terrorist attacks — the numbers fall and never return.

"My concern is this is yet another step, a big jump down that we're not going to get back to where we were in 2024 anytime soon, and maybe not ever."

Residents divided over Trump's tactics

The ongoing fight over tariffs and Lake Ontario's name puts residents of Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor in a complicated position. The two areas fall within St. Lawrence County and Jefferson County, respectively — both of which Trump has won by more than 10 points in previous presidential elections.

Outside a Walmart in Ogdensburg, Greg Barr told The House he visits Canada all the time and has never had any issues with Canadians. But when asked about the trade war, he said he thinks the U.S. has been "way too generous."

"Not [just] to Canada but to other countries," Barr said. "[Trump's] getting things more even, to me. Maybe he has a different way of doing it, but he does get results."

Jim Rupert, who runs a taxi service that takes clients back and forth from Canada all the time, echoed Barr's view that Trump's tactics are a means of equalizing the playing field.

Taxi operator Jim Rupert says Trump's tariffs are a way of equalizing the economic playing field, and Canada can do more to improve its standing by developing more of its natural resources. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC News)

"I hate to listen to [Trump] half the time because he rambles, he rants, he does this and that, but the policies are solid."

But Carol and Gary Davis, who say they've noticed how much more their groceries cost nowadays, say they can't make sense of Trump's actions.

"When he got elected, gas was going to be cheap, food was going to be cheap," Gary said. "It's just the opposite."

Carol, who voted for Trump in the last election, said she's disappointed with the president — though she felt there weren't better options when she cast her ballot.

"So, yeah, I guess I do have regrets now."

Carol and Gary Davis say Trump promised to make gas and food more affordable — but the opposite has happened. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

Local Republican lawmaker weighs in

Scott Gray, a Republican assemblyman who represents Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor, is aware of residents' concerns. He told The House he's not opposed to tariffs, but doesn't want them to harm either his residents or Canadians.

"We have enjoyed a long-time exchange in our economy and our trade, and I think we should try to maintain that," Gray said.

He said he hopes some key irritants, like U.S. access to the Canadian dairy market, can be corrected through trade negotiations. But tariffs, he added, can be disruptive — as are counter-tariffs.

Gray pushed back on behaviour from the White House, including Trump repeatedly calling Canada the 51st state and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth belittling two female Canadian cadets.

WATCH | Democratic senator calls Hegseth's comments 'deeply disrespectful': Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator | Duration 1:37 Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego says recent comments regarding Canada's military by U.S. cabinet secretaries are 'deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with [the U.S.].'

But he also placed some blame at Canada's feet, like when Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump could "kiss my ass" in response to tariff threats.

"We need to make sure there's a fair trade deal, and we need to do it without creating animosity and friction, which is largely caused by whatever antics that you want to describe out there," Gray said.

Back at the marina in Sackets Harbor, Morgia questions whether the U.S. government will stop antagonizing its northern neighbour. He's sympathetic to Canadians' calls for Americans to step up and pressure their leaders to back off on punishing their country.

"I guess not until [midterm elections in] November. People are trying, but right now the Republicans control most of the government. And until that changes, I don't think he's going to be held to account."

World.title: Alberta independence group releases its ‘transition plan’ to become a country
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An independence group has released a “transition plan,” sketching out what it sees as a roadmap should Albertans vote in the future to become a sovereign nation.

The Alberta Transition Council released the 214-page report on Thursday, laying out a series of proposals tied to how life in Alberta might look in the event of a future “yes” vote on independence.

The report also touches on a range of regulations and institutions the group identifies that would need to transition to Alberta’s control through negotiation, including with Ottawa.

Those proposals vary in scope, from the continuity of social programs to air traffic control to the implementation of a new constitution and the relationship with First Nations.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who leads the Alberta Transition Council and is also a leader with the independence group Let Alberta Decide, says the aim is to outline how Alberta’s exit from Canada could run smoothly.

“What we need to remember is we’re not starting from scratch, right? Those people who work at the airports, we’re not going to blow up the airport. It’s still there,” Wilson said. “All we’re doing is changing the payroll.”

But one critic argued any transition planning is far off and the plan is “unrealistic” about what are certain to be complex negotiations.

“Many of those issues would take many, many years, potentially, to be fully discussed and possibly never come to a conclusion,” said Errol Mendes, a professor of constitutional and international law at the University of Ottawa.

Not all in Alberta's control, report says

Albertans go to the polls on Oct. 19 to vote on whether Alberta should stay with Canada, or hold a second, binding referendum to separate.

Polling suggests a minority of Albertans presently support the idea of secession.

The guiding idea, according to the group, is to not approach the transition as the creation of a country “from scratch.”

“Alberta independence would not eliminate Alberta’s relationship with the rest of Canada,” the report reads. “It would change the legal and governmental framework within which that relationship operates.”

Let Alberta Decide co-leaders Keith Wilson, left, and Tanya Clemens are pictured at the launch of Alberta independence organization Let Alberta Decide in Calgary on June 19. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

At the same time, the report acknowledges not all of this is in Alberta’s control.

Debt, mobility, energy infrastructure, pensions, borders, and assets are among the areas where negotiation would be needed with Canada, First Nations and others.

Outcomes cannot be known or guaranteed, the report states.

The document claims 45 Albertans in fields including banking and currency, law, international trade, First Nations and policing contributed to the preparation and review of the package.

However, the identities of those individuals were not made public.

Wilson said confidentiality was put in place to ensure contributors don’t face “cancel culture" or harassment.

“The report will speak for itself. And Canadians, and many people in the world, are growing leery of the ‘experts say’ stuff anyway,” Wilson told CBC News. “People will be able to evaluate it.

“Each one of us have our own level of life experience that we’ll be able to hone in on — something we’re very familiar with — and say, ‘Hey, do the base facts seem accurate? Does this analysis make sense?’”

The document is one of several released recently that explore the various ways Alberta separating from Canada could impact people’s daily lives.

From currency to mortgages to military

In the introductory section of the paper, a series of questions is posed.

“How will laws continue? How will courts operate? How will salaries and pensions continue to be paid? How will money continue to move through banks? How will airplanes continue to fly?”

The group offers some ideas. For instance, take currency. On day one of independence, the group suggests using the Canadian dollar “because it minimizes contract, pricing and consumer disruption.”

“Other possibilities — including use of the U.S. dollar, dual-currency arrangements or a future Alberta currency — remain longer-term or contingency choices,” the report reads.

U.S. banknotes are shown in a file photo. The Alberta Transition Council suggests using the Canadian dollar as a starting point, but leaves the door open to transition to the U.S. dollar or a future Alberta currency. (Sertac Kayar/Reuters)

In many cases, a full resolution isn’t offered yet. On pensions, the group proposes to keep pension payments going for now, leaving the negotiations over future plans for pensions and asset transfers for later.

What would happen to mortgages in the event of a separation vote has been a big question in the run-up to the referendum. Earlier this year, analysts told CBC News there are a lot of unknowns involved in what is likely to be a complicated process.

The plan proposes offering the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation the opportunity to continue its services in an independent Alberta.

“If they’re not interested in that, Alberta would stand up, in advance of independence … the Alberta housing mortgage corporation,” Wilson said. “And a transition would occur where the Alberta entity would agree to transfer the mortgage guarantees … so that the banks remain whole.”

An aerial photo of Lewis Estates in Edmonton. (David Bajer/CBC)

Earlier this week, in a separate report , the Calgary-based public policy think-tank Canada West Foundation calculated that debt per person in Alberta could rise to between $80,000 and $95,000 post-separation, compared to $27,000 per person in 2024, based on the increased debt share Alberta could assume.

The Alberta Transition Council, while not recommending a final federal debt figure, suggests that Canada shouldn’t propose that Alberta assume a share of the debt based primarily on population.

“Such an approach would ignore Albertans’ historical fiscal contributions, which should be taken into account in any fair calculation methodology,” the report reads.

Similarly, the report doesn’t include a detailed costing of the broader dollars and cents tied to the prospect of independence, promising a companion report on those matters in the coming weeks.

The report also acknowledges First Nations have constitutionally-recognized rights and are treaty partners.

“Nothing automatically happens to reserve land merely because Alberta becomes independent,” the report reads.

Should an independence vote be successful, the report presents four “relationship pathways” for First Nations, including "Option A," which would allow a First Nation to “keep its current relationship with Canada as much as possible.”

The report also suggests the Alberta Sheriffs could be expanded into a full provincial police force to replace the RCMP, and proposes an initial 2,100-member defence force, which would consist of 300 full-time permanent members and a separate, 1,800-member “territorial force.”

'I don't doubt that it's rosy'

In its report earlier this week, the Canada West Foundation stated that negotiations for Alberta to secede from Canada would be complex, with no guaranteed outcome.

Setting up an independent Alberta would cost more than $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion annually, estimated former Treasury Board senior manager Lennie Kaplan.

Canada West Foundation President Gary Mar said he has yet to read the Alberta Transition Council’s full report. However, on both the “leave” and “stay” sides, there’s too much certainty, in his view, with each side seeming to be fully sure of their assumptions.

“We’ve looked into the complications of both sides, staying and leaving, and have come to conclusions,” Mar said. “I think that Mr. Wilson’s work, I don’t doubt that it’s rosy. But that’s what he’s advocating for.”

Canada West Foundation President Gary Mar said people on both the ‘stay’ and ‘leave’ sides of the debate promote a future of fantastic opportunity with too much certainty. (CBC)

Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of the Forever Canadian movement and former deputy premier of Alberta, said he viewed the plan as “ridiculous.”

“He is the guy that thinks that he can divorce and then show up the next day and say, ‘What's for dinner, honey?’” he said. “Well, it doesn't work like that. This is a divorce.”

Wilson said his group’s report was optimistic “in the sense that we assume that the federal government and the provinces and the First Nations would enter into good-faith negotiations.”

“We know each of the services and functions that the federal government provides. We can plan for the transition of them, just as ordinary businesses do when one business acquires another. The customer is not disrupted,” he said.

Over the coming weeks, Albertans can expect even more numbers and predictions about the province’s future.

That includes the University of Calgary's study of the potential costs of Alberta leaving Canada, commissioned by the provincial government.

That report is expected to be released later this month.

World.title: How public institutions — like schools and transit — are handling Quebec's new secularism law
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

From university halls to garages in Montreal's Metro network, public institutions across Quebec are quietly locking prayer rooms and rewriting employee guidelines as the province’s expanded secularism law takes full effect.

Law 9 significantly broadens the reach of Bill 21 and extends restrictions.

The religious symbols ban passed into law in 2019 now applies to daycare staff and prayer spaces are now forbidden in places like university campuses, or the facilities of a transit agency like Montreal's Société de transport de Montréal.

But as institutions rush to comply with the changes, administrators and legal experts warn that the government has left them navigating a complex legal grey zone with few clear guidelines on how to actually enforce the rules.

Law 9 took effect on Sept. 1.

Prayer rooms closed, chapels can stay

Concordia University — which had a large prayer room, according to the Muslim Student Association — says it no longer has any places set aside for prayer.

McGill University says it intends to comply with its legal obligations as well. Dawson College declined to comment.

“All the signs have been taken down,” said Ezekiel Montoya Desjardins, the vice-president of external affairs at the Dawson Student Union, who managed the prayer rooms there.

Signage and some furnishings, like carpeting, have been removed and the rooms are empty now. Montoya Desjardins said he understands the government’s position, but secularism doesn’t need to be defined as no religious activity.

“I think that it means there is neutrality in all religions at school,” he said, noting that the prayer rooms were mostly used by the Muslim community, but were open to everyone.

Law 9, adopted by the Quebec government in the spring, puts limits on praying in public. (Radio-Canada)

As for Vanier College, Benoit Morin, the school’s director general, said the small prayer room has been locked since the start of August. A notice on the door says Muslim students can head across the street to a mosque to pray.

While prayer rooms like that one close, religious practice in chapels, like the one at Université Laval, Concordia, McGill and Bishop’s University, is allowed.

Vanier catching up with the law

Morin said the school is still working on two important steps included in the law. The first is establishing a process whereby religious accommodations can be requested and determined by management, and initiating a complaints process as well.

Before, students would ask professors for religious accommodations. Now that request will go up to Morin's office, for him or someone he delegates to decide.

And when it comes to complaints about someone not operating in line with the multiple existing secularism laws, there needs to be a new, separate registry for Law 9 complaints that can be audited by the ministry, he said.

The school also created new training for security guards to teach them about Law 9 and give warnings to people if they see something that isn't in line with the law, he said.

LISTEN | Exploring some of the effects of Quebec's expanded secularism law: Let's Go 10:08 Secularism law expansion goes into effect for STM, daycare workers New rules are going into effect as of today as part of Law 9, the latest expansion of Quebec's secularism laws. We'll go over what changes concretely for places like schools, daycares, and even the STM. Let's Go researcher Sarah Jesmer breaks it down.

Morin said the new measures are affecting Vanier's ability to teach students the importance of living peacefully together.

“It was and still is fairly complex to determine the fine print as to how it should live within the walls of Vanier,” he said. “And we've been working hard throughout the summer to make sure that we can be compliant.”

The hope is schools like Vanier will be consulted more before such laws are adopted in the future as “it has a deep impact on communities that have been built over several years,” he said.

Daycare union keeping close eye on enforcement

The law also bars workers in subsidized daycares and private schools from wearing religious symbols. Those already in their positions are exempt.

A spokesperson for the federation representing health and social service workers is looking into the impact on its 13,000 daycare workers across 400 subsidized daycares.

In a statement, Lucie Longchamp, the spokesperson for the Fédération de la santé et des services sociaux-CSN, said it has asked its member daycares to identify Law 9's impacts and the federation “will closely monitor developments in the coming weeks.”

Lucie Longchamp is the spokesperson for the Fédération de la santé et des services sociaux-CSN. (Radio-Canada)

She said the federation expects to hear about a breakdown of services, departures and hiring difficulties. From there, the federation will have more to say on the matter.

The spokesperson also said the FSSS-CSN will continue to “advocate for an open, pluralistic model of secularism that does not further jeopardize the provision of non-profit educational services.”

STM closes prayer space, adjusts policies

Montreal's public transit agency is telling employees they can no longer pray on workplace property.

The Société de transport de Montréal (STM) says it has four rooms that employees can use for silent activities such as meditation and yoga but can no longer be used for prayer.

The agency says signs have been posted outside the rooms to remind people of the ban, and said supervisors who witness religious practices should address the matter with the employee.

The STM union representing maintenance workers declined to comment.

Inside the transit network, musicians can still sing about their beliefs and wear whatever they want, but they can't "manifest any religious practice" or lead a worship service with music in the Metro.

STM spokesperson Amélie Régis said the agency’s special constables, with new training, will be intervening if any Metro performers are praying or evangelizing.

The union representing professionals like engineers and architects said there are resource rooms used for prayer at STM garages. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

Groups like Jehovah's Witnesses will still be allowed to operate, even talking to people about their beliefs. Since they aren’t forcing their beliefs on people, but instead waiting to be engaged by passersby, the STM isn’t going to prohibit the practice.

“It is our understanding that discussing a belief is not a religious practice,” she said.

Régis said constables will intervene by "prioritizing an awareness-raising approach," so warnings will be given to those who don’t follow the rules.

Lawyer says there’s a ‘grey zone’

The penalties laid out in Law 9 are fines that, in general, range between $125 and $1,125.

The law outlines how the province is going to enforce the law, with inspectors who can go into an institution, take photos and report back.

However, the onus is still on employers to ensure compliance.

Constitutional lawyer Frédéric Bérard said Law 9 represents a significant expansion of both where government oversight applies and what measures are enforced.

"You can say that it goes, you know, way beyond Bill 21," Bérard said. "One should ask the following question: What was the objective behind that?"

He argued the government cannot point to concrete examples of public prayer in places in the Metro causing disruptions, calling the legislation political pandering rather than a response to real needs.

While Bill 21 targeted authority figures like teachers and police to prevent state influence, Bérard said extending restrictions to cafeteria workers, janitors and transit employees reveals a shift toward removing visible religious presence entirely.

"So what's the next step, actually?" he asked. "Are we going to ban Muslim women from wearing veils in public, on the street? Are we going to go that far?"

Bérard added that public institutions are left navigating a legal grey zone without clear rules on enforcement or handling non-compliant employees.

It offers no guidance on what to do if an employee refuses to comply.

"What do we do with people who keep wearing their religious symbols? Do we fire them? How do we do that?" Bérard said. "Those institutions are not quite clear about what they have to do in order to respect the new bill."

CBC News reached out to the office of the minister responsible for secularism and was told they would respond soon. The story will be updated.

World.title: Some Great Lakes sturgeon may be 400 years old. Scientists are rethinking how to save them
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some of the lake sturgeon swimming around in the Great Lakes today may have been alive when Samuel de Champlain first reached Lake Huron more than four centuries ago.

New research suggests these ancient-looking, armoured fish may live far longer than scientists previously thought — in some cases, more than 400 years.

But despite their extraordinary longevity, lake sturgeon — which can weigh up to 180 kilograms and grow up to two metres long — have barely survived us. In Ontario, lake sturgeon are listed as a species at risk, and endangered in the Great Lakes specifically.

Overfishing and destruction of their spawning habitat wiped out an estimated 99 per cent of the lake sturgeon's historic population. More than a century later, populations in parts of the Great Lakes still rely on human beings raising and releasing young fish to help them recover.

The new study uses more than four decades of data from lake sturgeon caught and recaptured across the Great Lakes, suggesting recovery could be a much longer project than scientists anticipated.

A new way to count sturgeon birthdays

"We're pretty comfortable saying that there are potentially 400-year-old lake sturgeon swimming around," said Ed Baker, a fisheries scientist with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources who led the study.

Traditional estimates suggest lake sturgeon can live for as long as 150 years. But figuring out how many birthdays a sturgeon has had isn't as easy as counting candles on a cake.

WATCH | Trevor Pitcher introduces us to a Great Lakes giant: Meet the ancient giants of the Great Lakes | Duration 1:13 University of Windsor biologist Trevor Pitcher introduces us to a young lake sturgeon and explains what makes these ancient fish so remarkable — and so difficult to age.

Scientists have typically estimated a sturgeon's age by counting annual growth rings in a cross-section of its fin ray. But the older a sturgeon gets, the more slowly it grows — and the harder those rings become to distinguish.

Instead of counting growth rings, Baker and his colleagues used 44 years of capture data to calculate how much individual sturgeon grew between one capture and the next — then modelled how long it would take them to reach adult size.

A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service employee holds a lake sturgeon in the water. As Canada's largest freshwater fish, they can grow more than two metres long and weigh up to 180 kilograms. (Sharon Rayford/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

In one remarkable case, a male sturgeon measured 117 centimetres when researchers caught the fish in 1990. When the same fish was caught again 34 years later, it had grown just seven centimetres, or about 0.21 centimetres per year.

When researchers used those real-world growth rates to calculate how long it would take a fish to reach full size, some of the resulting ages stretched into centuries.

"It's a completely unexpected result," Baker said. "But it's one that's supported by the data, for sure."

The very long game of saving sturgeon

For Trevor Pitcher, a University of Windsor biologist who has spent years trying to rebuild lake sturgeon populations, the finding raises a much bigger question: What does it mean to conserve an animal whose lifespan may be measured in centuries?

"I think it changes everything," he said. "Assuming they do live, let's say 200 to 400 years, we need to reframe the way we do conservation."

Lake sturgeon were once abundant across the Great Lakes before overfishing and habitat destruction wiped out an estimated 99 per cent of their population. New research suggests some could live for more than 400 years. (Zach Melnick/Inspired Planet Productions)

Canada's existing conservation plan is a century long, Pitcher said, with the expectation the work will outlast the individuals who started it. If the new longevity estimates hold up, the assumptions behind that plan may have to change, he said.

"We would have to readjust some of our plans about restoration, and some of the habitat work would certainly be different."

A lake sturgeon fingerling rests across the palm of a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service employee. If it survives, this tiny fish could become enormous over a life span that could last centuries. (Jennifer Johnson/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

Pitcher said sturgeon eat large numbers of invasive quagga mussels and gobies, helping hold those populations down. Because historic overfishing and habitat destruction by humans reduced sturgeon to roughly one per cent of their former population, he said, "we kind of shot ourselves twice in the foot."

"When you take out a key species like sturgeon, it changes everything in the food web."

Pitcher's work is already extending beyond his own lab. His team is helping train people in Georgian Bay and Walpole Island First Nation to raise lake sturgeon themselves — spreading the expertise needed to rebuild populations around the Great Lakes.

A spiritual connection that runs deep

For Perry McLeod-Shabogesic, an elder and knowledge keeper from Nipissing First Nation, about 40 kilometres west of North Bay, Ont., the importance of lake sturgeon extends far beyond their role in the ecosystem.

"Because of their longevity, they were considered like a grandfather fish."

Perry McLeod-Shabogesic spoke to CBC News from his home in Nipissing First Nation, on the shores of Lake Nipissing in northern Ontario. (CBC)

A fish that can live for centuries experiences and witnesses things across generations, he said, and it's the reason sturgeon are regarded as elders in Anishinaabe tradition.

"They're seen as elders — fish elders, if you will," he said.

Their appearance adds to that sense of age. Lake sturgeon belong to a lineage of fish that stretches back more than 150 million years — long before humans appeared.

It was only relatively recently that their numbers collapsed, as habitat destruction and commercial fishing nearly wiped them out across the Great Lakes.

Lake Nipissing once teemed with sturgeon. McLeod-Shabogesic remembers older fishermen describing spring spawning runs, when the fish crowded the Sturgeon and French rivers so thickly that their backs broke the surface.

"You could walk across the river, they were so thick," he said.

'Duh'

For McLeod-Shabogesic, the unusual traits also place the fish in another category; he describes sturgeon as beings that live "in between" — neither like other fish nor anything else in the lake.

Workers with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources measure a lake sturgeon captured as part of the agency's long-running monitoring program. Decades of capture and release data allowed scientists to estimate how slowly the fish grow and how long they may live. (Michigan Department of Natural Resources)

In Anishinaabe teachings, he said, things do not always fall on one side or the other; between male and female is two-spirit, between hot and cold, there is warm. Sturgeon, he said, occupy a similar space.

That idea appears in an old Nipissing story McLeod-Shabogesic learned from his father. A family staying on the Manitou Islands caught and ate a mysterious black fish. By the next morning, they had transformed into serpent-like beings and disappeared beneath the ice.

The story, he said, speaks to the sturgeon's place in between worlds, and to its power and medicine.

"They weren't a fish completely and they weren't a snake completely. And then their age — they were different from the other fish."

So when McLeod-Shabogesic heard scientists now believe lake sturgeon may live for centuries, he wasn't surprised. "Duh," he said, laughing.

"It validates things to a certain degree," he said. "These are things that we already knew that our teachers and my ancestors — my grandparents and those fishermen that have fished this lake for a long time — they all knew these things already."

World.title: A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's just past noon at Richfield Bowl on the outskirts of Flint, Mich., and already the sounds of rolling bowling balls and crashing pins fill the large hall.

Here, strikes and spares are serious. So are splits. And not just when two pins are left standing.

"President [Donald] Trump's trying to keep American people working instead of sending it overseas," said Scott Holmes, moments before his turn to bowl.

"My son just lost his job a few months ago because they sent it over to Africa."

His teammate Dick Hunt sees the U.S. president's tariffs another way.

"The people, we end up paying for it," he said.

WATCH | Michigan residents react to the Canada-U.S. trade war: How the Canada-U.S. trade war is playing out in Michigan | Duration 1:55 Michigan has been one of the states hit hardest by the Canada-U.S. trade war, something that could turn into a big issue for voters in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

CBC News recently travelled to Michigan to get a temperature check on how Americans are feeling about the tariff war with Canada — the state's largest export market.

MAGA supporter Tina Bentley says she trusts the president's handling of the economy.

"I think he's a smart man. And I think that he cares 100 per cent about America," she said.

"The way I look at it is God didn't use perfect people to do his work. He used people like Trump to do his work."

Tina Bentley says she trusts U.S. President Donald Trump — and God — to do well by America. (Gian Paolo Mendoza/CBC)

A few lanes down, longtime bowler Peggy Banks can't disagree more.

"Our tariffs have not done anything for the people except make everything more expensive," she said.

Bowling league-mate Lisa McFadden nodded along.

"I think now everybody is starting to see it regardless of if you're a Democrat or a Republican because now it's affecting everybody's pocket," she said.

Trump's tariffs on the ballot

Michigan, heart of the auto industry, is one of the states hardest hit by the trade dispute. Just this month the U.S. National Taxpayers Union Foundation published a study suggesting Michigan households face the highest per-household tariff costs in the country.

That puts the already hotly contested race for U.S. Senate this November in the shadow of an escalating trade war.

Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is not running for re-election this year. Holding Michigan's seat is crucial for the Democratic Party if they want to regain control of the Senate during the second half of Trump's term. The Republicans are hoping to flip the seat red.

So far, polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck.

Nods to Flint's auto manufacturing history are prominent throughout the city. (Gian Paolo Mendoza/CBC)

Abdul El-Sayed, considered a progressive-left choice for the Democratic Party, is hoping to capitalize on Michiganders' frustrations with the trade war. He's been pushing Canada into the conversation while campaigning, repeatedly calling Trump an "asshole" for starting a trade war with the country's northern neighbour.

"People don't want to have to keep paying more for stuff that they need to buy. And this is the logical outcome of an illogical trade war. So here we are," El-Sayed told CBC News during a campaign stop in Waterford, Mich., on Thursday.

WATCH | Trump's 'vanity trade war' not popular with Michigan voters: Abdul El-Sayed: Abdul El-Sayed says Michigan voters not happy with Trump's 'vanity trade war' | Duration 12:31 Canada’s dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs are set to come into effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on Sept. 8. How will the country's largest retaliation yet be received south of the border? CBC has an exclusive interview with the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, and Power & Politics speaks with former U.S. ambassador to Canada James Blanchard.

The Democrat — who was quick to raise his childhood memories of watching Hockey Night in Canada and his love of lacrosse, Canada's other national sport — isn't ruling out all tariffs.

He cited duties on windmill parts or solar rigs as an example of tariffs he would keep if it would help build up his state's renewable energy industry.

"But it's because you're being very particular about exactly what kind of industries you're trying to protect. This is just across the board, ridiculousness, for no particular reason," El-Sayed said.

"So I can't quite explain it. Except for that everything Donald Trump does is ham-fisted, chaotic and self-serving."

His Republican rival has largely stayed away from talking about Trump's tariffs on the campaign.

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers speaks during a campaign event on Aug. 20 in Detroit. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

Mike Rogers's camp didn't respond to CBC's request for an interview, but was recently asked by Fox News if he supports Trump's handing of the trade deal with Canada and backed the president's objectives.

"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," Rogers said in an interview on Fox & Friends on Monday. "I think they think that the Republicans are going to lose in the midterms, and then that the Democrats are going to open up the borders again and absolutely undercut the people who build cars and car parts right here in Michigan."

Voters mixed on if tariffs play into their vote

Residents in Genesee County were mixed on whether the tariffs will impact their votes.

Carl Olson, teammates with Holmes and Hunt, offered a quick "no."

"I think eventually everything will level out and everything will go back to normal," he said.

Carl Olson, who doesn't see tariffs affecting his vote in the midterms, gets ready to bowl in Flint. (Gian Paolo Mendoza/CBC)

"If anything, it made it stronger that I will never vote Republican," said Joan Castor, when stopped in the Flint downtown core.

Down the street, Matt Zastrow said work and housing are his main concerns. If he votes, it will be for the Republican candidate.

"I think Trump's doing a good enough job right now. I'm not sure where we would be if we had somebody else in there," he said.

Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, stands in front of a view of the Michigan side of the Gordie Howe International Bridge. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

So far, industry in the region is largely staying out of politics. Businesses CBC contacted didn't want to speak on the record, citing the atmosphere.

Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, said businesses he speaks to want to see the cloud of uncertainty this trade war has brought cleared.

"Politics is not what this is about," Stevens Jr. said. "This is about making cars, in our perspective, moving lumber, moving energy, moving agriculture to the market and employing people.

"So the politics and the rhetoric are one thing, and that's at a crescendo right now, but the economics really are what speaks."

World.title: Friend holds out hope for Canadian runner missing on Matterhorn
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A friend of a Canadian athlete who went missing on the Matterhorn says Squamish, B.C.'s mountain running community is hoping for her safe return.

Kalie McCrystal, an elite mountain athlete from Squamish, was last seen on Sept. 1 above the mountain's Jean-Antoine Carrel hut, located at an altitude of roughly 3,830 metres.

Search and rescue crews were mobilized to find her, but recently declared they would suspend the helicopter operations after a full day of aerial searches on Thursday turned up no trace.

"We just want her to come home safe," said Duncan O'Regan, a friend of McCrystal. "And we miss her here. So we're just crossing our fingers."

He described her as a fixture in the local mountain running community.

Speed record in sight

McCrystal, a 38-year-old lawyer, was training to climb and descend the Matterhorn in less than five hours via the Lion Ridge, the main route from the Italian side. She had her eye on attaining the fastest known time.

"I know that this objective was well within her capabilities," said O'Regan, who is a mountain runner. "She's done much more difficult things, and this is not something that is beyond her capabilities. She's comfortable in this terrain."

O'Regan said the Matterhorn objective is something she's been training and rehearsing. One of the most recognizable peaks of the Alps, the Matterhorn straddles Italy and Switzerland, standing 4,478 metres tall.

Canadian mountain runner Kalie McCrystal, 38, of Squamish, B.C., in an image posted to Instagram on Aug. 7. McCrystal was last seen on Tuesday. (kalie_mcc/Instagram)

McCrystal is known as an expert skyrunner — a discipline which combines trail running and mountaineering.

"It's sort of like blending running a very long distance with scrambling," said Jacob Cook, a professional climber based in Squamish. "Sort of like rocky mountaineering terrain. And it quite quickly, often blends into, like, real climbing."

Cook said he doesn't know McCrystal personally but is aware and impressed with her accomplishments on the local circuit.

An accomplished athlete

In July, McCrystal bagged the fastest known female time of Squamish's Tantalus Traverse at nine hours and 40 minutes, crushing the previous record by three hours, according to the Fastest Known Time database.

"To do the Tantalus Traverse in the time that she did represents a really incredible level of athleticism," said Cook, who'd done the route a day after her.

McCrystal tested herself in competitions and mountains abroad.

Recently, she placed fourth in the women's division of the Trofeo Kima skyrunning race, which forces athletes through 52 kilometres of extremely technical mountainous terrain in Italy.

On Aug. 14, McCrystal completed a solo ascent and descent from Zermatt via the Swiss Hörnli Ridge in six hours, 47 minutes and 33 seconds, according to the Fastest Known Time database.

McCrystal is known as an expert skyrunner, a discipline which combines trail running and mountaineering. (Randall Hackley/The Associated Press)

Global Affairs aware of situation

Capilano University, where she is a faculty member, expressed its sympathy.

“Our thoughts are with Kalie’s family, friends and colleagues, and with everyone involved in the search efforts during this incredibly difficult time," said Jason Dewling, president and vice-chancellor of the university.

Global Affairs Canada says it's aware of a missing Canadian and is in contact with local authorities.

"Everyone here in Squamish is just really missing Kalie and hoping that she comes back soon," said O'Regan.

World.title: Cape Breton hit by over 200 millimetres of rain, leading to washouts and flood risks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A slow-moving weather system is dropping significant rainfall on northeastern Nova Scotia, especially Cape Breton this weekend.



Environment and Climate Change Canada has issued orange and yellow alert level rainfall warnings for these regions.



Heavy downpours and thunderstorms are bringing rainfall rates of 10 to 20+ millimetres per hour with the risk of localized flooding and hazardous travel conditions.

More than 21,000 Nova Scotia Power customers were without electricity late Saturday morning, with more than half the outages located in Cape Breton.



Cape Breton



The system has already dropped very heavy rainfall across the island with widespread amounts of 100-200 millimetres being recorded as of Saturday morning. Some private weather stations have already exceeded 200 millimetres in Richmond County with reports of washouts and localized flooding.



The community of Eskasoni picked up 20-30 millimetres per hour overnight and was also nearing the 200-millimetre mark as of mid-Saturday morning.



Rain will continue at times heavy for the Island through Saturday. Generally another 15-to-30 millimetres is expected throughout the day. However, with downpours and thunderstorms, another 50 millimetres locally isn't out of the question. The greatest risk for higher totals will be in Victoria County and also in Cape Breton County near the Atlantic coastline.



The rain continues Saturday night with generally another five-to-15 millimetres, however higher local amounts are still possible. Once again, Victoria county and coastal Cape Breton county will be at the greatest risk for these higher amounts overnight.



The system is also bringing winds gusting 60-80 km/h to the Island, which have brought some power outages.



Sunday both the rain and wind look to ease, however lighter rain and showers will continue with winds gusting to 50-60 km/h.

Northeastern regions

Guysborough, Antigonish, Pictou, as well as northern Colchester and Cumberland counties have also already picked up a lot of rain. Widespread totals of 40 to 70 millimetres have been recorded, with localized amounts nearing 100 millimetres in some areas as of mid-Saturday morning.



Periods of rain at times heavy with the risk of thunderstorms will continue in the east today with generally another 10-to-20 millimetres, however heavier amounts are possible locally, especially near the Northumberland Strait.



The periods of rain will continue tonight and right into Sunday with totals of 70 to 150 millimetres possible by the end of Sunday.



Central regions



Periods of rain will continue throughout Saturday and into Saturday night with lingering showers in the forecast for Sunday.



Generally, additional rainfall totals of 5-10 millimetres are expected for most of the central region by Sunday evening. However, as noted above, higher amounts look more likely for northern Colchester and Cumberland counties.

Temperatures in central areas will struggle with highs in the mid-teens for Saturday and Sunday with northerly winds gusting 50 to 60 km/h.

Monday should bring a mix of sun and cloud with a lingering chance of showers and milder temperatures.

(Ryan Snoddon/CBC)



Western regions



Further west, areas like the western Annapolis Valley, South Shore and Tri-County can expect just some lingering showers for Saturday and Sunday. However some sunny breaks are also likely for this region, especially Annapolis, Digby, Yarmouth, Shelburne and Queens counties. This region will see the mildest conditions, with highs in the mid-to-upper teens for Saturday and Sunday. Winds gusting 40–50 km/h will keep the fall feel in the air for both days.

Monday here will be great with lighter winds, lots of sunshine and temperatures popping into the upper teens and low 20s.
