The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast tackles expat money habits and mistakes
World.content:
Money affects everyone living in or traveling to Mexico. It is with that in mind that Mexico News Daily has launched a new weekly series called “Mexico and My Money.” You can read about the thinking behind the series here: Mexico and My Money: A new series MND on personal finance.

Our team recently conducted a survey of over 700 expats living in 25 states throughout Mexico about how they handle money while living in the country. The results were striking: Despite wariness of Mexican banks, 71% of respondents own a home in Mexico and nearly eight in 10 have made some kind of investment here — in real estate, a business, stocks or bonds. Nearly one in five respondents said they’d been victimized by a financial crime, with stories ranging from a landlord who kept a deposit “without cause” to a household employee who stole from a family over eight years. You can see the full results here: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups.

In this week’s episode of “Confidently Wrong,” George and I dig into those results. We talk about banking in Mexico, cash and credit cards, the money mistakes expats wish they’d avoided. You will learn what are others doing differently and about best practices for money in Mexico. Check it out!

Confidently wrong about Mexico and my money: Episode 7 - Season 3

Watch this video on YouTube

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Here is a mindblowing number to think about: If the peso had performed similarly from 2020 to the present as it did in the previous 25 years (from 1995 to 2020), the current exchange rate would be near 37 pesos to the US dollar!

That statistic puts into perspective how incredible the current exchange rate of 16.86 (as of Friday) really is. With the peso back near record highs in what seems like an unbreakable trend, I thought it would be a good time to do a refresher on the topic of the MXN:USD exchange rate.

For decades, the peso reliably lost about 10% of its value against the dollar every year. Although that devaluation was bad for some and good for others, its consistency and predictability allowed businesses, governments and families to plan around it. The fact that the past five-plus years have been so dramatically different — so unpredictable — has had some real impacts on Mexico.

With that in mind, I thought I would share some of the top columns I have written about the peso over these past several years to help us understand why its its happening, if it might continue, and what we can do about it. Each one tackles a different angle of the story. Please enjoy.

When will the Mexican peso begin to behave rationally again? — Why the peso stopped following its old, predictable rules — and what “rational” behavior would even look like now.

Is the peso punching above its weight? The results of our latest MND Peso Index™ — Our MND Peso Index™ compares real prices in Mexico and the U.S. to understand the real value of the peso.

Mexico in Numbers: The peso’s wildest swings since 2000 — A numbers-driven look back at 25 years of exchange rate history.

What’s next for the peso? — A forward-looking read on where the exchange rate could realistically head next.

World.title: 135 doctors sickened by salmonella outbreak at Mexico City’s General Hospital
World.content:
A salmonella outbreak at Mexico City’s General Hospital has sickened 135 doctors, leaving 41 hospitalized, including 15 who find themselves in the intensive care unit.

The doctors began showing symptoms last week, but the authorities initially ignored them, according to a source cited by the newspaper Reforma. However, as more and more physicians reported abdominal pain, diarrhea, low-grade fever and vomiting, an investigation was carried out.

The hospital’s dining room was finally shut down on Monday after bacterial infection and E. coli coinfection were confirmed, but administrators are receiving criticism after disregarding the initial complaints.

Reforma reported that as a result of the delayed care, the conditions of several of the doctors worsened, with some developing kidney failure and hypovolemic shock.

A shelter that previously housed family members of long-term patients was converted into a ward for the sick doctors. The area had been closed since the COVID-19 pandemic, but as the emergency room was overflowing, it was reopened.

Officials cited by the newspaper El País said that all those affected had received medical attention and were in stable condition, although 41 remained hospitalized as of Thursday.

Health Minister Dr. David Kershenobich downplayed the reports that doctors were admitted to intensive care, saying on Friday that it was “not related to the severity of their symptoms, rather it was a matter of making available any space we had to receive the staff and hydrate them.”

The hospital has two cafeterias, one for health care staff and workers, and another for resident physicians, which is outsourced. Early analysis suggests contaminated eggs caused the infection.

Once the source of the outbreak was confirmed, hospital administrators ordered the suspension of the outsourced dining service.

Management is actively searching for and monitoring those potentially exposed to the contaminated food.

El Financiero newspaper reported that Restaurantes Grogi, a commercial food service and catering company, holds the food preparation contract for the dining room that was shuttered.

The company holds two federal contracts worth over 333 million pesos (US $19.7 million) to run medical dining halls. The contracts require the company to perform routine bacteriological testing on all prepared food.

With reports from Reforma, El País and El Financiero

World.title: The super peso is back. What does that mean for Mexico?
World.content:
Listen to this article

The peso gained against the dollar in early trading on Friday, hitting its strongest point in 28 months and highlighting recent assertions that the “super peso” is back.

But before Mexico’s currency gets fitted for a cape, it’s worth examining what the peso’s surge means for Mexico.

At 10 a.m. Mexico City time on Friday, the spot exchange rate hit a new yearly low of 16.863 pesos to the US dollar, a gain of 6.5 centavos compared to Thursday’s close of 16.928 pesos.

With the peso on track to gain nearly 10 centavos this week and last month’s 1.87% gain pushing yearly appreciation to nearly 6%, it’s no wonder that talk of the super peso has been revived.

What is driving the peso appreciation?

The peso — one of the most-traded emerging market currencies — is not unusually strong compared to other emerging market currencies, Graham Stock, an analyst at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, told Reuters.

Instead, “the dollar has been weak compared to previous cycles.”

If the peso’s strength were purely a result of dollar weakness, however, it would be rising alongside other currencies. Instead, it has gained against other major currencies.

Alejo Czerwonko, emerging markets analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, says this is “a sign that domestic factors, not just broad dollar weakness, are at play.” Those factors include lower trade-risk premiums, political stability and solid macroeconomic conditions, Czerwonko said.

Marco Oviedo, senior strategist for Latin America at XP Investments, said that after Mexico’s 2024 election many long-term investors, such as pension funds and insurers, stepped back from the peso and have largely stayed away.

Recent gains have been stoked primarily by “fast money” investors (i.e., hedge funds and short-term traders) rather than by the ⁠reappearance of longer-term institutional buyers — an important distinction, analysts say, since the type of investor can shape how long a rally lasts.

Investors, strategists and economists have also issued warnings about trade policy.

For instance, RBC BlueBay’s Stock cites “clear uncertainty” around how the U.S.-Mexico trade ⁠relationship plays out after the Trump administration declined to approve a 16-year extension for the USMCA free trade agreement.

It remains to be seen what the USMCA will look like afterward, Stock said, particularly as Mexico pursues separate bilateral discussions.

So what are the positives and negatives?

A stronger currency can be a mixed blessing.

On the positive side, there are lower import costs, less inflationary pressure, cheaper inputs and greater purchasing power for those who buy products from abroad.

On the negative side, there is lower value in remittances, pressure on exporters’ margins and a loss of competitiveness for domestic producers against cheaper imports.

The stakes are high since Mexico sends more than 80% of its exports to the United States. A stronger peso benefits sectors that import a significant portion of their inputs, machinery and equipment. The agricultural export sector, meanwhile, faces a less favorable outlook because its costs are not linked to imported inputs, preventing it from compensating for losses when exporting.

“About 77% of Mexican imports are intermediate goods … [and] used to produce other goods,” Ana Karen García, a researcher at the Mexican Institute for Competitiveness (IMCO) told the newspaper El Economista. “This protects the manufacturing sector, since although it loses money when exporting, it pays less for these goods when importing.”

As a result, states with strong manufacturing sectors integrated into global supply chains, such as automotive, electronics, electrical and machinery, stand to benefit, García said.

On the other hand, states dominated by the agriculture sector lose out. Many of those states — such as Michoacán — rely on remittances which often shrink in the face of the super peso.

With reports from El Economista and Reuters

World.title: Led by Quintana Roo, Mexico’s tourism GDP ranks fourth globally, according to the  World Travel & Tourism Council
World.content:
Mexico has been ranked fourth globally by the World Travel & Tourism Council in tourism-generated revenue as a contribution to the GDP, both overall and in the specific category of leisure tourism.

The high-level performance places Mexico behind only the United States, China and Germany, and makes it the only Latin American nation in the top 10 in both rankings.

“It is a pleasure to announce that Mexico ranks fourth in both rankings, which reflects its consolidation as an international tourist destination,” head of the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) Gloria Guevara said during the presentation of the rankings in Cancún, Quintana Roo.

The famous beach resort was a fitting site for the presentation, as it is part of its state’s Caribbean coast that the data shows is the driving force behind Mexico’s tourism dominance.

In the indicator of direct contribution of travel and tourism to GDP, Mexico registered US $149.4 billion in 2025. This figure includes the value generated directly by activities such as lodging, transportation, restaurants, travel agencies, attractions, and services contracted by visitors.

The U.S. topped the list with US $885.8 billion, followed by China with US $434.8 billion and Germany with US $202.9 billion.

Mexico also ranked fourth globally in visitor spending on leisure and recreation travel (as opposed to other travel categories, such as medical, cultural, adventure, ecological, etc.). This indicator, which considers mainly visitors on vacations and short breaks, again places Mexico behind the three largest economies in the ranking.

Guevara, a former Mexican tourism minister, mentioned that Mexico was the fastest-growing market in North America, ahead of Canada and the United States, where tourist spending contracted due to fewer travelers.

The WTTC ranked Mexico sixth in the Americas in growth of international visitor spending compared to 2019, with an increase of 1.7%. That percentage is above the world average but below Cuba, Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, and Brazil for that period.

Quintana Roo strengthened its position as one of the driving forces of tourism in Mexico. According to Guevara, the state maintains its momentum with its sun and beach offerings, connectivity, and collaborative efforts between the state government, hoteliers and the WTTC itself.

With reports from El Economista and SPD Noticias

World.title: Panama Now Hosts 192 Multinational Headquarters
World.content:

PANAMA · BUSINESS

Key Facts —What happened: Panama’s commerce ministry says 192 multinationals now hold SEM regional headquarters status. —How big it is: The list, updated to May 2026, was announced on September 2, 2026. —What it means: SEM offers tax breaks and immigration perks to attract corporate regional hubs. —The catch: The ministry did not confirm how many jobs or how much investment these firms bring. —Who it hits: Foreign executives and their families can get residency through the program. —What comes next: A newer EMMA regime extends similar benefits to manufacturing services.

Panama’s SEM scheme now counts 192 multinational headquarters. The ministry says they have created about 10,000 jobs, roughly half filled by Panamanians.

What is the SEM regime?

SEM stands for Sedes de Empresas Multinacionales, which means Multinational Company Headquarters in Spanish. It is a special status that Panama gives to foreign companies that set up a regional office in the country.

The goal is to make Panama the home base for a company’s Latin American operations. In return, the company gets tax breaks and easier immigration rules for its staff.

The program is run by a special unit inside the Ministry of Commerce and Industries, known as MICI. That unit tracks every company that holds the status.

Panama created this regime to attract high-value corporate jobs. It wants to be the place where global firms manage their regional business.

The new numbers

On September 2, 2026, the Ministry of Commerce and Industries (MICI) announced that 192 companies now hold SEM status. The list was updated to May 2026.

Panama closed 2025 with 188 SEM companies, so four have joined since. The ministry did not name them.

The ministry published the news on its own website. A Panama newspaper repeated the same figure the next day.

MICI publishes SEM and EMMA companies on the same list, which runs from 2007 to May 2026.

What SEM offers

Panama created SEM under Law 41 of 2007 and reformed it under Law 57 of 2018. Headquarters pay 5% income tax on what they earn serving group companies abroad.

The regime also brings immigration perks. Executives and their families get faster visas and residency.

These perks make Panama more attractive than other Latin American hubs. Executives can move with less paperwork and keep more of their income.

The benefits are not automatic. Companies must apply and meet specific requirements set by the ministry.

How EMMA fits in

EMMA is a newer regime, created by Law 159 of August 31, 2020. It is aimed at multinationals that provide manufacturing-related services, not just headquarters.

EMMA offers similar terms, including a 5% income tax rate and relief from Panama’s sales tax, the ITBMS, on certain services. It also provides immigration perks like permanent residency.

Tax advisers describe EMMA as a version of SEM built for manufacturing services. It lets companies do more than manage regional offices.

The two programs are tracked together on the ministry’s public list. That list covers both SEM and EMMA firms from 2007 to May 2026.

Jobs and investment

The ministry says these companies provided 8,359 direct jobs in 2024. It puts the running total at about 10,000 jobs by early 2026, roughly half held by Panamanians.

Investment totals are still not published. Jobs are, and about half of them go to Panamanians.

Earlier reports from March 2026 mentioned 13 new licenses in 2025. They projected US$37.3 million in investment.

Infobae reported in January that multinationals were weighing new investments in Panama. That suggests the pipeline of new companies is still active.

Who benefits

The main beneficiaries are foreign executives who get to live and work in Panama with their families. The regime makes it easier to obtain visas and residency.

Panama also benefits from the jobs and spending these companies bring. Local professionals get opportunities to work for global firms without leaving home.

Local service providers also gain. Lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents serve the needs of these multinational teams.

The program aims to create a multiplier effect. Each headquarters can support many local jobs beyond its own staff.

The bigger picture

Panama has long positioned itself as the logistics and business hub of Latin America. The SEM regime is a key part of that strategy.

The country’s dollar-based economy and strategic location help. But the tax and immigration incentives are what seal the deal for many multinationals.

Panama is not the only country courting regional headquarters. But it has the longest-running scheme in Central America.

The SEM regime is one tool in a broader plan. Panama wants to diversify beyond the canal and become a knowledge economy.

What the ministry has not said

The ministry did not confirm which companies were the latest to join the SEM regime. It also did not provide a breakdown by sector.

The MICI portal keeps a public database of SEM and EMMA companies from 2007 to May 2026. That is the best place to check the full list.

The tax terms sit in the law rather than in the announcement. Law 57 of 2018 sets the 5% rate.

Investment totals are still not published. That makes the programme’s full return hard to judge.

What comes next

Panama is likely to keep promoting both SEM and EMMA to attract more multinationals. The government sees these regimes as a way to create professional jobs and diversify the economy.

For foreign companies, the message is clear: Panama wants to be your regional home. The SEM regime is the door, and EMMA widens it.

The ministry may release more details in future announcements. Investors should watch for updates on new licenses and policy changes.

The government has signaled it wants to keep both programs active. That suggests stability for companies already in the system.

Why Panama targets multinationals

Panama’s economy depends heavily on services like banking, logistics, and trade. Multinational headquarters bring high-value jobs that support those sectors.

These companies also create demand for local lawyers, accountants, and other professionals. That helps Panama move beyond its historic reliance on the Panama Canal.

The canal alone cannot sustain the country’s growth. Panama needs new engines of economic activity.

Multinational hubs also bring global connections. They link Panama to corporate networks across the region.

How the SEM regime works in practice

A company applies to MICI for SEM status. Once approved, it can set up a regional office that manages operations across Latin America.

Companies must meet minimum staffing and spending commitments. Those details are not public in the latest announcement.

The application process involves several government agencies. It can take months to complete.

Once approved, the company must renew its status periodically. That keeps the regime accountable.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The jump from 188 to 192 companies shows steady, if slow, growth. But it does not prove that Panama is winning a race against rivals like Costa Rica or Colombia.

The company count on its own says little. The jobs figure is the more useful number, and it points to about 10,000 posts since the scheme began.

The four new companies could be small or large. The count does not reveal their economic weight.

Jobs are the better measure, and the ministry now publishes them. Export and investment totals are still missing.

What foreign investors should watch

Investors should watch for updates from MICI on new SEM and EMMA licenses. They should also look for changes in tax law that affect these regimes.

The government has signaled it wants to keep both programs active. That suggests stability for companies already in the system.

Investors should also monitor the political climate. Changes in government could alter the incentives.

Finally, watch how Panama’s neighbors respond. If they sweeten their own deals, Panama may need to adjust.

How Panama compares with neighbors

Costa Rica and Colombia also offer incentives for regional headquarters. Panama’s edge is its location and dollar-based economy.

But those countries have lower labor costs in some sectors. Panama must compete on more than just tax breaks.

Panama’s canal and banking sector give it unique advantages. No other country in the region has both.

The SEM regime is just one factor in a company’s decision. Infrastructure, security, and quality of life also matter.

The role of the Ministry of Commerce

The Ministry of Commerce and Industries, known as MICI, runs the SEM program. It processes applications and keeps the official list.

MICI also promotes the regime abroad. It works with investment agencies to attract new companies.

The ministry’s announcement on September 2 led on jobs rather than on the company count. It said about half of the posts go to Panamanians.

For more information, companies can contact MICI directly. The ministry’s website has contact details and the public list.

Historical growth of the regime

The SEM regime started in 2007. Since then, it has grown steadily to 192 companies.

The public list covers the full history from 2007 to May 2026. That shows how the program has evolved.

Early years saw slower growth. Recent years have added a few companies each year.

The growth is not explosive, but it is consistent. That consistency may appeal to investors.

Potential risks and limitations

The SEM regime depends on government policy. A change in leadership could alter the benefits.

Global economic downturns could also slow new investments. Multinationals may delay expansion plans.

Panama faces competition from other hubs. If rivals offer better deals, companies may go elsewhere.

Investment totals are still not published. That makes the programme’s full return hard to judge.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does SEM stand for? SEM stands for Sedes de Empresas Multinacionales, which translates to Multinational Company Headquarters. It is a special status Panama grants to foreign firms that set up regional offices. How many companies are in the SEM regime? As of May 2026, 192 companies hold SEM status. The Ministry of Commerce and Industries announced this on September 2, 2026. What benefits does SEM offer? SEM offers a 5% income tax rate on qualifying income, plus easier visas and residency for executives. The exact details are set in the law. What is the EMMA regime? EMMA is a newer regime for multinationals providing manufacturing-related services. Created by Law 159 in 2020, it offers similar benefits to SEM, including a 5% income tax rate and residency options. Where can I find the list of SEM companies? The Ministry of Commerce and Industries (MICI) publishes a public list on its website. It covers SEM and EMMA companies from 2007 to May 2026.

World.title: El Salvador Budget Shift Moves US$97 Million It Can Still Borrow
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

EL SALVADOR · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: The Finance Ministry asked Congress on September 3 to add US$97 million to the 2026 budget. —How big it is: The amount is under 1% of El Salvador’s US$10.56 billion budget for 2026. —What it means: The funds come from unused bond authorizations, not new debt or surplus. —The catch: This is not new money; it’s leftover permission to borrow that was already approved. —Who it hits: Eleven state institutions, including security, agriculture, and tourism agencies. —What comes next: The finance committee takes up the request first, then the full Assembly votes.

The government says it needs the money for prisons, farms and ID cards. The request also shows how El Salvador handles debt under its IMF programme.

What the government is asking for

On September 3, the Finance Ministry sent a request to the Legislative Assembly, which is El Salvador’s Congress. The request asks to reform the national budget and add US$97 million for the second half of 2026.

The Finance Ministry calls the costs ‘priority and unavoidable obligations’ for 11 state institutions. The full list is not public, but the largest items are known.

Where the money comes from

The US$97 million is not new borrowing. It comes from two domestic bond issues that Congress approved earlier but were not fully used.

The first issue was approved in November 2025 for US$344 million. The government used US$267 million, leaving US$77 million.

The second issue was approved in April 2026 for US$100 million. It left US$20 million unused.

Together, those leftovers make up the US$97 million. This is an important distinction.

The funds are pending authorizations, not surplus from bonds that were already sold. The government is asking for permission to use the remaining borrowing capacity it already has.

How the money would be spent

The largest single item, US$37 million, goes to the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Reports differ on the exact use, from farm markets to running costs.

The next largest, US$30 million, is for prisoner rehabilitation. About US$19 million goes to the interior and territorial development ministry, split between running the ministry and social programmes.

Smaller sums go to the Attorney General’s office, the economy ministry and public works. The National Registry of Natural Persons gets US$1.19 million to issue free national ID cards for first-time applicants.

Other recipients include the environment ministry, tourism ministry, and CORSATUR, the state tourism promotion corporation. The decree does not say how long the bonds would run or what interest they would pay.

Why Congress must approve it

In El Salvador, changes to the national budget require approval by the Legislative Assembly. This includes using existing bond authorizations.

The request reached the Assembly as a formal letter from the Finance Ministry. The Assembly’s finance committee has been called to take up the request early next week.

A plenary vote would follow if the committee backs it. The Assembly could still change the request or reject it.

The IMF program behind the budget

El Salvador is under a 40-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) with the International Monetary Fund, approved in February 2025. The program provides about US$1.4 billion in loans.

In exchange, the government agreed to cut spending and raise revenue. The goal is to reduce public debt to about 83% of GDP by 2028.

That means running a primary surplus, which is revenue minus spending before interest payments. The IMF program also limits new debt.

Under the deal, the government cannot issue Bitcoin-linked bonds or other crypto-related guarantees.

El Salvador’s approved 2026 national budget is US$10,555.6 million. The request would move money inside that total.

How this request fits the IMF deal

Using leftover bond authorizations is a way to get cash without going to international markets. Fitch Ratings, a credit rating agency, said in May 2026 that it does not expect new Eurobond sales before 2027.

Instead, El Salvador relies on domestic borrowing and multilateral lenders like the IMF and World Bank. This request fits that pattern.

The IMF’s 3 September statement on the second and third reviews does not mention this request. The two are separate steps.

The bigger picture: fiscal consolidation

The IMF program requires deep spending cuts. El Faro, an independent Salvadoran outlet, reported that the IMF-backed plan implied social spending cuts of about US$623 million in 2025.

It put the cuts at over US$1 billion in 2026 and US$1.4 billion in 2027. The government says it is committed to fiscal consolidation.

In December 2025, an IMF staff statement praised the government’s ‘strong’ commitment. It said the 2025 primary balance target was on track.

But some targets have been missed. Fitch notes that the 2025 domestic debt reduction goal was not met.

A Q1 2026 indicative target was also missed. The end-2025 primary balance target, however, was achieved.

What this means for foreigners

For investors and expats, this request shows how El Salvador manages its public finances under the IMF program. It is a mix of domestic borrowing, multilateral support, and strict spending controls.

The US$97 million is under 1% of the 2026 budget. It is a small sum, but the government still needs permission to spend it.

The request also signals that the government is avoiding new international debt for now. It also means less new debt sold abroad this year.

It also means the IMF programme sets the limits.

What to watch next

The key date is when the finance committee meets, likely early next week. If approved, the money will be distributed to the 11 institutions.

Also watch for the IMF’s final approval of the second and third reviews. That would release the next tranche of loan funds.

The government has not said when it will issue the remaining bonds. The interest rate and the term of the bonds have not been published.

How El Salvador’s budget process works

El Salvador’s national budget is a law passed by Congress each year. The Finance Ministry proposes it, and lawmakers approve it.

If the government needs more money mid-year, it must ask Congress to amend the budget. This request is a formal step in that process.

The Legislative Assembly has 60 seats. The ruling party, Nuevas Ideas, holds 54 of them, so approval is likely.

Mid-year top-ups are routine. In June the Assembly approved a separate US$118 million reinforcement funded by higher tax collection.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The US$97 million is under 1% of the 2026 budget. It is a small sum, but the government still needs permission to spend it.

The request is significant because it shows the government’s cash flow challenges. It needs to use leftover borrowing authority to pay for basic services.

The numbers do not prove that the government is in crisis. They show that it is managing within the limits set by the IMF program.

However, the missed targets on domestic debt reduction suggest some strain. The government is walking a tightrope between spending needs and fiscal discipline.

Who is affected and how

The US$97 million would reach several groups. Farmers would benefit from the agricultural market programs.

Prisoners would get rehabilitation services, which the government lists as a priority cost. First-time applicants would get their national ID card, the DUI, free of charge.

Tourism agencies would organize international events to attract visitors. The money is still borrowed, and it is borrowed at home.

Local banks and pension funds are the usual buyers.

The role of domestic bonds in El Salvador

Domestic bonds are debt securities sold to local investors, such as banks and pension funds. They are a key source of funding for the government.

In 2025 and 2026, Congress authorized two domestic bond issues. The government did not sell all the bonds, leaving US$97 million in unused authorization.

Now it wants to use that leftover permission to borrow. This is a common practice in many countries, but it requires legislative approval.

Domestic bonds are different from Eurobonds, which are sold on international markets. Eurobonds are more expensive and subject to foreign investor sentiment.

What is still missing

The specific terms of the bonds, such as interest rates and maturity dates, are not public. The government has not released that information.

It is also not clear whether the IMF has explicitly approved this budget reform. The staff-level agreement does not mention it.

Only the largest recipients among the 11 institutions have been named so far. The Assembly could still change the request or reject it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the US$97 million a surplus from an existing bond? No. It comes from unused balances of two domestic bond issues approved in 2025 and 2026. The government is asking for permission to use that remaining borrowing capacity. What will the money be used for? The largest amounts go to agriculture (US$37 million) and prison rehabilitation (US$30 million). Smaller sums go to ID card issuance, environment programs, and tourism events. Why does Congress need to approve this? In El Salvador, any change to the national budget requires approval by the Legislative Assembly. This includes using existing bond authorizations. How does this relate to the IMF program? The IMF program requires fiscal consolidation and limits new debt. Using leftover bond authorizations helps the government avoid new international borrowing, which fits the program’s goals. When will Congress vote on this? The finance committee was due to take it up in the week of 7 September. A plenary vote would come after that.

World.title: São Paulo Builder You,Inc Faces Negative Equity
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · REAL ESTATE

Key Facts —What happened: You,Inc, a São Paulo developer, is delaying deliveries and has negative equity of R$312.7 million (about US$61 million). —How big it is: The company’s net debt reached R$779.8 million (about US$153 million) in the second quarter. —What it means: Negative equity is an accounting measure, not a finding of insolvency. —The catch: You,Inc is not in judicial recovery. —Who it hits: Buyers in several You,Inc projects in São Paulo report stalled works and late deliveries. —What comes next: Brazilian law allows buyers to seek contract termination and refunds, but recovery depends on the company’s finances.

You,Inc’s own second-quarter accounts show it burning cash. Buyers on several projects say deliveries have slipped.

What negative equity means for You,Inc

Negative equity sounds technical. It is not.

It means a company’s debts are bigger than its assets.

For You,Inc, that gap was R$312.7 million at the end of June 2026. That is about US$61 million.

At R$5.11 to the US dollar, the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX rate of Friday 4 September 2026.

A year earlier, You,Inc had positive equity of R$2.4 million (about US$0.5 million). The swing took just 12 months.

You,Inc’s financial troubles in numbers

You,Inc’s net debt rose from R$663.1 million to R$779.8 million between the first and second quarters of 2026. That is about US$130 million to US$153 million.

Equity turned more negative in the same period. It went from minus R$221 million to minus R$312.7 million (about minus US$43 million to minus US$61 million).

The company burned R$116.7 million of cash in the second quarter, about US$23 million. That was up from R$71.7 million (about US$14 million) in the first quarter.

Gross sales fell 68.1% year on year in the second quarter, to R$94 million (about US$18 million). Contracted sales are not the same as booked revenue, but the fall shows how little new money is coming in.

Delayed deliveries and stalled works

Buyers have protested over works that Brazilian outlets report as stopped or slowed on several projects. Portas, a Brazilian property title, names one specific site: Authentique Perdizes, stopped since March 2025.

You,Inc has not launched any new projects in 2026.

There is no public total for how many buyers are affected. Portas counted at least 15 court cases specifically over delivery delays.

Dozens more over contract revision and damages, and at least 106 complaints on Reclame Aqui in six months.

A consumer law site lists about 19 You,Inc worksites. These are ordinary civil disputes, not a formal bankruptcy process.

What happens to your money if a Brazilian developer fails

Brazilian developers can ring-fence a single project under a rule called ‘patrimônio de afetação’. It walls that project’s assets and buyer payments off from the rest of the company.

Ring-fencing is optional, not automatic. Buyers should check their own contract and the project’s registry record to see whether it applies.

Where a project is not ring-fenced, buyers rank alongside other unsecured creditors if the developer fails. That is the general rule in Brazil.

If the developer goes bankrupt, you may have to join a queue of creditors to get your money back. Protection is not absolute.

Your rights as a buyer in Brazil

Under Law 13.786/2018 a buyer may terminate and seek a refund. Developers may keep a penalty, and there is a 180-day grace period on delivery.

How much is refunded depends on the contract.

This process is called ‘distrato’. You can also demand compensation for delays.

Lawyers who handle these cases say the first step is written notice. Timing and the exact contract terms then decide what follows.

If the developer does not respond, you may need to go to court. Legal action can be slow, but it is often the only way to enforce your rights.

Is You,Inc in judicial recovery?

Judicial recovery is a Brazilian process similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It gives a company protection from creditors while it tries to restructure.

No court has placed You,Inc in judicial recovery, and no filing has been reported. This is a cash and delivery problem, not an insolvency case.

Being in judicial recovery would freeze most lawsuits against the company. It would also give You,Inc time to negotiate with creditors.

Without that protection, buyers can pursue their claims individually. Nothing in the public record indicates the company plans to file.

What the company says

You,Inc has not published a project-by-project response to the delays. Its chief executive, Abrão Muszkat, has described an operational and financial restructuring at the company.

The financial figures come from the company’s own disclosures.

Estadão has reported that builders in this segment, You,Inc among them, are selling projects to cut debt. You,Inc has not confirmed any sale.

Commentators quoted in the Brazilian press. Including Roberto Pereira of ATEX Investimentos and Adenauer Rockenmeyer of Corecon-SP, describe the company as heavily indebted.

Selling land or projects is the usual route out for a developer in that position.

What buyers should do now

If you have a contract with You,Inc and the delivery is delayed, you can send a formal notification to the company. This is the first step in a distrato process.

You may also want to seek legal advice. A lawyer can help you understand your rights and the best way to get your money back.

Keep all documents related to your purchase, including contracts and payment receipts. These will be essential if you go to court.

The company has announced no new delivery dates and no refund schedule. This is general information, not legal advice.

The bigger picture for Brazil’s real estate market

Estadão has reported that builders which bet on the middle class are now heavily indebted and selling projects. You,Inc is one of them.

The pattern is a warning for foreign buyers. A big market does not make a small developer safe.

The middle-class segment was once seen as a growth area. But economic downturn and high interest rates have hit these developers hard.

Some of these companies are selling projects to reduce debt. Others may need to restructure or face bankruptcy.

How You,Inc got here

You,Inc expanded in the São Paulo market. The company targeted middle-income buyers with residential projects.

The company’s debt grew as it financed new projects. When sales slowed, the debt became harder to manage.

Net debt kept rising while sales fell. The company has launched nothing new in 2026.

You,Inc reported a landbank of about R$1.8 billion (roughly US$352 million). One account of the same results puts inventory at R$1.58 billion (about US$309 million).

What is not yet known

Neither the company nor the courts have published a figure for affected units. The exact number of buyers remains unknown.

You,Inc has not published a detailed response to the delays. Its plans for new delivery dates or refunds are not public.

The negative equity figure of R$312.7 million comes from You,Inc’s own financial reports. These are public documents filed with regulators.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does negative equity mean? It means a company’s liabilities are bigger than its assets. For You,Inc the gap was R$312.7 million, about US$61 million, at the end of June 2026. Can I get my money back if You,Inc delays my property? Brazilian law allows a buyer to terminate and seek a refund once the delivery date and grace period have passed. A process known as distrato. Is You,Inc bankrupt? No. You,Inc is not in judicial recovery as of 5 September 2026, and no filing has been reported. How many buyers are affected by You,Inc delays? There is no public total. Portas counted at least 15 active delay cases, and a consumer law site lists about 19 worksites. What protections do Brazilian buyers have? Some projects are ring-fenced under ‘patrimônio de afetação’, which separates that project from the developer’s other business. It is optional, so buyers need to check whether their own project has it.

World.title: Brazil Regulator Approves Oi Fixed-Line Sale With Conditions
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · TELECOMS

Key Facts —What happened: Brazil’s telecom regulator Anatel approved the sale of Oi’s fixed-line business to Método. —How big it is: The deal is worth R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million), bid as a single upfront payment. —What it means: Oi’s fixed-line customers will eventually be served by Método, but only after conditions are met. —The catch: Oi remains responsible for fixed-line service until all conditions are fulfilled, which may take months. —Who it hits: Fixed-line customers in remote towns where Oi is the only operator. —What comes next: Método must present guarantees and plans to Anatel before the transfer is finalized.

Anatel’s conditional approval moves Oi’s fixed-line sale forward, but the bankrupt carrier remains responsible until all conditions are met.

What Anatel approved

On 3 September 2026, Anatel’s board gave prior consent for Método to take control of Oi’s fixed-line unit. The approval is conditional, meaning Método must meet several requirements before the deal is final.

Anatel is Brazil’s telecommunications regulator. It does the job America’s Federal Communications Commission does.

Who is Oi and how did it get here

Oi was once Brazil’s largest fixed-line telephone company, serving millions of customers across the country. But years of heavy debt and competition led to financial collapse.

In 2023 Oi filed for court protection from creditors for the second time. In August 2026 a Rio court ended that process and declared the company bankrupt.

The fixed-line unit was sold through a judicial auction. That is a court-supervised process.

Who is Método

Método Telecomunicações e Comércio Ltda. is a telecom company based in Minas Gerais, a state in southeastern Brazil. It won the auction for Oi’s fixed-line unit with a bid of R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million).

Método beat another company, Sercomtel, to win the auction.

The conditions Anatel imposed

Anatel’s approval comes with several conditions. Método must formally take over Oi’s regulatory commitments.

Those are the obligations Oi had to provide service in certain areas. Método must also sign an addendum to an existing agreement with Anatel.

It must present a guarantee to ensure service continuity. It must also submit a plan for transferring phone numbers.

These conditions are designed to protect customers. They are there to keep essential services running.

One approval is still outstanding. Cade, Brazil’s competition regulator, has not yet cleared the deal.

Método itself named Cade clearance as a suspensive condition in July. Until it comes, the sale is not final.

Why service continuity matters

In many remote areas of Brazil, Oi is the only fixed-line operator. This is known as being the Carrier of Last Resort.

That means Oi is required to provide service even where it is not profitable. Anatel’s conditions require that voice service in these areas continues through December 2028.

That matters for people who rely on a landline to call for help.

What happens to customers now

For now, Oi’s fixed-line customers continue to be served by Oi. Anatel has made clear that Oi remains responsible for the service until the transfer is fully completed.

That means customers should not see any immediate change. Over time, as Método meets all conditions, customers will gradually migrate to Método’s control.

But there is no set date for that yet.

The cost of keeping services running

Anatel’s technical analysis estimates that keeping the fixed-line services running through the end of 2028 will cost around R$160 million (US$31.3 million). That is more than double the sale price.

This highlights the financial burden of operating a fixed-line network, especially in rural areas. Método must post guarantees covering that cost.

It is the hardest condition to meet.

What this means for Oi’s bankruptcy

The sale of the fixed-line unit is part of Oi’s bankruptcy proceedings. The court approved the sale in April 2026.

Anatel’s approval is another step in the process. However, Anatel’s decision does not change that.

Oi was declared bankrupt in August and a court-appointed administrator is now selling what is left.

The company still has other assets to sell and debts to pay. The exact impact on Oi’s overall restructuring is not yet clear.

What comes next

Método must now present the required guarantees and plans to Anatel. The regulator will review them and decide whether to give final approval.

The process could take months. Until then, Oi remains the legal operator.

Customers should continue to receive service as usual. The date to watch is December 2028.

Anatel’s conditions run to then, and it has not said what follows.

How the auction process worked

The fixed-line unit was sold through a judicial auction in April 2026. A court in Rio de Janeiro supervised the process to ensure fair bidding.

Método’s bid of R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million) was the highest. The court approved the sale, but regulatory approval was still needed from Anatel.

What is a UPI in bankruptcy sales

In Brazilian bankruptcy law, a UPI is an isolated productive unit that can be sold separately. This allows a company to sell parts of its business without halting operations.

Oi’s fixed-line unit was structured as a UPI. This made it easier to sell while keeping services running for customers.

The role of the bankruptcy court

The 7th Business Court in Rio de Janeiro is overseeing Oi’s bankruptcy. It approved the sale and has also ordered Método to pay the auction price promptly.

In July 2026 the court ordered Método to pay R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million) within five days. A 50% penalty applies if it did not.

Método has disputed parts of the payment terms.

Background on Brazil’s telecom market

Brazil’s fixed-line market has been shrinking for years as mobile phones replaced landlines. Many operators have struggled to make money from fixed-line services.

Oi’s network covers vast rural areas where mobile coverage is thin. This makes the fixed-line sale a delicate balance between business and public service.

Why regulators care about ownership changes

Anatel’s job is to make sure telecom services work for everyone, not just for shareholders. When a company changes hands, the regulator checks that new owners can meet obligations.

Anatel’s release says the conditions exist to protect the public interest and vulnerable users. This is why Anatel imposed conditions on the Oi fixed-line sale.

What the numbers do and do not show

The sale price of R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million) seems low for a national network. But the cost of keeping it running is R$160 million (US$31.3 million) through 2028.

That gap shows why Oi struggled financially. It also explains why Anatel demands guarantees from Método before allowing the transfer.

How customers might be affected in practice

Most fixed-line customers will not notice any change for a while. Oi will keep billing and maintaining the network until the transfer is complete.

If Método meets all conditions, customers will eventually get new bills from Método. Phone numbers should stay the same, but billing and customer service may change.

The bigger picture of Oi’s restructuring

Oi’s bankruptcy is one of the largest in Brazil’s history. The company has been selling assets to pay creditors and reduce debt.

Oi sold its mobile arm to Claro, TIM and Vivo in 2022. What remains is mostly fiber and property.

The fixed-line sale is just one piece of that plan. Other parts of Oi’s business may also be sold in the future.

What is still uncertain

It is not clear how long the final approval will take. Método must present guarantees and plans, and Anatel will review them.

The court and Anatel may also disagree on details. Any dispute could delay the transfer further, leaving customers in limbo.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will my fixed-line service be interrupted during the transition? No, Anatel has required that service continuity be maintained. Oi remains responsible until the transfer is complete, and Método must provide guarantees to keep services running. Who is Método Telecom? Método is a telecom company based in Minas Gerais, Brazil. It won the auction for Oi’s fixed-line unit with a bid of R$60.1 million (US$11.8 million). Why did Anatel approve the sale with conditions? Anatel wants to ensure that customers, especially in remote areas, continue to receive service. The conditions require Método to assume Oi’s obligations and provide guarantees. When will the sale be finalized? There is no set date. Método must meet all conditions, including presenting guarantees and plans, before Anatel gives final approval. What happens after December 2028? Anatel’s current conditions run to December 2028. The regulator has not said what happens after that.

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Says US Ground Operations Would Help
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

COSTA RICA · SECURITY

Key Facts —What happened: President Laura Fernández said such a deployment in Costa Rica could help security. —How big it is: No plan exists, and any deployment needs approval from Costa Rica’s Congress. —What it means: The country without an army is weighing foreign troops on its soil. —The catch: Costa Rica has had no army since 1949, and any deployment needs two-thirds of Congress. —Who it hits: Costa Ricans who cherish their demilitarized identity and oppose US involvement. —What comes next: No proposal has reached Congress, and votes to approve one do not exist.

Costa Rica’s president is open to US ground operations in Costa Rica against drug trafficking. A constitution with no army makes it a distant prospect.

A surprising statement from a president

Costa Rica’s president said on Friday that US ground operations in Costa Rica would be very beneficial. She was talking about fighting crime and drug trafficking.

The comment answered a direct question about US forces operating on Costa Rican soil.

Laura Fernández, who has been president since May, made the remarks in an interview with Reuters at the presidential palace. She quickly added that no concrete plans exist.

Any deployment would require approval from the Legislative Assembly, the country’s congress.

What exactly did she say?

Fernández said it “would obviously be very good for national security” if it pursued a common objective. That objective would be against transnational crime, drug trafficking and terrorism.

She also stressed that nothing concrete is under way.

She said nothing has been proposed and no request has reached the Assembly. The votes to approve one do not currently appear to exist.

Reuters published the interview on 4 September. The Tico Times followed a day later.

A country without an army

Costa Rica abolished its army in 1949, a decision that shapes its national identity. Article 12 of the constitution outlaws a permanent military.

The country relies on police and coast guard forces instead.

The constitution gives the Legislative Assembly power to authorise foreign troops. Any US ground operation would need a two-thirds vote there.

That is a high hurdle in a country that prizes its demilitarised status. The abolition came after a brief civil war in 1948.

The context: US security cooperation in 2026

Costa Rica already cooperates with the US on security, mainly through maritime and law-enforcement efforts. In December 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved port calls by up to 195 US vessels for anti-drug work during 2026.

It is a routine annual authorisation.

The country also participates in ‘Escudo de las Américas’ (Shield of the Americas), a US-led regional initiative against organized crime. None of that has involved US ground troops.

No US ground deployment is under way. The remarks come as the US pushes similar security cooperation with Ecuador.

What the December 2025 vote allowed

The December 2025 vote was narrow in scope. It allowed US Coast Guard vessels to dock at Costa Rican ports for anti-drug operations.

It did not authorise any ground missions or troop presence. The approval was for maritime cooperation only.

That distinction matters for the current debate. Ground operations would require a separate and much broader vote.

The vote reflected years of joint patrols against drug smuggling. Such cooperation has been routine since the 1990s.

US military activity in the Caribbean in 2026

Across the Caribbean, US military activity in 2026 has focused on maritime interdiction. The US Coast Guard and Navy have worked with regional partners to stop drug shipments.

There is no public evidence of US ground combat units operating in the region. The cooperation has been mostly at sea and in the air.

Costa Rica’s role has been as a host for port calls and joint exercises. That pattern continued through 2026.

Fernández’s remarks about ground operations are a departure from that norm. They are hypothetical, not a description of current activity.

What Chaves said before her

Rodrigo Chaves, president until May 2026, had raised the subject earlier in the year. In March, he defended Costa Rica’s part in Escudo de las Américas.

He said he did not rule out requesting US military support if necessary. He also insisted nobody was necessarily talking about military force.

He stressed support for the police.

In March, Chaves brushed off a constitutional challenge from the PLN with a dismissive remark about critics. The challenge came from Miguel Guillén, secretary general of the National Liberation Party.

Reaction at home: legal and political pushback

The prospect of US troops on Costa Rican soil has already sparked legal challenges. In March, the Constitutional Chamber took up a case against the US security agreement.

It asks whether the deal breaches the ban on an army.

Miguel Guillén, secretary general of the National Liberation Party, filed a separate constitutional challenge against Escudo de las Américas. Former president and Nobel laureate Óscar Arias has also warned that aspects of the agreement may violate the constitution.

Government defends cooperation

Public Security Minister Mario Zamora has defended the US-backed cooperation. He says it respects sovereignty and aims to fight organized crime.

He argues it does not reintroduce an army or violate constitutional limits.

The legal challenges show deep unease about foreign military involvement. Costa Rica has prided itself on peace.

What happens next?

For now, Fernández’s comments are hypothetical. No formal proposal has been made, and no request has reached the Legislative Assembly.

Constitutional hurdles and political opposition make any US ground operation unlikely soon. But the debate itself reflects the tension between security needs and a cherished demilitarized identity.

How the Legislative Assembly would decide

The Legislative Assembly is Costa Rica’s single-chamber congress, with 57 members elected every four years. Under Article 121 of the constitution, it must authorize the entry of foreign troops into the country.

Approval requires two-thirds, or 38 of 57 deputies. Humanitarian missions clear a lower bar of 29 votes.

Currently, no such proposal exists. Fernández herself said the votes to approve one do not appear to exist.

In practice, the assembly has approved US Coast Guard vessels for 2026. Ground troops are a different matter, and the bar for approval is much higher.

Who would be affected if troops came

A US ground operation would affect Costa Ricans directly. Many take pride in having no army, and any change would be deeply felt.

The debate also affects the political scene. Opposition parties are ready to challenge any move, as the National Liberation Party has shown.

An election year adds pressure

Costa Rica holds its next presidential election in February 2026. That vote is now only months away.

Fernández is not running, but her party’s candidate will face the consequences. Security issues often dominate campaign debates.

Opposition candidates have already used the cooperation agreements to attack the government. They call it a threat to sovereignty.

The timing of her remarks may complicate the government’s position. Voters will watch how the debate unfolds.

What remains uncertain

No source confirms any specific US ground operation was proposed. The president’s words were about a possibility, not a plan.

It is also unclear whether any US official has asked Costa Rica for such access. No such request has been reported.

The legal challenges are still pending before the courts. Their outcomes could shape any future decision.

For now, the debate is about ideas and principles. There is no concrete proposal on the table.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who said US ground operations would help Costa Rica? President Laura Fernández, in a Reuters interview published on 4 September 2026. She said such operations could be good for national security if they targeted transnational crime. Does Costa Rica have an army? No, Costa Rica abolished its army in 1949. The constitution outlaws a permanent military, and the country relies on police and coast guard forces. What would it take for US troops to operate in Costa Rica? Any deployment would require approval from the Legislative Assembly, Costa Rica’s congress. Currently, no proposal exists and votes are lacking. What is Escudo de las Américas? It is a US-led regional security initiative against organized crime and drug trafficking. Costa Rica participates, but it has not involved US ground troops. Why are some Costa Ricans opposed to US military involvement? Many see it as a threat to the country’s demilitarized identity and constitutional principles. Legal challenges have been filed against security agreements with the US.

World.title: Kast Approval in Chile Hits Lowest Yet at 34%
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CHILE · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Kast’s approval fell to 34%, his lowest since taking office in March. —How big it is: Disapproval hit 61%, the highest of his term so far. —What it means: Voters are unhappy with the economy and security, pollsters say. —The catch: Official crime data show homicides falling, not rising, this year. —Who it hits: Kast’s government, which promised a tough crackdown on crime. —What comes next: Kast has no election to face until October 2028, giving him room but no deadline.

Six months in, Chile’s president has his lowest approval yet. Voters blame the economy more than crime.
