A rocky start for Chile’s most right-wing leader since Pinochet

José Antonio Kast took office on 11 March 2026, promising a hard line on crime and immigration. He is Chile’s most conservative president since Augusto Pinochet, a description that shapes expectations.

Six months later, the mood has soured. The Cadem tracking poll, a widely watched survey, shows approval at 34% and disapproval at 61%.

What the approval numbers say

The 34% approval is a drop of four points from the previous Cadem reading. It is also the lowest level since Kast was inaugurated.

Disapproval was already at 60% in July, so the move is small. The direction is what matters.

Cadem’s own numbers show why. Some 82% rate household purchasing power badly, the worst since 2014, and 91% expect employment to worsen.

The economy is a drag

One clear factor is the economy. Chile’s monthly activity index, the Imacec, shrank 1.5% in July 2026 against a year earlier.

That was its worst fall in over three years, driven by mining and bad weather. The contraction is the only hard economic number directly linked to Kast’s falling approval in the sources.

Full GDP, unemployment, and inflation figures for his first six months are not confirmed. But the July Imacec alone is enough to worry voters.

Security: a tale of two trends

Kast ran on a promise to crack down on organized crime. But the data is mixed.

In his first month, from 11 March to 6 April, the prosecutor’s office recorded 26 homicide or attempted homicide cases. That was up 36.8% from the same period in 2025, when there were 19.

The government’s answer on crime

The government says that short-term spike is misleading. Crime Prevention Subsecretary Ana Victoria Quintana noted that from 1 January to 5 April 2026, total homicides actually fell 14.2% versus 2025.

She also pointed to 2025 ending with an 11.5% drop in completed homicides. That continues a downward trend since a peak in 2022.

What the longer-term data shows

By early September 2026, official figures showed homicides down 17.2% year-to-date, or 117 fewer cases. Violent robberies fell 13.2%.

Kast’s June state-of-the-nation address cited 378 homicide victims through May 31, down from 444 in the same period of 2025. A July balance put the number at 442 through June 28, down 13% from 508.

Why critics still cry foul

Independent analysts note that Chile’s homicide rate had already fallen for three straight years before Kast arrived. That complicates his claim of a turnaround.

They argue that his security narrative is not always backed by the data. The criticism is that policy is driven by political messaging rather than evidence.

What six months does and doesn’t tell you

Six months is a short time to judge a president, especially one facing inherited problems. Chile’s economy was already slowing before Kast took office, and crime trends were improving.

The approval drop is real, but it reflects perceptions as much as results. Voters may be reacting to news of economic contraction and a security narrative that doesn’t match their daily fears.

What to watch next

Kast’s government will need to show progress on both fronts to rebuild support. The next municipal and regional elections are in October 2028.

That is a long runway, and a long time to stay unpopular. For now, the numbers are a warning, not a verdict.

Understanding the Cadem poll

Cadem is a Chilean polling firm that surveys public opinion weekly. Its tracking poll is widely cited by media and politicians as a barometer of presidential popularity.

The poll released on 3 September 2026 surveyed a national sample. Cadem’s published summary does not give a margin of error.

Poll results can shift quickly and are sensitive to recent news. A single bad month can drag approval down, even if longer-term trends are stable.

Cadem is a private polling firm, not an official measure. But it shapes political narratives in Chile.

How Chile’s presidency works

Chile’s president serves a four-year term and cannot run for immediate re-election. The president holds significant power but needs Congress to pass laws.

Kast’s coalition does not control Congress on its own. That forces him to negotiate with opposition parties on key reforms.

The presidency is based in La Moneda palace in Santiago. The next presidential election is set for 18 November 2029.

Understanding this balance of power helps explain why Kast’s agenda faces hurdles. He must build coalitions to deliver on his promises.

Who is affected by Kast’s low approval

The low approval affects Kast’s ability to push his agenda. Lawmakers may be less willing to support unpopular measures.

Investors watch approval ratings as a sign of political stability. A weak president may struggle to implement economic reforms.

Ordinary Chileans feel the impact through public services and security policies. Their daily concerns drive the poll numbers.

The October 2028 municipal and regional elections are the next real test. Kast’s party could lose ground if approval stays low.

What the numbers do and do not prove

The 34% approval is a snapshot, not a trend. It shows current dissatisfaction but does not predict future performance.

The data do not prove that Kast’s policies have failed. They only show that voters are unhappy right now.

Similarly, the crime data show declines but do not capture all forms of crime. Perceptions of insecurity may lag behind statistics.

How Chilean presidents’ approval typically moves in the first year

Chilean presidents often enjoy a honeymoon period after taking office. Approval tends to start high and then decline as difficult decisions take effect.

Historical patterns show that first-year approval can drop sharply. Economic troubles and security issues often accelerate that slide.

Kast’s decline fits a common regional trend. New leaders face high expectations that are hard to meet quickly.

But each presidency is different. Kast’s numbers are low, yet he still has time to recover before the next elections.

What Kast promised on security and what has been enacted

Kast campaigned on a promise to crack down on organized crime and illegal immigration. He pledged a tough ‘mano dura’ approach from day one.

Since taking office, he has pushed for stronger police powers and tougher sentences. Some measures have been enacted, but many require congressional approval.

His government has highlighted falling homicide rates as proof of progress. Critics say the decline started before he arrived.

The gap between promises and results fuels the debate. Voters may judge him on what they see, not just statistics.

The economic numbers behind the criticism

The main economic figure tied to Kast’s approval drop is the July Imacec contraction. That index fell 1.5% compared to a year earlier.

This is the only hard economic number confirmed in the sources. Full GDP, unemployment, and inflation data are not yet available.

Cadem’s poll shows deep pessimism about household finances. 82% rate purchasing power badly, the worst reading since 2014.

These perceptions matter as much as official data. Voters feel the squeeze even if some statistics lag.

Who the named critics are and what they say

The Nationcraft analysis, an independent commentary, argues Kast’s security narrative is a ‘mirage’. It says policy is not aligned with crime data.

That analysis points out that homicides had fallen for three years before Kast. This complicates his claim of a new turnaround.

Other critics focus on governance style. They say his ideological agenda clashes with the need for consensus in Congress.

These are expert opinions, not official statements. They reflect a broader debate about Kast’s approach.

What the government says in its own defence

Government officials reject the idea that security is worsening. They point to falling homicide rates as evidence of progress.

Subsecretary Ana Victoria Quintana has relativized short-term spikes. She emphasizes the longer-term downward trend since 2022.

Kast’s own addresses cite declining homicide numbers. He frames these as results of his policies.

The government argues that perceptions lag behind reality. It says crime data will eventually change public opinion.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kast’s approval rating after six months? His approval is 34%, according to a Cadem poll released on 3 September 2026. Disapproval stands at 61%. Why did Kast’s approval drop? Cadem links the fall to negative economic news, including a 1.5% contraction in July’s Imacec. Security concerns also weigh on public opinion. Is crime actually up or down under Kast? Official data show homicides down 17.2% year-to-date as of early September. But a spike in his first month raised alarms. What does the government say about the crime data? Officials say short-term increases are misleading and point to longer-term declines. They highlight a 14.2% drop in homicides from January to early April. What are the main criticisms of Kast’s government? Critics cite a security narrative not backed by data and a difficult economy. These are themes from expert commentary, not a single unified assessment.

World.title: Guyana Deportee Deal Begins as First Six Arrive From the US
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

GUYANA · MIGRATION

Key Facts —What happened: Guyana and the US finalised a migration framework, and the first six deportees arrived on Friday. —How big it is: Up to 12 people a month for an initial 12 months, with no carry-over of unused places. —What it means: Guyana temporarily hosts people while their immigration status is resolved, not permanent resettlement. —The catch: The deal is not a labour scheme; it is a temporary hosting arrangement under a voluntary-return programme. —Who it hits: Deportees from the US, plus Guyanese opposition worried about sovereignty and transparency. —What comes next: More arrivals are possible monthly, but the full framework text has not been published.

Guyana has begun taking in people deported from the United States under a new framework. The first six, Cubans and Afghans, arrived on Friday.

What happened

Guyana and the United States have finalised a migration cooperation framework. The first six people, Cubans and Afghans, arrived in Guyana on Friday.

The joint statement from both governments confirms the deal. Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud said the six were vetted by Guyana and had no criminal records.

This is a temporary hosting arrangement, not a permanent resettlement. People stay while their immigration status is resolved elsewhere.

The United States bears the relocation costs and the International Organization for Migration covers housing and support. The agency says it does not take on the government’s own responsibilities for admission or removal.

Who are the first arrivals

The first six people are Cubans and Afghans deported from the US. They were deported mainly over immigration issues, not crimes.

Persaud said Guyana vetted each person and approved them. He did not name the individuals.

These people arrived on Friday, 4 September 2026. Their identities have not been made public.

They are part of a larger group of third-country nationals. The US has been seeking places for them across the region.

The terms of the deal

The framework runs for an initial 12 months. Up to 12 people can arrive each month, with no carry-over of unused places.

The United States bears the relocation costs and the International Organization for Migration covers housing and support. The agency says it does not take on the government’s own responsibilities for admission or removal.

This programme helps people return voluntarily to their home countries. But these deportees cannot go home, so they stay temporarily in Guyana.

Neither government has set out what legal status or rights the arrivals hold in Guyana while they wait.

What this deal is not

The framework describes the people it covers as vetted, skilled and non-criminal. But it is a temporary hosting arrangement, not a work programme.

The joint statement says the stay is temporary and does not constitute permanent resettlement. People stay while their cases are processed, then go home or move on.

The people are not coming to work in Guyana. They are waiting for decisions on their immigration status.

The United States has deported them from its soil. Guyana is simply a temporary stop while their future is decided.

Guyana’s right to refuse

Guyana keeps the right to reject anyone proposed for relocation. The US cannot offload people without Guyana’s approval.

The announcement says people relocated under the framework keep the right to seek international protection. This right to refuse is a key part of the deal.

It means Guyana controls who comes in. The framework also says people will not be sent to a country where they face danger.

That is a standard protection in such agreements. The International Organization for Migration says it does not assume government responsibilities for admission or removal.

What has not been published

The two governments have not published the full text of the framework. Neither side has released a cost figure.

Third Country Deportation Watch, which tracks these arrangements, lists Guyana among the deals it cannot categorise. The text has not been disclosed.

No one has said how long each person will stay. The review process after 12 months is also vague.

Neither government has published the selection criteria beyond the requirement of no criminal record.

Why this matters

Guyana is the latest Caribbean nation to take in US deportees. St Kitts and Nevis and Belize have already received people, and St Lucia is expected to take its first group this week.

The US pays through the International Organization for Migration, which handles reception and housing. This model may be used elsewhere.

This deal shows a new pattern in the region. The US is finding third countries to host people it cannot easily deport.

For Guyana, it brings international attention. The country must balance its oil wealth with its duties as a host.

What comes next

More arrivals could come in the coming months, up to the monthly cap. The framework will be reviewed after 12 months.

Observers will watch how Guyana handles the arrivals and whether opposition pressure forces more transparency.

The first six are just the start. Up to 12 more could arrive each month for a year.

The deal’s success will depend on clear rules. Without them, confusion and criticism will grow.

How the deal works in practice

The arrangement is part of the Assisted Voluntary Return Programme run by the International Organization for Migration. That agency handles the logistics of moving people.

The United States funds the programme fully. Guyana provides the temporary home.

People are housed and supported while their cases are processed. The goal is for them to eventually return home or go to a third country.

This is not a quick process. Some people may stay for months while their status is resolved.

Regional context

Other Caribbean nations have made similar deals with the US. Antigua has discussed accepting a small number of deportees.

The US has been pushing for such arrangements across the region. It wants to reduce the number of people it holds in detention.

Each country sets its own terms. Guyana’s deal includes a cap of 12 people per month.

The regional pattern is clear. Small nations are being asked to help with a US problem.

What Guyana gets out of it

Guyana gets financial support from the US for hosting. The exact amount is not public.

Officials say the deal helps address skills gaps in the economy. But the first arrivals are not necessarily skilled workers.

The real benefit may be diplomatic. Guyana strengthens its ties with the US.

Neither government has announced aid or trade concessions alongside the framework. The main gain is the relationship.

What is still unclear

The full text of the agreement has not been released. No one knows the exact legal status of the arrivals.

The cost to the US is unknown. The length of stay for each person is also unclear.

Neither government has published the selection criteria beyond the requirement of no criminal record.

The review after 12 months is vague. No one has said what criteria will be used to judge the deal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Guyana-US migration deal signed? Yes. Both governments finalised the framework and announced it in a joint statement. Who are the first deportees in Guyana? They are Cubans and Afghans deported from the US. They were vetted by Guyana and have no criminal records. How many people can come under the deal? Up to 12 people a month for an initial 12 months. Unused places do not carry over. Who pays for the programme? The United States pays all costs through the International Organization for Migration. Guyana pays nothing. Is this a labour migration deal? No. It is a temporary hosting arrangement for people whose immigration status is being resolved. It is not permanent resettlement.

World.title: Brazil Court Fines Ex-Governor Cabral Over Prison Perks
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: A Rio appeals court found ex-governor Sergio Cabral liable for administrative improbity over prison perks. —How big it is: Cabral must pay a fine of 12 times his last salary plus R$1 million (US$195,300) in damages. —What it means: This is a civil case, not criminal, so it adds fines but no prison time. —The catch: Cabral is free with an ankle tag, and his lawyers say they will appeal the ruling. —Who it hits: Six others, including a former prison secretary, were also found liable and fined. —What comes next: Further appeals would go to Brazil’s higher courts, while Cabral fights other convictions.

A Rio appeals panel found ex-governor Sergio Cabral liable for the perks he enjoyed in his cell. The penalty is money, not more prison time.

A new ruling in a long legal saga

Sergio Cabral governed Rio de Janeiro from 2007 to 2014. On 4 September 2026, an appeals court found him liable in a civil case.

The 4th Public Law Chamber of the Rio de Janeiro Court of Justice ruled against him. The charge was administrative improbity, a Brazilian legal concept covering misconduct by public officials.

This is not a criminal conviction. Administrative improbity is a civil offense, so the punishment is financial, not prison time.

Cabral must pay a fine equal to 12 times his last government salary. He also owes R$1 million (US$195,300) in collective moral damages.

What is administrative improbity?

Administrative improbity is a legal tool in Brazil. It punishes public servants who abuse their positions for personal gain.

It is separate from criminal law. A person can be found liable for improbity even if criminal charges fail.

Penalties usually involve fines, loss of public office, and suspension of political rights. In this case, the reported penalties are financial only; no suspension of political rights has been reported.

The prison luxuries that led to the ruling

The case centers on the ‘Cabral video library’. That was a 65-inch TV and home theater system in his cell.

Court documents also list a special mattress, banned foods, gym equipment, household appliances and easier visits. Prosecutors said officials falsified records to hide these benefits.

Prosecutors also alleged unregistered visits and night-time trips out under guard. All this happened while he was serving time for other corruption crimes.

Who else was found liable

Six other people were found liable alongside Cabral. Among them is Erir Ribeiro Costa Filho, the former state penitentiary secretary.

The others are prison officers Alex de Lima Carvalho, Fabio Ferraz Sodré. Sauler Antonio Sakalen, Fernando Lima de Farias and Nilton Cesar Vieira da Silva.

Each of the six must pay a fine of five times their salary. They also owe R$100,000 (US$19,530) in collective moral damages.

Cabral’s defense responds

Cabral’s lawyers said the civil ruling is unreasonable. They noted he was acquitted of criminal accusations related to the same facts.

In a statement, they said: ‘The former governor was acquitted of the unfounded accusations in the criminal sphere. The civil conviction is unreasonable, and an appeal has already been filed.’

Cabral’s other convictions, most still on appeal

Cabral is among the most-convicted politicians in Brazil. Many of those rulings are still under appeal.

His convictions total more than 400 years in prison. These convictions are for crimes like corruption, money laundering, and criminal association.

Most come from the Rio arm of Operation Car Wash, run under names like Calicute and Eficiência. Prosecutors said he took bribes on state contracts, including the Maracanã rebuild and favela works.

How did Cabral end up in prison?

Cabral was arrested in November 2016, two and a half years after leaving office. He was accused of leading a criminal organization that siphoned millions from public contracts.

His arrest marked a turning point in Brazil’s fight against corruption. It showed that even powerful governors could face justice.

Since then, he has been in and out of prison. Sometimes under house arrest, but always facing new charges.

What this means for Brazil’s justice system

The ruling covers conduct inside prison rather than the contracts that put him there. The court treated the perks as an abuse of public office.

It also highlights the complexity of Brazil’s legal system. Civil and criminal cases run in parallel.

Cabral is at liberty while his convictions are appealed. This civil case adds a financial penalty he will have to pay from whatever assets he has left.

The catch: no new prison time

Administrative improbity is a civil matter. The punishment is purely financial.

Cabral’s lawyers are appealing. They say he was acquitted of the criminal charges over the same facts.

The civil ruling may be overturned. For now, it stands as another mark on his record.

What comes next for Cabral

Cabral left prison in December 2022. The Supreme Court ruled his preventive detention had run too long without a final judgment.

He is at liberty under precautionary measures. These include an electronic tag, a surrendered passport and a ban on leaving the country.

This civil ruling does not change that. Further appeals would go to Brazil’s higher courts, the Superior Court of Justice and the Supreme Court.

Some of his sentences have been reduced, but the total time he faces is still immense. Brazilian law caps time actually served at 40 years, raised from 30 in 2020.

The older 30-year cap still applies to crimes committed before then. For foreign observers, this case shows that Brazil’s justice system, while slow, does eventually hold powerful people accountable.

The man behind the rulings

Cabral was elected twice and spent heavily on Rio’s infrastructure. He led Rio’s preparations for the 2014 World Cup and the 2016 Olympics, resigning months before the first kicked off.

His fall from grace was swift after corruption allegations emerged. He went from hosting global events to sharing a cell, a dramatic reversal of fortune.

How the process works in Brazil

In Brazil, public officials can face separate civil and criminal cases for the same act. Civil cases focus on financial penalties, while criminal cases can lead to prison.

This dual system means a person might be acquitted in one court and found liable in another. Cabral’s lawyers say he was cleared of the criminal charges over the same facts.

The Rio court still found him liable in this civil case. The ruling came from the 4th Public Law Chamber of the Rio de Janeiro Court of Justice, an appeals panel.

The rapporteur, appeals judge Caetano Ernesto da Fonseca Costa, wrote that those involved ‘acted consciously to conceal official acts’. He added that the conduct offended impersonality and society’s trust in the prison system.

The impact on Cabral’s assets

The fines from this ruling add to the financial penalties Cabral already faces. Courts have ordered him to repay millions in past corruption cases.

His assets have been frozen, and authorities have seized properties and luxury goods. Courts have not published a figure for what remains of his assets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is administrative improbity in Brazil? Administrative improbity is a civil offense that punishes public officials for misconduct, such as corruption or abuse of power. It is separate from criminal law, so penalties are financial, not prison time. What privileges did Sergio Cabral have in prison? According to the ruling, Cabral had a 65-inch television and home theatre. A special mattress, banned foods, gym equipment and household appliances in his cell. Is Sergio Cabral in prison now? No. Cabral left prison in December 2022 and is at liberty under precautionary measures. Including an electronic tag and a ban on leaving the country. Will this ruling add to Cabral’s prison time? No, this is a civil ruling, so it only adds fines. Cabral was ordered to pay a fine and damages, but no additional jail time. What is the ‘Cabral video library’? It is the nickname for the home theater system, including a 65-inch TV, that Cabral had installed in his prison cell. It was part of the privileges that led to this ruling.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Two Biggest Soccer Clubs Meet Saturday Night in Alajuela
World.content:
Costa Rica’s two most popular soccer clubs, Alajuelense and Saprissa, play each other Saturday night in Alajuela. Kickoff is at 8 p.m. at the Estadio Alejandro Morera Soto, Alajuelense’s home ground. Costa Ricans call this game the Clásico Nacional. It happens a handful of times a year, and it stops the country in a way no other match does.

Saprissa comes in first place. They have won five of their six games so far and lost one, which gives them 15 points. They have also scored more goals than anyone else in the league. Their most recent game was a 2-1 win over Escorpiones, and they have had five days off since.

Alajuelense sits fourth with 11 points, from three wins, two draws and one loss. They haven’t won in their last two games — both were draws, not losses — and that’s why Saprissa has pulled ahead. Here’s why Saturday matters more than a normal game. Four teams are bunched within four points of each other at the top. Cartaginés is second with 12 points and Sporting FC is third with 11, level with Alajuelense.

So, the result swings things a long way. If Alajuelense wins, they close to within a single point of first place. If the game ends in a draw, nothing changes. If Saprissa wins, their lead grows to seven points, which is a real cushion this early on. That matters because of how the season is set up. Each team plays 18 games, and only the top four go through to the semifinals at the end. Herediano, who won the last title back in the first half of the year, is also in the mix.

Alajuelense should take some confidence from playing at home. They have won four of their last five games at the Morera Soto, and three of the last four times they hosted Saprissa there. The wider record between the two is closer than that suggests. Their last five meetings produced two draws and three wins split between them, most recently a 1-1 draw in April.

Neither coach is missing a player through suspension, so Hernán Medford at Saprissa and Ismael Rescalvo at Alajuelense can both pick the team they want. Juan Gabriel Calderón will referee, with Juan Carlos Mora and Andrés Arrieta as his assistants and Brayan Cruz as the fourth official.

Saprissa has another big game coming quickly after this one. They are still in the Copa Centroamericana, a regional club tournament, and they play Cartaginés on Wednesday at their own stadium in Tibás. Medford may hold something back on Saturday with that in mind. The game is on FUTV and TDMAX in Costa Rica. If you are watching from the United States, that’s 10 p.m. Eastern, 9 p.m. Central, 8 p.m. Mountain and 7 p.m. Pacific.

The two clubs meet again on November 1, that time at Saprissa’s stadium. Depending on how Saturday goes, that one could matter even more.

World.title: Thousands of Olive Ridley Turtles Come Ashore in One of the Year’s Largest Arribadas
World.content:
One of the largest arribadas of the year began in the early morning hours this morning at the Ostional National Wildlife Refuge in Guanacaste, as thousands of olive ridley sea turtles emerged from the Pacific to nest on the beach long known as their favorite stretch of Costa Rican coastline.

Guides and residents alike described this week’s event as among the biggest seen so far in 2026. More turtles were expected to continue arriving through Friday night and into Saturday morning. The spectacle draws both Costa Ricans and tourists eager to watch the turtles come ashore, dig their nests, lay their eggs and return to the sea. That cycle has made Ostional one of the most closely watched nesting sites in the world.

The timing fits a well-established seasonal pattern as well as arribadas occur throughout the year at Ostional, but September, October and November typically bring the largest events, when more than 100,000 turtles can come ashore in a single night and a single arribada can stretch on for up to two weeks.

Dry season arribadas, running roughly from January through July, are considerably smaller. Those events usually bring fewer than 20,000 turtles over three or four nights. Friday’s event also arrived on schedule as arribadas at Ostional cluster around the last quarter moon, which fell on September 4, and can begin two days before or after that phase.

The refuge is patrolled daily by park guards who track nesting activity along the beach. When the number of turtles climbs to around 1,000 in a given arribada, the Asociación de Desarrollo Integral de Ostional, the local community development association, can declare what is known as an arribada aprovechable.

That designation sets several things in motion at once. It triggers Costa Rica’s official monitoring operation and allows members of the local community to carry out a legal, regulated harvest of a portion of the eggs. It also closes the beach to anyone not accompanied by a certified local guide, with groups capped at nine visitors.

The guide rule is not a formality but a nesting female that is startled will abandon the attempt and return to the water without laying, and a beach at this density is packed with fresh nests that are easily crushed underfoot. Flash photography and white flashlights are prohibited for the same reason.

The harvest itself is limited to the first days of an arribada, when eggs laid early are likely to be dug up and destroyed by the waves of females arriving behind them. The model has operated at Ostional for more than three decades and remains one of the only sites in the world where a regulated harvest of sea turtle eggs is permitted.

The refuge covers 468 hectares (1,156 acres) of land and 8,000 hectares (19,768 acres) of ocean along 16 kilometers (10 miles) of coast, taking in not only Ostional but also the beaches of Nosara, Pelada and Guiones. Final turtle counts and nest totals for this week’s arribada were not yet available. Those figures are typically released by Costa Rican wildlife authorities and the local association once monitoring concludes, generally a few days after the largest nightly arrivals taper off.

Anyone planning to travel to Ostional in the coming days should confirm tour availability with the local guide association before setting out. Access during an arribada is by guided group only, and slots fill quickly when a large event is underway.

World.title: Watch Spider Monkeys Return to Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula
World.content:
Costa Rica is famous for its biodiversity. There’s an incredible amount of life packed into this tiny country. However, this diversity of species isn’t uniformly present throughout the nation. Many factors, including habitat type and the impact of human beings, affect the presence of a certain species present in a given area.

I’ve spent the last 8 years or so using camera traps to sample the level of species diversity around the country, but I’ve mostly focused on a specific part of the country, Guanacaste. After many camera revisions from locations throughout Guanacaste, I’ve come up with an informal gradient of species diversity that’s based on the animals that my cameras are best at recording, mammals.

Areas with the very highest levels of species diversity are still home to Costa Rica’s largest mammals, the white-lipped peccary, the jaguar, and Baird’s tapir. As the level of species diversity begins to drop, the white-lipped peccaries are the first to disappear, followed by the jaguars and tapirs. In my experience, the first primate species to disappear when dropping down a level of diversity are Central American spider monkeys.

These levels of diversity are nothing official, just patterns I’ve noticed while carrying out camera trap projects throughout Guanacaste. At this point, when I begin a new project, I have a pretty solid idea of what species are going to be missing from the environment based on results from work I’ve done in that general area.

This year, when I had the opportunity to work with a coalition of organizations including the Fondo de Biodiversidad Sostenible and FONAFIFO on a wildlife monitoring project in the Nicoya Peninsula, I thought I knew what species were going to present on the properties. The project is still ongoing, but my assumptions were proven incorrect during the revision of the very first camera.

As I scrolled through species that I knew were going to be present, agoutis, ocelots, nine-banded armadillos, one video stopped me in tracks. It featured two Central American spider monkeys fleeing from the ground up into the trees, either frightened by the presence of my camera or something else nearby.

I was shocked. The nearest property where I had recorded or seen spider monkeys was in northern Guanacaste some 100 kilometers from the place I was sitting. On top of that, I had done some internet sleuthing in the past about locally extinct species on the peninsula and had read that spider monkeys were amongst the species, like jaguars and Baird’s tapirs, that had disappeared decades ago.

Obviously delighted to be wrong, I did some more research when I got home and found that Rescate Wildlife Rescue Center (formerly Zoo Ave) had a reintroduction program that had done some work in the Nicoya Peninsula and one of the species that they had focused on was spider monkeys. Excited about learning more, I reached out to Rescate Program Director Amy van Esch to tell her about my camera trap video and learn more about the program. Amy confirmed that they had been working on wildlife reintroductions for years and even offered to share some more information about their work. Here’s what she had to say –

“Rescate Wildlife has been working in the Nicoya region for over 35 years. Within the foundation we have a large protected area of over 800 hectares (about 2,000 acres) that we use as a release site for many different species.The spider monkey was completely extinct in this region at that time.

In the year 2000 we released a group of 44 spider monkeys, 31 former pets (who came to our rescue center through the pet trade), and 13 born onsite through our endangered species breeding program. Fast forward 26 years and we now have various wild troops with over 100 individuals! It’s pretty amazing to think, this population has all come out of animals that were formerly pets, now living wild, reproducing and dispersing into other areas.

This last year we also started something completely new: we built one of the world’s largest pre-release enclosures, over 4 hectares in size. We currently have a troop of 12 individuals preparing for release (all former pets, some even arriving dressed in baby clothes). This will be the first time we release new spider monkeys in over 15 years.

This enclosure is unique in its size, which is full of large growth trees, allowing them to learn “to fly” between trees and gain real agility before being released into the wild. It’s something we are really looking forward to in the coming year: finally seeing them fully wild!“

How cool is that? Check out the ten second video below that proves that all of their hard work has resulted in spider monkeys once again living wild on the Nicoya Peninsula.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica.

World.title: Costa Rica Renews Push to Make Chirripó Its First UNESCO Global Geopark
World.content:
Costa Rica and the State Distance University are renewing an effort to have Chirripó recognized as Costa Rica’s first UNESCO Global Geopark, a designation intended to protect its geological heritage while spreading tourism benefits to nearby communities.

The State Distance University (UNED), is working with the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), to develop the proposed Chirripó Global Geopark. The project would combine scientific research, environmental education, local culture and sustainable tourism across Chirripó National Park and its surrounding communities.

The proposed territory covers more than 105,000 hectares, equivalent to about 405 square miles. It includes Cerro Chirripó, Costa Rica’s highest point at 3,822.6 meters, or approximately 12,541 feet, above sea level. The mountain’s landscape still carries evidence of the glaciers that covered the area during the last Ice Age Its U-shaped valleys, moraines, terraces and glacial lakes give scientists a record of how Costa Rica’s highest mountains developed over thousands of years.

UNED and SINAC currently describe Chirripó as an “aspiring” geopark. That means organizers are building the management structure, documenting geological sites and working with communities before seeking final approval. It does not mean UNESCO recognition has already been granted.

Chirripó is not among the 14 new geopark applications that UNESCO received for formal evaluation in 2026, and authorities have not announced when they expect to submit a new application. UNESCO’s process normally stretches across three calendar years, beginning with a letter of intent and a formal application, followed by document reviews, a field visit and a final decision.

This is also not Costa Rica’s first try to get the designation for Chirripó. It submitted an application in 2017, followed by a UNESCO evaluation visit in July 2018. The UNESCO Global Geoparks Council later concluded that the proposal did not meet the program’s requirements and rejected it. Recommendations included creating a clearer identity for the geopark separate from the national park and improving its visibility and organization.

The renewed initiative appears designed to address some of those weaknesses by giving local organizations a larger role. A committee now includes representatives from universities, SINAC, municipalities, schools, community groups and local businesses. The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock and MINAE’s Directorate of Geology and Mines are also participating.

During a recent meeting at SINAC’s Villa Mills station, committee members spoke with representatives of UNESCO’s Costa Rica office about the project’s progress. Working groups have also been created to focus on geological education and the management of risks at important sites. Organizers are planning a workshop to begin designing tourism routes around the region’s geological attractions.

UNED natural resources specialist Zaidett Barrientos Llosa said the project should involve schools, community businesses and residents rather than being managed solely by government agencies and scientists. Environment and Energy Minister Mónica Navarro Del Valle made a similar point, saying residents should become the principal participants and beneficiaries in managing the area.

The idea is to offer more than the demanding hike to Costa Rica’s highest summit. Enzo Vargas Salazar, administrator of Chirripó National Park, said geological routes and educational activities could draw attention to the area’s lakes, valleys, rock formations, biodiversity and cultural heritage while generating income for surrounding communities.

UNESCO Global Geoparks are territories where geological sites of international importance are managed through conservation, education and sustainable development. The program emphasizes local participation and requires applicants to show that the territory has already functioned as a geopark before submitting a formal application.

UNESCO currently recognizes 241 Global Geoparks in 51 countries. Costa Rica does not yet have one. The designation would be separate from Chirripó’s existing international protections. The park is already part of the Talamanca Range–La Amistad Reserves World Heritage Site, which Costa Rica shares with Panama.
