World.title: International News: U.S. strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after attacks on Navy ships
World.content:
International News: U.S. strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after attacks on Navy ships

By Zoila Palma: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers today after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy vessels, according to the U.S. military. The attacks reportedly caused no injuries among American personnel.

U.S. Central Command said an American aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer evaded multiple attacks launched by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In response, U.S. forces targeted three vessels, saying two crude oil carriers were permanently disabled.

The vessels identified were the M/T Downy, struck off the coast of Kharg Island, and the M/T Stark 1, targeted near Jask, NBC reports.

CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said the U.S. response was intended to impose an economic cost on Iran while defending American forces. He warned that the United States would continue to defend its personnel and could target Iran’s exposed oil fleet if necessary.

The strikes further raise tensions around Kharg Island, a strategically important hub for Iran’s oil exports in the Persian Gulf.

World.title: International News: Drone attack in Colombia kills 3 soldiers
World.content:
International News: Drone attack in Colombia kills 3 soldiers

By Zoila Palma: At least three Colombian soldiers were killed and four others wounded following an attack involving explosives dropped from drones and a subsequent clash inside a military compound in northeastern Colombia, the country’s army today.

The attack occurred late Friday at a military unit in Ocaña, Norte de Santander, near the Venezuelan border. Local authorities attributed the assault to the National Liberation Army (ELN).Two soldiers died at the scene, while a third succumbed to injuries after receiving medical attention, AP reports.

President Abelardo de la Espriella condemned the attack and vowed that the government would respond with the full force of the state against those responsible.

The ELN, an armed group that has been active in Colombia since 1964, maintains a significant presence in the Catatumbo region.

The region has experienced ongoing violence as the ELN and dissident factions of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) compete for control of territory and lucrative coca-producing areas near the Venezuelan border.

World.title: When scrolling becomes an addiction: Growing risk for children!
World.content:
When scrolling becomes an addiction: Growing risk for children!

By Zoila Palma: Meta’s reported $17.1 billion settlement has renewed attention on the growing concerns surrounding social media use among children and teenagers, particularly the ways digital platforms may encourage young users to remain online for extended periods.

According to Jason Nagata, M.D., MSc, a pediatrician and youth screen-time researcher at the University of California, San Francisco, frequent overnight social media notifications can disrupt teenagers’ sleep and have been linked to depression, lower cognitive performance and suicidal behaviors. He said the settlement represents a meaningful step because it places greater responsibility on social media platforms, rather than solely on children and parents.

Under the agreement, Meta has committed to measures including default time limits, restrictions on nighttime notifications, options for non-personalized feeds and stronger age-assurance measures. Nagata emphasized, however, that not all screen time is harmful, noting that digital platforms can also support education, communication, social connection and access to health information.

Research involving thousands of adolescents has found that problematic social media use is associated with a range of health and developmental concerns, including depression, suicidal behaviors, sleep disturbances and difficulties with memory and language.

Researchers also note that children and teenagers may be particularly vulnerable because their brains are still developing and they can be highly influenced by peer feedback, likes, notifications and personalized content.

Nagata encouraged parents to focus less on simply counting screen hours and more on how social media affects their children’s daily lives.

He recommends establishing screen-free periods during meals and bedtime, keeping phones outside bedrooms at night and modeling healthy technology habits.

He also stressed the importance of ongoing conversations with children about cyberbullying, problematic content and difficulties controlling social media use, while calling for independent research to determine whether platform changes actually improve young people’s health and well-being.

World.title: Words Make People Part 1 -Protecting Our Children
World.content:
Words Make People Part 1 -Protecting Our Children

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Nuri Muhammad: More than fifty years ago, Imam W. Deen Mohammed introduced a simple idea that has stayed with me: “Words make people.”

To understand what he meant, we first have to understand his use of the word “word”. A word is not only something spoken from the mouth or printed on a page. In the Imam’s methodology, a word can be anything that communicates meaning to the human consciousness through the senses. What we hear is a word, but what we see can also be a word. A picture, an image, a gesture, music, a taste, a touch and even our environment can communicate meaning. Everything that reaches our consciousness and leaves an impression upon the mind is, in that larger sense, speaking to us.

Another expression frequently heard from Imam Mohammed was “Man means mind.” He was not giving us an English-language etymology. He was directing our attention to the consciousness, intelligence and capacity for thought that distinguish the human person. Put the two ideas together and an important principle emerges: Words make people. Man means mind. Therefore, we must be concerned about what we allow to enter the mind. The eyes and ears are not merely windows through which we observe the world; they are gateways through which the world enters us.

Long before algorithms, smartphones, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, Imam Mohammed was teaching us to pay attention to the language environment in which human beings are formed. Today we have created perhaps the most powerful language environment in human history, and we have placed it in the hands of our children.

When I was growing up, parents worried about the company their children kept. We understood the old saying, “Show me your company and I will tell you who you are.” Parents wanted to know: Who are you talking to? Where are you going? Who are your friends? Today a child can be sitting quietly in his or her bedroom while keeping company with thousands of people, and behind those people is something even more powerful—the algorithm.

The algorithm studies the child. What makes him stop scrolling? What makes her look again? What makes him angry or curious? What image holds attention? What video produces another click? It learns and then feeds the user more. The commercial objective of these platforms is not primarily the development of a healthy child. Their business depends heavily upon attention, engagement, data and advertising. The longer we remain engaged, the more commercially valuable that attention becomes.

In the language of Imam Mohammed, therefore, we should be asking: Who is selecting the words, pictures, sounds and experiences entering the consciousness of our children?

This is no longer simply the concern of old-fashioned parents complaining that children spend too much time on their phones. The scientific and medical warnings have become substantial. The U.S. Surgeon General reported that up to 95 percent of teenagers ages 13 to 17 use social media, with about one-third saying they use it “almost constantly.” Young people spending more than three hours a day on social media faced double the risk of poor mental-health outcomes, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. Concerns have also been raised about sleep, attention, social comparison, body image, self-esteem, exposure to inappropriate material and the displacement of healthy activities.

We should be careful not to make the science say more than it says. Social media is not the only cause of depression, anxiety or behavioural problems among children, and not every child who uses social media will be harmed. There are educational, social and creative benefits. But when credible scientific authorities identify meaningful risks to developing minds, we cannot simply wait until every question has been answered.

Other countries have decided that waiting is not good enough. Australia now requires major social-media platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent children under 16 from maintaining accounts. Significantly, the responsibility is placed upon the platforms rather than simply punishing children or their parents.

Mexico is also moving seriously in this direction. In July 2026, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced national discussions aimed at developing proposals for regulating children’s and adolescents’ use of digital platforms and social media. Proposals before the Mexican legislature have included age restrictions, parental consent for younger users, stronger privacy protection, restrictions on personalized advertising to minors and controls on digital designs intended to keep children continually engaged.

The point is not that Belize should copy Australia or Mexico word for word. The point is that governments are beginning to recognize that protecting children in the digital environment is a legitimate responsibility of the State.

Meanwhile, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, is facing major litigation in the United States over allegations concerning the effect of social-media products on children and young people. Thousands of claims involving Meta and other technology companies allege that social-media platforms were deliberately designed in ways that encourage compulsive use and contributed to harm among young users. Meta strongly disputes these allegations and maintains that it has invested heavily in protections for children and teenagers.

We do not have to wait for the final American court decision to begin asking our own questions in Belize. Must Australia act before Belize becomes concerned? Must Mexico legislate before we begin discussing legislation? Must American courts first tell us how dangerous these products are? Are our children not of the same value as children anywhere else on this planet?

Our children are exposed to the same Facebook, Instagram and other platforms, the same infinite scrolling, carefully selected images, social pressures and sophisticated techniques designed to hold attention. A Belizean child’s developing mind is no less valuable than the mind of a child in Sydney, Mexico City, London or Los Angeles. In fact, as a small developing country, we should perhaps be even more protective because the minds of our children are among our greatest national resources.

I am not suggesting that we smash the phones, close down the Internet or pretend that we can return our children to the world of the 1960s. That world is gone. Neither should concern for children become an excuse for government censorship of adults or political speech. Any legislation must respect privacy, freedom of expression and legitimate access to information.

But surely Belize can seriously examine legislation establishing a minimum age for social-media accounts, meaningful parental consent, privacy protections for minors, restrictions on targeted advertising to children, controls on deliberately manipulative design features and meaningful penalties when companies fail to protect children. Schools must also be part of the discussion, along with parents, teachers, religious communities, NGOs and the children themselves.

We also have to recognize that parents cannot fight billion-dollar algorithms by themselves. We tell a mother or father to “control your child,” while on the other side of the telephone screen are some of the richest corporations in human history employing sophisticated technology, behavioural science, artificial intelligence and enormous quantities of user data to discover what keeps human beings looking. That is not a fair fight. Government has a legitimate role—not replacing parents, but giving parents protection against forces far more powerful than the individual family.

And so I return to Imam W. Deen Mohammed. Fifty-one years ago, when he assumed leadership of the community following the passing of the Honorable Elijah Muhammad, there was no Instagram, Facebook or TikTok. There were no smartphones sitting in the hands of eight-year-olds. Yet the methodology he taught gives us an extraordinary way of understanding the problem confronting us today.

Words make people. And a word is more than something spoken. A word is a carrier of meaning. Pictures, videos, music, s and the entire digital environment are speaking, and day after day they are speaking directly into the consciousness of our children.

If “man means mind,” then protecting the developing mind is part of protecting the developing human being. The question is not whether our children should participate in the modern technological world. Of course they should. The question is who will help determine what enters their minds while those minds are still being formed—their parents, their community and their country, or an algorithm whose principal responsibility is to a corporation seeking to profit from our ignorance?

Fifty-one years later, the warning contained in those few words may be even more relevant than when I first heard them: Words make people. If we care about the people our children are becoming, then Belize must become much more concerned about the “words” that are making them.

World.title: Protecting households today while securing Belize’s Electricity Future
World.content:
Protecting households today while securing Belize’s Electricity Future

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Dr. Leroy Almendarez: Cabinet’s decisions represent a balanced economic response to two interconnected challenges facing Belize’s electricity sector: the immediate pressure of electricity costs on household budgets and the structural need to expand electricity supply as the economy grows. Rather than addressing affordability and energy security separately, the measures recognize that sustainable economic policy must do both. Households require relief today, while the country must simultaneously invest in sufficient generation capacity to meet tomorrow’s demand.

The increase in the GST exemption threshold on residential electricity bills from $100 to $200 per month provides broad-based and immediate relief. With more than 91,000 residential customers, representing approximately 96% of residential consumers, expected to benefit, the measure allows a significantly larger share of Belizean households to retain more of their disposable income. The economic benefit extends beyond the electricity bill itself. Money that households no longer pay in GST can instead be spent on food, transportation, education, housing and other necessities, supporting household consumption and circulating through the domestic economy. This is particularly meaningful because electricity is an essential service and represents a recurring expenditure that households have limited ability to avoid.

The decision to support an expansion of the Social Rate eligibility threshold from 60 kWh to 80 kWh per month strengthens the targeted component of the relief package. Approximately 17,000 residential customers would qualify for the preferential tariff under the expanded threshold. Economically, this is important because lower-income households generally spend a larger proportion of their income on basic necessities. Reducing the electricity burden for these consumers therefore produces a proportionately greater improvement in household welfare. It also recognizes that the amount of electricity required to meet basic household needs has evolved as appliances, connectivity and other electrical services have become increasingly integral to everyday life.

Importantly, however, affordability cannot be sustained without adequate electricity supply. Cabinet’s approval of an Emergency Declaration to facilitate the procurement of additional generation capacity therefore addresses the supply side of the equation. The projected electricity shortfall in 2027 is not simply an energy-sector concern; it represents a potential constraint on economic growth. Electricity demand rises as households expand consumption and as tourism, construction, agriculture, manufacturing, commercial activity and other productive sectors grow. If generation capacity does not expand alongside demand, the result can be reduced reserve margins, greater exposure to supply interruptions and ultimately a constraint on investment and economic activity.

Additional generation should therefore be viewed as economic infrastructure. Reliable electricity is fundamental to business productivity, investment confidence and competitiveness. Hotels, farms, manufacturers, retailers and service businesses cannot expand efficiently if electricity supply is uncertain. The economic cost of insufficient generation can ultimately exceed the cost of securing additional capacity because interruptions affect production, employment, investment and household welfare.

There is also an important distinction between reducing the electricity burden on consumers and artificially suppressing the underlying cost of supplying electricity. The GST measure provides relief through fiscal policy rather than requiring the electricity utility to absorb the cost. This helps protect consumers while avoiding further pressure on the financial sustainability of the electricity system. It therefore represents a more transparent allocation of the cost of social relief: Government deliberately foregoes some tax revenue so that households can retain more income, while the electricity sector remains better positioned to finance reliable service.

The three measures consequently work together as a coherent economic strategy: the GST exemption provides broad household relief; support of the expansion of the Social Rate provides deeper and more targeted assistance to lower-consumption households; and additional generation capacity addresses the structural supply constraint that could otherwise undermine economic growth and electricity reliability.

Ultimately, the policy objective is not simply to make electricity more affordable today. It is to build an electricity system capable of supporting the Belizean economy of tomorrow. Relief without investment would be temporary; investment without attention to affordability would place excessive pressure on households. By pursuing both, Government is balancing affordability, reliability and economic growth providing relief now while building the generation capacity necessary to secure Belize’s energy and economic future.

World.title: Government explains Belize Revenue Authority plan
World.content:
Government explains Belize Revenue Authority plan

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Ministry of Finance has issued a detailed statement on the proposed Belize Revenue Authority, addressing questions raised by employees and the public.

The Authority would replace the Belize Tax Service Department with a semi autonomous body established by law.

Government says the current public service structure was not designed around the operational needs of a revenue administration. Recruitment processes can be lengthy, specialised positions do not fit easily within traditional job classifications, and there is limited flexibility to attract and retain technical skills.

Modern tax administration now requires expertise in compliance risk management, forensic auditing, data analytics, international taxation, transfer pricing, cybersecurity and digital services.

On the question of autonomy, the statement is clear that the BRA will not have authority to create or impose taxes. Taxes and fees will continue to be established through legislation, with the Authority administering those laws.

The Minister of Finance remains responsible for fiscal and revenue policy. An Advisory Board will provide oversight, while a Chief Executive Officer manages day to day operations.

Existing employees will be required to apply for positions within the BRA under a redesigned structure.

World.title: International Day highlights Rights, Resilience and Leadership of Indigenous women and girls
World.content:
International Day highlights Rights, Resilience and Leadership of Indigenous women and girls

By Zoila Palma: Today, September 5, marks the first International Day of the World’s Indigenous Women and Girls, highlighting their leadership, resilience, knowledge and vital contributions to Indigenous communities and society.

Indigenous women and girls serve as leaders, knowledge keepers, caregivers and stewards of their lands and territories. They play an important role in preserving Indigenous languages, traditional knowledge, governance systems and biodiversity, while contributing to the well-being and resilience of their communities.

Despite these contributions, Indigenous women and girls continue to face significant structural inequalities, including poverty, limited access to education, healthcare, land and resources, justice and decision-making. They are also disproportionately affected by trafficking and other forms of gender-based violence.

The United Nations General Assembly established the International Day through Resolution A/RES/80/10 on November 26, 2025, designating September 5 as an annual day of observance.

World.title: ‘Unfair and illegal’
World.content:
The Jamaica Gazette, dated April 1, 2014, states that all certified motor vehicle dealers must ensure that the warranty provided on motor vehicles imported and sold by them is not materially less than that offered by the manufacturer.

PRESIDENT of the Jamaica Used Car Dealers’ Association Lynvalle Hamilton is headed to court to challenge what he says is an unfair and illegal policy being implemented by the Trade Board to govern warranty that players in the sector must give their customers.



Hamilton, who is the owner of Auto Channel Limited, told the Jamaica Observer that it is important for him to seek to block the policy from taking effect any further as it is a big setback for businesses.

According to Hamilton, other players in the industry are running scared and even though they are not happy with the policy, they refuse to join him in protest over fear they may become targets.

“With this policy in particular, the Trade Board compels us to give a certain warranty and that is not consistent with the law, the Sale of Goods Act. This clearly gives us the right to choose the warranty that we want to give to the customer,” said Hamilton.

“The customer can also rely on our expertise to get warranty, but the Trade Board’s policy wants us to give warranty on every occasion and outlines a particular warranty that we are to give, which is totally unfair. That’s unlawful. They are acting as if they are a law unto themselves as is the case with many agencies and entities in Jamaica. This has to be challenged,” added Hamilton.

He charged that because of his refusal to comply with the policy, his certification has been blocked.

“They use the certification as a weapon [and] it is ruining business. This is my livelihood. This is an abuse of power. The other players in the industry are afraid because, listen, not everybody will stand up to the Government in situations like this. You have to stand up for your rights and also get the Government to abide by the law,” he argued.

“The Government can’t make the laws and then want to be a law unto themselves, and that’s what they are doing now. The dealers, although they know it is wrong, they still comply just to keep their business going,” lamented Hamilton, who is being represented by attorney Hugh Wildman.

Wildman, who has filed the challenge in the Supreme Court, told the Observer that the warranty policy has been proving difficult for players in the industry to adhere to and even more than that, it is illegal.

“The Sale of Goods Act is what governs the buying and selling of goods. When they import motor vehicles from abroad and they are going to sell it to the customer, the customer examines the vehicle before to see whether or not they wish to buy it. Whatever warranty is given to them by the dealer, that is it,” argued Wildman.

“They have come up with this motor vehicle policy now, where they will try to impose warranties on the dealers, but that is not contained within the Act. They are saying that they must prescribe what warranty the dealer must give the customer, outside of what the legislation is saying. Mr Hamilton is challenging that policy which affects him,” added Wildman.

He charged that players in the industry are not pleased, especially because those who disagree with the policy and wish not to adhere to it could find themselves without a licence to operate, as is the case with his client.

“If they don’t get with this policy then they will not certify them to import vehicles,” Wildman said as he told the Observer that an application to challenge the policy was filed on Tuesday.

On Friday, the Observer visited Jamaica Trade Board to get a reaction from Chairman Sean Azan. However, he declined to comment, noting that the matter is now before the court and as such he did not wish to prejudice the case. At the same time, he shared a copy a section of the Jamaica Gazette dated April 1, 2014 that outlines the policy on motor vehicle imports.

Under the section that deals with warranty, the document states that all certified motor vehicle dealers must ensure that the warranty provided on motor vehicles imported and sold by them is not materially less than that offered by the manufacturer. According to the document, manufacturer’s warranty on labour, parts, time owned, or distance driven must be passed on to the consumer. This requirement applies to dealers certified as importers of new motor vehicles and those certified as importers of used motor vehicles but who wish to participate in the importation and sale of new motor vehicles.

The gazette also states that all certified used motor vehicle dealers and brokers must provide warranties in accordance with guidelines determined by the vehicles’ age and odometer reading.

Class A warranty is applicable to vehicles manufactured fewer than four years before the sale date with an odometer reading of less than 53,000 kilometres (km)/32,934 miles.

Class B Warranty is applicable to vehicles manufactured more than four years but fewer than seven years before the sale date, with an odometer of less than 106,000km/65,867 miles.

Class C warranty is applicable to commercial vehicles manufactured more than six years but fewer than 11 years before the sale date with an odometer reading of 178,000km/110, 607 miles.

The warranty covers vehicle parts such as the engine, transmission, differential, steering gear, drive chain, front end, major electronic components including computers, air conditioning system, general electric system, and suspension system.

World.title: Distress signal
World.content:
Researchers have compared data from 2010, 2017 and 2026 showing that mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression.Photo: Adobe stock

BY ALICIA DUNKLEY-WILLIS Senior staff reporter dunkleywillisa@jamaicaobserver.com

THE 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey’s finding of increased suicidal thoughts and attempts among students in grades nine to 11 — with girls outpacing boys in both — is “a distress signal from our children” and a warning of a crisis that “did not happen overnight”, according to a child and adolescent development expert.

“When more than one in three grade 11 girls says she has thought about ending her life, and nearly one in three grade 9 girls says she has actually tried, we are not looking at an anomaly, we are looking at a generation in crisis,” Therrain Davis, lecturer in the Child and Adolescent Development Programme at the University of Technology, Jamaica’s College of Health Sciences, told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

According to researchers, in comparing the 2010, 2017 and 2026 survey results, “mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression”.

For Davis, the crisis now unveiled had been announcing itself from over a decade ago.

“The survey compared data from 2010, 2017, and 2026. Each wave brought worse news. More suicidal thoughts, more anxiety, more depression. That means this has been building for at least 16 years while, as a society, we have largely looked away,” the scholar noted.

She said several factors account for the findings.

“Many of our young people are carrying wounds they cannot name — abuse, neglect, violence in the home or the community. These experiences do not stay in the past. They follow children into classrooms, into friendships, into the way they see themselves and the world. Research tells us that children who grow up in these conditions are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts. Jamaica’s own data confirms this pattern. Yet our systems, schools, health services, communities are rarely set up to recognise or respond to this kind of pain,” the educator reasoned.

According to Davis, the “enormous amounts of time” spent online with almost no guidance is another fatal factor.

“The survey found that nearly nine in 10 students have a mobile phone, and two in three spend three or more hours on screens every single school day. Only 39 per cent have parents who set rules around social media. This matters because the research is clear: Heavy social media use, especially for girls, is linked to rising depression, anxiety, sleep problems, harmful comparisons, and cyberbullying. The Internet is not neutral territory for a hurting teenager,” the university lecturer declared.

She also argued that the stigma attached to people experiencing mental health challenges in Jamaica is another hurdle.

“In Jamaica, mental health struggles are still too often treated as weakness, madness, or something to hide. That silence costs lives. Young people who need help are not getting it, not because they do not want it but because the judgment is too great and the services too few,” Davis said.

She, however, noted that while dire, the problem is “not without solutions” as “other countries and communities have faced similar crises and pulled back from the edge”.

“Here is what the evidence shows works: Start in schools. Schools are where our children spend most of their waking hours [so] they are the most logical places to provide early mental health support: counselling, safe spaces to talk, trained teachers who can spot a child who is struggling. A school counsellor should not be a luxury. Right now, it largely is,” Davis said.

Other proven solutions, she said, include training parents and communities how to talk about mental health, recognise warning signs, and set healthy boundaries around screen time.

Additionally, Davis advanced as another solution making it easier to ask for help through anti-stigma campaigns that speak in the language and culture of Jamaican communities, with buy-in from churches, community organisations, schools, and media.

Creating clear pathways for children in crisis to find help, so that referrals actually work with minimal wait times and service availability across communities, is another strategy.

In addition, Davis said “what lies beneath” must be addressed, as mental ill-health does not exist in a vacuum and is fed by poverty, violence, and unstable homes.

“The release of this survey is an opportunity not to write reports that gather dust, but to act. Every child who checked ‘yes’ to suicidal thoughts on that questionnaire is someone’s daughter, son, niece, nephew, student, or neighbour. The question is not whether Jamaica can afford to respond. The question is whether we can afford not to,” Davis emphasised.

“Policymakers must move beyond awareness to investment in school-based mental health services, in trained professionals, in community programmes, and in the families — who are the first line of support for every young person. But this is not only a Government responsibility; it belongs to all of us. Check on the young people in your life. Have the hard conversations. Ask directly, ‘Are you okay?’ and mean it. Remove the shame. Create space. Listen,” she added.

Said Davis: “Our children are telling us something. The only question is whether we are willing to hear it — and to act before more lives are lost.”

World.title: ‘Something doesn’t sound quite right’
World.content:
.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Five people walked free from the St James Parish Court on Wednesday after the prosecution offered no evidence in a case stemming from a police operation at a Montego Bay nightclub.

The accused include three women from the Dominican Republic who were charged with working without permits and two Jamaicans, alleged to be their employers, who were charged with aiding and abetting the offence.

The case arose from an August 1 operation conducted by members of the St James Police Division and the Trafficking in Persons Unit. The team went to a nightclub on Barnett Street in Montego Bay following reports of suspected human trafficking activities at the establishment.

The five individuals appeared before Parish Judge Kaysha Grant-Pryce on Wednesday. They are Marsol Beaz Beaz, Yahaira Jimena Tejeda Sanchez and Naiomi Perez, all from the Dominican Republic, along with Jamaicans Camoy Spence and Nicholas Ricketts. They were represented by attorney-at-law Adrian Dayes.

The three women were charged with working without a permit, while Spence and Ricketts faced charges of aiding and abetting that offence. However, the matter took an unexpected turn when the court was informed that the prosecution would not be proceeding with the charges.

Judge Grant-Pryce asked what had changed.

“How it was explained to me, your honour, is that they entered the club and were dancing but several other persons were dancing around them as well,” the clerk of court responded.

The judge then asked the clerk what the prosecution intended to do. The clerk reiterated that the prosecution intended to offer no evidence, but explained that the difficulty was that defence counsel Dayes had indicated that he would provide his own translator, who was not available on Wednesday.

“I was not prepared to have our translator today. They do understand, though, the difference between guilty and not guilty and if the court wishes to proceed we could do so,” Dayes said.

The five accused were subsequently called upon to plead and each pleaded not guilty.

The prosecution then offered no evidence against all five, bringing the proceedings to an end.

However, before allowing the accused to leave, Judge Grant-Pryce issued a stern warning.

“Something doesn’t sound quite right, Madam clerk, but I am going to tell the two Jamaican nationals that these girls are not supposed to be working here,” the judge said.

She further warned the locals that they could find themselves before the court not only in relation to the women working without permits, but also on matters involving trafficking in persons.

“Trafficking in persons is a serious offence. The world is having an issue with that. Vulnerable persons are being used for work of all kinds. You can find yourself on the other side of the law. You are lucky this morning; these girls were dancing,” she added.

According to the allegations, when the police entered the nightclub, several patrons were seen dancing and consuming alcoholic beverages. Several female exotic dancers were also observed, including the three women from the Dominican Republic.

The women were reportedly dressed similarly to the other females at the establishment.

The police subsequently communicated with the women using

Google Translate on their mobile phones and asked whether they had valid work permits. The women reportedly indicated that they did not. The managers were also questioned and allegedly confirmed that they were not in possession of the required permits. The five were subsequently arrested and charged.

During an earlier hearing, Dayes had told the court that his clients were lawfully in Jamaica and were not working at the time of the police operation.

The prosecution’s decision to offer no evidence on Wednesday resulted in the matter being brought to a close.

World.title: Saint International crowns male and female Fashion Face of the Caribbean winners
World.content:
Rajae Shirley (left) and Talleta Gregory were crowned male and female winners of the Saint International Fashion Face of the Caribbean at AC Hotel on August 29, 2026. .

Rajae Shirley, a 25-year-old resident from the hilly community of Thompson Town in Clarendon, and 17-year-old Ascot High School sixth-form student Talleta Gregory of Portmore were last Saturday night chosen as Fashion Face of the Caribbean Male and Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female, respectively, in the Saint International Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition.

The finals of the competition, which saw 45 females and 38 males competing for the titles, took place inside the ballroom of the AC Hotel in New Kingston.

During the event, nine designers showcased 10 collections in the segment dubbed ‘Riddim Runway Fashion Collections’ and which was sponsored by the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport.

Designers included UK-based Jamaican designer David Newell, Kaydian Nicely, Janseen Graham, Lucien Harrison, Tamia Carey, Errice Alicia, Nina Levy, Shades of Africa, and Andre Shirley.

The judging panel tasked with selecting the winners consisted of some of the world’s most powerful agents. Corrie Caster – Elite World (Europe); Price Stephen – Soul Artist Management (New York); Agel Raya – No Smoking Period (New York, London, Milan, Paris); and Monika Kielczewska – The Society Models (New York).

And when it came down to the announcement of the winners, you could feel the tension in the air.

“I honestly did not expect to win, but I knew for sure that my presence in the competition would make an impact because of my confidence. Everyone else had time to prepare their outfits, while my clothes were actually purchased by my wife on the same day of the event,” Rajae told the

Jamaica Observer post-event.

Rajae, who said he felt unprepared, had decided to withdraw from the competition due to financial and personal challenges.

“I felt a bit unprepared and out of place. So coming back on the day of the competition after the Saint coordinator called and told me that Mr Peters requested my presence, I decided to show up, be myself, and give it my best,” he shared.

He recalled that when his name was announced as the winner, it made him reflect on events leading up to the finals.

“My mind immediately went back to what Mr Peters had said to me that very same morning. For about three mandatory sessions leading up to the event, I was not present because my daughter had gotten sick and was in the hospital. At that point, I had decided to withdraw from the competition because of the personal difficulties I was facing, and I was still without a sponsor. Then, on the very same day of the event, they had secured a sponsor. I came to Kingston for prejudging, and when I arrived, he told me very firmly that I must never give up on myself and that he believed in me. He said I should give it my best shot because this could be a life-changing moment for me and my family. So when my name was called, all of those words came back to me. I couldn’t help but think about everything that had happened just to get me there. It was a very emotional and unforgettable moment for me,” he said.

Rajae said that it was his wife who encouraged him to enter the competition.

“We were at home one evening and she said, “They like you.” I asked her, “Who?” and she told me it was the agent from Saint International. She went ahead and submitted my picture to their

Instagram post where they were searching for new faces. She knew that modelling had always been a dream of mine, and she wanted to see me finally bring that dream to reality. I decided to take the chance and see where it could lead me,” said Rajae, who described the experience as transformative.

“It challenged me mentally, physically, and emotionally. I had to learn how to take directions, work with the other contestants, and remain composed under pressure. The training sessions were very intense, and I learnt a whole lot. The experience also gave me the opportunity to meet some very talented people and learn more about the fashion industry. Most importantly, it showed me that I am capable of much more than I initially thought, and that sometimes you just have to step out of your comfort zone and give yourself a chance.”

Talleta described being named as the winner of Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female as surreal.

“Honestly, it feels surreal. I was surprised that I won, so hearing my name announced as the Fashion Face of the Caribbean Female was definitely a ‘wait…did they just call my name?’ moment. I’m extremely grateful for the opportunity and proud of myself, especially because I entered mainly to enjoy the experience, meet new people, and grow as a model. Winning was just the beautiful surprise at the end,” she shared.

“When I heard my name announced, I immediately started crying! I was honestly shocked because I really didn’t expect to win. Earlier, I had been chosen as the winner for the Blue Denim Remix Challenge [for all the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competitors] so I thought that would probably be my only big moment for the night. My family and friends had been telling me that they believed I could win, which gave me some confidence, but I still wasn’t expecting it. It was a tough competition, many amazing people; I went into the competition mainly for the experience, to have fun, meet new people and grow as a model.”

Talleta explained her decision to enter the competition.

“I’ve always loved art and fashion, and modelling is something I’m genuinely passionate about. When Saint discovered me at my school, Mr Peters told me that he believed I could be a star, but he did say it required a lot of work and discipline. So when I heard about Fashion Face of the Caribbean, it felt like an opportunity I couldn’t pass up. I wanted to challenge myself, gain more experience, and step outside of my comfort zone. I definitely wasn’t going into it thinking I’m coming home with the crown. I was really just there to enjoy myself and see where the experience would take me. Every training session was different, I realised I was lucky to be with Saint,” she reasoned.

Deiwight Peters, founder, CEO of Saint International is pleased with the turn of events.

“I thought this year’s pool of talent was extraordinary. There were such diverse looks and interesting backgrounds. We had an Italian, Jamaicans, Cubans, British Jamaican, and a Jamaican American. But in terms of the different looks, very interesting. I am confident a number of them will be developed to become international stars using the tried and proven and unmatched Saint formula for making fashion stars. I am very excited to see what the future holds for these wonderful young people,” said Peters.

World.title: Rare trio of Pacific hurricanes fuelled by historic El Niño
World.content:
This handout satellite image obtained from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/GOES shows Hurricane Lowell (left), Hurricane Karina (centre), and Hurricane Marie (right) over the Pacific Ocean on September 4, 2026, at 16:51 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Hawaii is preparing for impacts from Hurricane Lowell, which could brush by the state’s westernmost islands from Monday evening, even as its exact path remains unclear. The storm was passing south of the island chain on Friday but is set to swing north over the US Labour Day long weekend, possibly putting Kauai and Niihau islands near its centre, according to the latest forecast from the National Hurricane Center (NHC). Lowell is one of three hurricanes in the Pacific Ocean right now, where a near-record strength El Nino climate episode warms the waters. Karina, around 1,000 miles east of Hawaii, was weakening in the Central Pacific and expected to dissipate next week. Marie, several hundred miles south-west off the southern tip of Baja California, was moving north-west away from land. Photo: NOAA/AFP

WASHINGTON, DC, United States — A rare trio of hurricanes were churning through the Pacific Ocean on Thursday, which scientists attributed to waters warmed by a historically strong El Niño phenomenon.

Tropical Storm Marie strengthened into a hurricane late Wednesday off the coast of Baja California, lining up behind hurricanes Karina and Lowell — both rated as major Category 4 — which were making their way westward across the Pacific.

Three tropical cyclones are “definitely rare to see”, Julia Cole, a climate scientist at the University of Michigan, told AFP.

“El Niño warming sets the stage for these storms, which are fuelled in large part by warm waters. When the tropical Pacific is warmer than normal, we see an increase in strong storms,” Cole said.

Lowell was about 450 miles (725 kilometres) south of Hilo, Hawaii, and “is expected to remain a major hurricane for the next several days” as it moves west, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

“Swells from Lowell are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions in portions of the Hawaiian Islands during the next several days,” the NHC said, adding that its long-range track and intensity forecasts were “more uncertain than usual”.

Hawaii is still recovering from the impacts of Hurricane Lala, which brushed past the southern part of the Big Island last month, bringing destructive winds and severe flash floods.

The NHC said late Wednesday that Karina weakened slightly as it moved north-west, but is likely to remain a hurricane for the next couple of days.

Lowell and Karina are trailed to the east by Marie, which was 380 miles south-west of the southern tip of Baja California, generating swells impacting portions of the coast of south-west Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula that will likely spread northward to southern California over the weekend.

Warm waters provide fuel for storms, and El Niño’s effect on the atmosphere leaves little vertical wind shear over the Pacific, creating favourable conditions for hurricanes to intensify, said Benjamin Kirtman, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Miami.

“The climate system has significantly warmed over the last 20 years or so,” he told AFP.

The sea surface temperature anomaly — how much warmer the ocean is compared to average — is already near record high, Kirtman added.

“There’s no other way to put it — it is juicy out there right now.”

A similar train of four tropical cyclones took place in 2015, another intense El Niño year, when Typhoon Kilo, Hurricane Ignacio, Hurricane Jimena, and Tropical Depression 14E crossed the Pacific at once.

This year’s El Niño has a 69 per cent chance of becoming the strongest on record, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and is already unleashing extreme weather across the globe even though it is not expected to peak until October-December.

Peru, the world’s largest catcher of anchovy, is facing a devastating blow from warming seas that have gutted production, according to industry officials. In Sudan, El Niño is blamed for delaying crucial rains that have led water levels in the Nile to drop precipitously.

El Niño is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific known as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and comes along every two to seven years.

It sets in when east-to-west trade winds ease, allowing warm water which normally piles up in the western Pacific Ocean to slide back east and rise to the surface.

When those warmer-than-average surface temperatures last for a few months, they cause more storms and clouds over the region, which in turn cause ripple effects through the entire global atmosphere: hotter and drier conditions in some places, cooler and wetter in others.

Climate change increases El Niño’s impacts. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so El Niño-linked rains can turn more extreme. It also dries out soils, deepening drought where El Niño brings drought.

World.title: Summer of possibilities
World.content:
Simone Fisher Sobers (left), founder of Winsome Wishes for KIDS, and Ronique Satchell, administrative assistant of JMMB Joan Duncan Foundation, engage in discussion about the activities that form part of the Winsome Wishes for KIDS Summer Fun Reading Literacy Boost Camp.

FROM strengthening reading skills and communication abilities to exploring marine science, leadership development, and financial literacy, hundreds of young Jamaicans spent their summer learning, growing, and discovering new possibilities through programmes supported by the JMMB Joan Duncan Foundation.

Approximately 970 children and youth benefited from the foundation’s support of seven summer initiatives across the island this year.

Recognising the important role that summer programmes play in providing safe, structured, and engaging environments for young people, the foundation partnered with community organisations, educational institutions, and youth groups to expand access to opportunities that nurture both personal and academic development.

The initiatives reached a diverse cross-section of children and youth, including struggling readers, students from underserved communities, children with complex communication needs, and young people seeking opportunities to develop leadership skills and build confidence.

Among the programmes supported was Camp Hello! which provides specialised support for children with speech and communication challenges, helping participants strengthen their ability to connect and engage with the world around them.

The foundation also supported the Winsome Wishes for KIDS (WWKIDS) Summer Fun Reading Literacy Boost Camp, which helped students reading below grade level improve their literacy skills through targeted interventions, digital learning tools, storytelling, and creative activities.

Young people also benefited from programmes that encouraged discovery and exploration. Through support for the Port Royal Marine Laboratory’s summer camp, participants were introduced to marine science and environmental stewardship, while students enrolled in the University of Technology (UTech), Jamaica Students’ Union’s Teach the Youth Summer Programme accessed academic support, financial literacy training, emotional intelligence sessions, and recreational activities across six communities.

Additional support was provided to Kingston YMCA’s summer camp and leadership development programme, Justice For Peace International’s literacy intervention initiative, and SEYA Camp, which offered young people opportunities for mentorship, character development, and positive social engagement.

Kim Mair, chief executive officer of JMMB Joan Duncan Foundation, said the organisation remains committed to supporting programmes that help young people reach their fullest potential.

“Summer should be a time when children and young people continue to learn, explore, and build meaningful connections. The organisations we partnered with this year created welcoming spaces where participants could develop new skills, discover their strengths, and gain experiences that can positively influence their future,” said Mair.

“We are especially grateful to the community organisations and volunteers who dedicate their time and resources to supporting Jamaica’s youth. Their commitment helps to create opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach for many children and families, and we are proud to support their efforts,” added Mair.

She pointed out that this year’s summer camp partnerships formed part of the foundation’s ongoing commitment to transformational development and community empowerment.

“By investing in programmes that support learning, inclusion, confidence-building, and personal growth, the foundation continues to help create pathways for young people to thrive,” Mair said.

World.title: Sandals Resorts’ back-to-school drive brings support and hope to families
World.content:
Children put their hula-hooping skills to the test during a friendly contest at the Beaches Negril Family Funday, where team members’ families gathered for a day of games, activities and community bonding.

FOR thousands of Jamaican children, the start of the new school year will come with a little more excitement — and for their parents, a little less worry — thanks to Sandals Resorts’ annual Back-to-School Drive.

Across Jamaica’s major tourism regions, Sandals Resorts have again extended its reach beyond the resort gates, providing backpacks, books and other school essentials to children from kindergarten through high school.

Team members and their families were also supported through resort-based back-to-school treats and distributions.

Across the Ocho Rios region, the back-to-school season combined education, family fun, wellness and community outreach.

Sandals Dunn’s River hosted a two-day Family Fun Day and back-to-school drive for team members and their children, featuring games, entertainment, food and educational activities, while more than 500 team members received backpacks and school supplies for their children.

The resort also joined Sandals Royal Plantation and the Steer Town Community Organisation for a family fun day in Steer Town, where more than 500 children received school bags and supplies. Sandals Royal Plantation sponsored lunch for children and elderly residents, while Sandals Dunn’s River provided complimentary back and neck massages for seniors.

Meanwhile, Sandals Ochi Beach Resort partnered with Sandals Foundation and the North East Regional Health Authority (NERHA) to stage a Back-to-School Treat and Wellness Extravaganza at Ocho Rios Primary School, serving approximately 400 children with school supplies and access to health services.

Parent Jasette Brown, who attended with her two daughters, welcomed the combination of educational and health support.

“My two girls had their medical check-ups, one got the HPV vaccine, both had their teeth cleaned, plus school bags bursting with supplies,” Brown said. “It was a convenient, all-inclusive service that saved me thousands of dollars.”

More than 700 of the resort’s team members also received school bags and supplies for their children.

In Montego Bay, Sandals and Beaches Resorts’ corporate team members and their families gathered at the Kent Avenue office for a Back to Brilliance treat, where children received backpacks, school supplies and vouchers for books, shoes and barber services.

SRI Human Resources Manager Leshon Simpson said the initiative was designed to provide practical support while reminding team members that their families matter.

“This was about more than giving out school supplies,” Simpson said. “We were intentional about including vouchers for school shoes, books and even the barbershop to help families with some of the real expenses of preparing children for school.”

For some families, the support has been particularly meaningful as they balance everyday household expenses while continuing to recover from the lingering effects of Hurricane Melissa which hit Jamaica last October.

Despite their resorts being closed for regular operations, teams from Sandals Montego Bay and Sandals Caribbean Cay, in partnership with Sandals Foundation, also ensured that more than 300 children from communities including Williams Street (Gully), Canterbury, and Norwood received school supplies, while selected schools benefited from electronic devices and appliances.

More than 1,000 team members from the two resorts also received backpacks and school supplies for their children.

In western Jamaica, Sandals Negril and Beaches Negril catered to more than 1,000 children of team members through their annual back-to-school treat, which combined school supply distribution with rides, games, and family activities.

Through Sandals Foundation, more than 1,500 pounds of school supplies were also distributed to communities across Hanover and Westmoreland, benefiting more than 1,000 students.

Narda Wilson, principal of Galloway Early Childhood Institute in Whithorn, Westmoreland, welcomed the continued collaboration.

“I appreciate the support we’ve had from Sandals and the Sandals Foundation over the years and how active they remain in our communities and our children’s welfare,” Wilson said. “I know our children will make good use of the supplies for the new term.”

At Sandals South Coast, more than 700 team members received school supplies for their children, easing back-to-school expenses as they anticipate the resort’s November reopening.

The three-day distribution offered flexible collection and timely support for families in East Westmoreland and St Elizabeth still recovering from Hurricane Melissa.

“It means a lot to know the resort is thinking about our families. This support makes things a little easier as many of us continue to recover, and we truly appreciate it,” shared Susan Johnson, laundry supervisor.

More than simply distributing school supplies, the annual initiative reflects Sandals’ wider commitment to connecting Jamaica’s tourism industry with the communities that help make the country a world-leading destination.

Regional public relations manager in Montego Bay Rochelle Forbes-Reid said the annual drive demonstrates how the benefits of tourism can extend well beyond employment and visitor spending.

“Tourism dollars have a ripple effect,” Forbes-Reid said. “When tourism does well, the communities around us feel that impact too. Whether through education, local collaborations, community programmes, or the volunteerism of our team members, our responsibility is to keep connecting those dots.”

From South Coast and Negril to Montego Bay and Ocho Rios, the annual Back-to-School Drive continues to turn that philosophy into reality — easing the burden on parents, equipping children for the classroom and ensuring that the benefits of Jamaica’s tourism industry continue to reach beyond the resort gates.

World.title: Resilient Petersfield High coming back stronger
World.content:
Omar Wright (right), lead, environment and community development at JN Foundation, hands over back-to-school-supplies to Roan Green, principal of Petersfield High School in Westmoreland.

Principal Roan Green has praised the resilience and unwavering commitment of his teachers at Petersfield High School in Westmoreland for their efforts to keep learning on track following the passage of Hurricane Melissa last October.

Green said the school’s complement of 85 teachers demonstrated remarkable dedication to their students despite facing personal hardships after the hurricane, which left a trail of destruction across western Jamaica.

“The impact of Hurricane Melissa on Petersfield High School was significant,” said Green.

“What has been documented is that the school served as a shelter for members of the community who were affected by the hurricane. What has not been widely documented, however, is the profound impact the storm had on individuals within our own school family, including both students and staff members,” added Green.

He explained that more than half of the teachers and support staff suffered damage to their homes, ranging from the loss of roofs to severe structural destruction, with some losing their homes entirely.

“Despite those setbacks, they still reported for duty and remained committed to educating our students.

“We had many students who did not return to school immediately after the hurricane, and we had to mobilise as a school community to locate and check on them. When we found them, we realised that many needed necessities such as food and clothing. Our staff stepped up in every way possible to support them. I must commend our teachers and support staff for their hard work, compassion, and resilience during this very difficult period,” said Green.

The principal pointed out that while Petersfield High served as a shelter during the disaster, the school itself sustained extensive damage.

“People are aware that we were a shelter, but what has not been fully revealed is the extent of the damage we suffered. We experienced significant loss to school property, educational resources and other critical material. Many of those items have still not been replaced, even as we prepare to begin a new academic year,” Green noted.

Despite the challenges, the principal said the school has remained focused on ensuring it is as prepared as possible to welcome students for the start of the new school year on Monday.

“We have been doing everything within our means to get ready. We have had several sponsors and well-wishers come forward to assist us through donations and other forms of support, and we are deeply grateful for what they have done so far,” he said.

Among the organisations that have stepped forward to support the school is JN Foundation which recently donated back-to-school supplies for students, along with other essential items for members of staff.

Commenting on the donation, Omar Wright, lead, environment and community development at JN Foundation, explained that the organisation was eager to assist because education remains a cornerstone of Jamaica’s development and plays a vital role in helping communities recover and become more resilient after disasters such as Hurricane Melissa.

“The road to recovery after Hurricane Melissa has not been easy. However, we continue to be inspired by the strength, determination, and resilience demonstrated by Petersfield High School and its staff members, who have worked tirelessly to help students and the wider community regain a sense of normalcy,” said Wright.

“The JN Group is deeply invested in the communities we serve. Through the JN Foundation, we have been intentional about helping Jamaica build back better. With the support of our partner, Lutheran World Relief, we have been able to provide back-to-school supplies, personal care kits, and quilts to individuals and families in need. Partnerships such as these enable us to expand our reach and continue supporting those who have been most severely affected,” Wright added.

Principal Green expressed heartfelt gratitude for the donation, noting that the supplies would help ease the burden on both parents and the school as preparations intensify for the new academic year.

“I am grateful to the JN Foundation for the items they have provided for our students and members of staff. These donations come at a particularly important time, with back-to-school preparations now high on the agenda. We still have students who are struggling, even though it has been nearly a year since Hurricane Melissa. The need remains real for many families. We are extremely appreciative of this support, and I can assure you that these items will be put to good use,” Green said.

World.title: Farage would use military to ‘crush’ Argentina in any Falklands dispute, senior ally says
World.content:
But last week, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he was reconsidering Washington’s support for Britain’s sovereignty over the islands. “I always review every position — that’s just one of many,” he told reporters.

Days later, on Friday, right-wing Argentinian President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, escalated the rhetoric over his country’s enduring claim to the islands, pledging to levy sanctions against companies drilling for oil nearby without approval from Buenos Aires.

Britain’s center-left Labour government immediately rejected Milei’s threat. A Downing Street spokesperson said the islanders have a right to self-determination and that the U.K. supports their right “to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit.”

Jenrick told journalists at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, Milei would not be doing what he’s doing. This is happening because Milei is weak, and he senses that we have a weak government too.”

He added: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, we would use every lever of the British state — our armed forces, our economic sanctions, everything — to defend the Falklands, and we would crush Argentina.”

Reform UK’s decision to turn on Milei over the issue contrasts with Farage’s previous praise for the Argentinian leader for his right-wing, small state ideology. In 2024, Farage described Milei’s agenda as “amazing,” “incredible” and “like Thatcherism on steroids,” adding: “I’m beginning to think about buying Argentinian bonds.”

World.title: Putin signs off on 72-hour ceasefire with Kyiv as US envoys visit
World.content:
“This is due to the preparation and conduct of American contacts in Kyiv,” Peskov said. Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent weeks. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up its hits on Russia’s oil infrastructure, in August reaching a monthly record for strikes since the start of the war in 2022.

Saturday’s pause order followed a broad Russian overnight attack across Ukraine that killed at least five people and injured six others, according to the Kyiv Independent.

“They were deliberate, for the first time in a long while,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram of the strikes targeting airports in Kyiv and Boryspil. “Clearly, Russia’s strikes on the airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations concerning the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine.”

The U.S. emissaries are scheduled to meet with Putin later on Saturday.

World.title: UN backs effort to depict Africa correctly on maps despite US opposition
World.content:
Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings. | iStock

The American delegation dismissed the resolution as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project.”

The United Nations on Friday largely endorsed a resolution to promote maps that reflect the true scale of continents after an African-led campaign to move away from the ubiquitous 16th-century Mercator projection.

The United States was the only country to vote against the initiative, denouncing it as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project” and urging “countries to instill common sense to this body.” Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.

Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Sahra Wagenknecht
World.content:
Endspurt im Wahlkampf in Sachsen-Anhalt: Zwischen Plattenbauten in Halle-Neustadt steht für das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) weit mehr auf dem Spiel als nur der Einzug in den Landtag. Sahra Wagenknecht skizziert ein Klima der extremen Polarisierung, in dem ihre Partei von zwei Seiten unter Beschuss gerät. Fällt die Brandmauer, oder zwingt das BSW die etablierten Parteien in völlig neue Bündnisse?

Im Spannungsfeld zwischen der AfD um Ulrich Siegmund und den Altparteien kämpft das BSW um Sichtbarkeit und beklagt eine mediale Blockade. Wagenknecht zieht scharfe rote Linien zu Björn Höcke, fordert eine leistungsgerechte Aufstiegsgesellschaft und rechnet mit der Agenda-Politik von Gerhard Schröder ab. Was bedeutet der Begriff „links“ heute überhaupt noch, wenn die einstige Linkspartei ihr traditionelles Milieu verliert?

Neben landespolitischen Fragen geht es um die große geopolitische Linie, von der Kritik an teurem US-Gas bis zur Forderung nach mehr Diplomatie. Ein Spaziergang, der die strategischen Ziele des BSW offenlegt und in der Gordon Repinski mit Wagenknecht auch ihre persönliche Prägung zwischen DDR-Vergangenheit und dem Bruch mit ihrer alten Partei beleuchtet.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.
