Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions – and now a US blockade of its ports – and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil. Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war – Iran’s nuclear program – was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June. Now diplomats say the US, Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

World.title: ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller Steve Barrett September 6, 2026 — 1:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Adelaide: The Western Bulldogs were brave, they were willing, but just lacked that touch of class that the competition’s top-shelf contenders possess. In a nutshell, the Bulldogs’ 22-point elimination final loss to Adelaide was a microcosm of their 2026 season. Aaron Naughton congratulates Taylor Walker after the former Crows skipper’s final Adelaide Oval game. AFL Photos Their evening couldn’t have begun more horribly when defender Michael Sellwood was concussed by a stray football during the warm-up. Their backline was summarily rejigged, their midfield – piloted brilliantly by Ed Richards and Joel Freijah – had a huge say in proceedings, but it was ultimately their forward efficiency (or lack thereof) that cost them a semi-final berth.



The Dogs chalked up repeat entry after repeat entry, especially early, with the Crows hemmed inside their defensive-50 at the river end. But the visitors just couldn’t make Adelaide pay – not early when they had all the ascendancy, and not at the start of the final term when they looked as though they had discovered a second wind to roll over the Crows. In the end, it was a familiar finish for Luke Beveridge and his Bulldogs. “We unfortunately lacked a bit of polish,” Beveridge said. “We couldn’t convert or complete some of our prime opportunities at different times. “On the flipside, we were giving them their opportunities too close.”



Meanwhile, for the Crows and coach Matthew Nicks – who entered the match with more noise than necessary surrounding his future – the proverbial monkey is well and truly off the back. Adelaide notched their first finals victory since 2018 to lock in a semi-final date with the Brisbane Lions at the Gabba next Saturday night. View post on X “We can’t wait – we actually cannot wait to get up there,” said Nicks, who received a booming ovation from the 51,370-strong crowd every time his broad-smiling face flashed on the big screen in the fourth quarter. “Our goal is to play for a month. We’re one down, and we’ve got three to go.



“I think it comes on the back of, 12 months ago, going through a fair bit of pain.” Izak Rankine, who missed last year’s finals while serving a suspension for directing a homophobic slur at an opponent, was masterful, while Josh Worrell played the game of his life behind the footy – racking up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions. After a topsy-turvy first half, the Dogs looked out of energy and options following a goalless third term, before suddenly bursting to life with three goals in five minutes early in the fourth. View post on X With the scores level and the visitors boasting all the momentum, Aaron Naughton soared for a spectacular mark for a shot at goal straight in front.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it Jon Pierik Sports journalist for The Age A third-straight Crow choke in a final was on the cards. But then Naughton let them off the hook, hitting the post for the third time to give the Bulldogs the lead by just that margin – one point. From that moment, the Crows wouldn’t be denied. Their big three forwards – all of whom had been held in relative check on a night favouring smaller crumbing types – stepped up in the crunch.



Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker – playing at Adelaide Oval for the last time – and Darcy Fogarty went bang-bang-bang in front of goal. And then there was that man Rankine. At long last playing the first final of his burgeoning career, he showed he has the capacity to be “Mr September” – much like a former Crow wearing the iconic No.23 jumper, the incomparable Andrew McLeod. Rankine put an exclamation point on a wonderful night by conjuring an incredible crumbing finish from the south-western pocket, before Josh Rachele added a fifth-straight goal for the fast-finishing Crows, pouring some more icing on a sweet-tasting cake. Despite bowing out at the elimination final stage for the third time in the past five years, Beveridge feels his team is tracking in the right direction.



View post on X “I believe the boys have come a long way, and it’s a good platform for the future,” he said. “It seems like it’s one that got away ... we did a lot right, we were just not good enough tonight. “It’s a bitter pill when you know you can measure up, but you ultimately come away without the chips.” Freijah, one of the Dogs’ best against Adelaide, agrees that the future is rosy at Whitten Oval.



“There’s a really strong bond of characters within this team,” he said. “As a group and club, we’ve had some challenges this year with injuries and guys being out. View post on X “I’m proud of us as a group. Although this was a disappointing night, we’re definitely going in the right direction, and I’m optimistic about what we can do going forward.” That future could include Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, who announced after the home-and-away season his intention to leave the Power and return home to Victoria.



The Bulldogs will in the coming days, and weeks, ramp up their pitch to Butters, who supported the Dogs and idolised Marcus Bontempelli while growing up in Darley. An invitation to have a hit with some of the Bulldogs’ keen golfers could be just the trick in enticing Butters, a regular at Glenelg Golf Club throughout his time in South Australia. “There are a few handy golfers who go pretty well, like Oskar Baker, Bailey Dale and Timmy English,” Freijah said. “Zak’s an awesome player with real integrity in his game. He’s one of the stars of the competition. “We’ll see what happens over the trade period, and we’ll go from there.”

World.title: Sometimes the best part of travel is shutting yourself into a hotel room
World.content:
I often use the hours before a midday checkout to sit and read, as a relaxing contrast to the usual busy travel day. On this occasion, I have a limited choice of onward trains: departing at either 5.30am or 12.30pm. I’ve already sampled everything this city has to offer in my research for a travel guidebook, but I don’t fancy dragging myself to the railway station before dawn. So I choose the later train, linger over the hotel’s lavish breakfast spread (the Poles do a good buffet breakfast, with lots of breads and meats and cheeses and pickles), then read in my room until checkout over a fruit tea (another excellent Polish specialty).

It’s not very rock and roll but not all travel has to be frantic. I sometimes enjoy a period of quiet time in a hotel room, to simply sit and cocoon, appreciating a break between commitments.

Do you have a kettle? My Polish is a bit rusty and I’ve had to look up the word for kettle, but my request is successful and I’m soon back in my hotel room in the mountain town of Jelenia Gora, brewing a herbal tea.

I’ve never been that fussed about hotel rooms as I’m usually travelling to experience a destination, and I don’t spend much time in my room. I don’t care if it’s big or small or luxurious or plain, it’s just a place to lay my head after I’ve been out and about all day.



However, every so often an editor needs a piece filed quickly to meet a deadline, so I carve out half a day from my on-the-road schedule and hole up in my room. The Do Not Disturb sign is hung over the door handle, the kettle and coffee sachets (if available) are put on standby, and I tap away at a portable keyboard and tablet.

Amid a busy travel schedule, there’s something calming about spending a few hours in one place, focused on a creative task. On my Eurail trek across Europe in 2025, for example, I spent a solid writing session in my pleasant single room with a skylight in Bucharest’s gorgeous Hotel La Boheme, writing an article about coping without my phone weeks earlier in London.

A few years before, while in the US, I shut myself up in a room at the Sheraton Grand Seattle to write a story about Australian food and coffee in Los Angeles, which I’d just visited. On another occasion in Wurzburg, Germany, I took on an urgent rewrite of a piece about Hawaii’s Tiki culture. Sitting in bed at 6am I furiously redrafted it via frenzied finger jabs on an iPad, before emailing it off and heading down to breakfast.

And in 2015, arriving on a different trip to Poland aboard a train from Vienna, I shut myself away in a Katowice hotel. My mission? Writing an urgently needed article about a tour of Sound of Music locations which I’d taken earlier in Salzburg, Austria, to mark the 50th anniversary of the popular movie. Unusually for a Polish hotel, the room had an electric kettle, so hot beverages were the go as I typed away. To paraphrase Maria, the hotel room was alive with the sound of typing; and that was one of my favourite things.

World.title: Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it Jon Pierik Sports journalist for The Age September 5, 2026 — 10:45pm

September 5, 2026 — 10:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

After doing it the hard way, through a wildcard final win over Collingwood at the MCG last week, The Bulldogs were right up against it at Adelaide Oval. But no one should ever write-off Luke Beveridge’s men and their never-say-die spirit. The Dogs charged to a one-point lead in the final term. But Adelaide, courtesy of their firepower up forward, responded in style – winning by 22 points in front of more than 51,000 screaming fans. Jon Pierik runs his eye over every player in this elimination final. Taylor Walker leaves the Adelaide Oval surface for the final time as an AFL player. AFL Photos



Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Had a crucial role as a defensive forward on Bailey Dale, but his attacking bent kicked in – literally – with a left-foot snap for the Crows’ second goal of the night. He is an energiser battery, and lifted the locals with a long-snap in the third term. 6.5/10 (3) Sam Berry: He was at his robust best in the midfield, but was prepared to push back defensively. Finished the night with 20 disposals. 6.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: The Brisbane Lions premiership player was recruited for nights like this, and used his left foot to deliver a steadying goal late in the second term. He was always dangerous when near the goal, and even spent time behind the ball late in the game to steady his side. 6.5/10



(6) Daniel Curtin: The big-bodied midfielder ran with Marcus Bontempelli early and did an excellent job, nullifying the Bulldogs great in the first term. Curtin complemented Jordan Dawson and Izak Rankine, finishing with 15 disposals and 340 metres gained. 7/10 Job done: Daniel Curtin and Josh Worrell. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: The bustling forward had a great record against the Bulldogs, booting 13 goals in four games. He was well held here by Rory Lobb until he took a strong mark and converted a set shot on a tight angle in the final term, regaining the lead. He found himself in more key contests, lifting when the game was on the line. 6.5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: The dynamic forward is the Crows’ leading goal-kicker, and loomed large all night. He had a crowd-pleasing moment with an opportunistic snap in the second term to extend his team’s lead. He was fortunate to not be concussed in a tackle in the third term, and finished with three goals. 7.5/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: The inspirational Crows skipper ripped the Bulldogs apart earlier in the season, but had a relatively quiet 13 disposals to half-time. Of concern was that he had failed to have a clearance in that period. He finished with 28 disposals and five tackles, but the Crows will look for a goal or two from him next week. 7/10



View post on X (13) Taylor Walker: In what was his final game at Adelaide Oval, the retiring forward was barely sighted in the first half until a strong mark midway through the second term led to a Brayden Cook goal. But this is a man who is never out of the contest. He lifted after half-time, his mark and long bomb – his 319th career goal at the venue – extending the Crows’ lead to double digits with just over 10 minutes remaining in the game and igniting the crowd. 6.5/10 (14) Jake Soligo: The busy midfielder/forward had 11 disposals and 309 metres gained in the first half. He botched a regulation set shot for goal in the third term which would have extended the Crows’ lead to beyond four goals. 5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The clever wingman held his line late in the first term to mark and goal, giving the Crows the lead. He was busy all night, including a slick pass to Rachele, who snapped a goal. Delivered a fine tackle late when the desperate Dogs were pressing. 6.5/10 (16) Max Michalanney: The young defender had the job on Arthur Jones, and was unlucky to cede a free kick – and goal – in the second term. Remained strong in the contest after the main break. 5.5/10



(23) Izak Rankine: Wow, what a night to remember for the dynamic midfielder, who banished memories of a controversial end to his 2025 campaign. In his maiden final, Rankine, the top-ranked player in the league since round 17, put on a show. He had the first clearance out of the middle, the Dogs opting not to tag him. He had 17 touches and 300 metres gained to half-time, finishing with 34 touches, seven clearances and two goals. 9/10 After missing last year’s finals series, Izak Rankine was superb in this elimination final. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: The robust defender was here, there and everywhere in what was arguably a best-afield effort with a whopping 19 intercept possessions. He not only silenced creative small forward Cody Weightman, but had 10 touches of his own in the first term. By half-time, he had nine interceptions and a game-high 19 touches, rising to 32 to three quarter-time. Why the Bulldogs did not do more to avoid him was baffling. 9/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: The hard-running utility was busy with 10 disposals to half-time. He continued to work hard after the break. 6/10 (28) Alex Neal-Bullen: The former Melbourne premiership star worked hard but did not have a great impact before half-time. His tackling pressure is elite, and that was reinforced in the third term. 6.5/10



(29) Rory Laird: The veteran midfielder had 13 disposals to half-time, and sent his team forward early in the second half. He was a solid contributor. 6.5/10 (30) Wayne Milera: Despite the inclement weather, the dashing All-Australian half-back was at his creative best. He finished with 27 disposals and 402 metres gained, and was a prime mover when the game was there to be won. 7.5/10 View post on X (32) Darcy Fogarty: Gave the Crows’ faithful what they wanted by delivering the game’s opening goal with a clever bunt in traffic. He worked hard all night, and was rewarded with a strong mark and long goal late in the final term that put the contest beyond the Bulldogs’ reach. 6.5/10 (35) James Borlase: The intercept-marking defender had only the four touches to half-time but played the role the Crows needed. 5/10



(40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The mid-season draftee has impressed at half-back since joining the club. That continued with 10 touches to half-time. He had the job on Buku Khamis in the final term. 6/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: The young ruckman was determined to flourish against Tim English, and had a solid evening. While he had only nine disposals, 30 hitouts and four clearances got the job done. 6.5/10 Marcus Bontempelli leads the Bulldogs off the field for the final time in 2026. AFL Photos (44) Isaac Cumming: The former Giant had eight disposals to half-time, but finished the night with a workmanlike 206 metres gained. He was a calm presence. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: The reliable defender delivered his typical run and rebound, and had 201 metres gained just in the first term. Had 22 touches and 426m gained by night’s end, and will be a man the Lions will need to curb next week. 6.5/10



Western Bulldogs (3) Cody Weightman: The flashy small forward had an early set shot snap from the boundary, but went to ground too often in the first term. While his endeavour could not be questioned, he needed to do better to negate opponent Josh Worrell, who was arguably best afield. 3/10 Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller (4) Marcus Bontempelli: Branded “the best Bulldog ever” by club great Brad Johnson during Kayo Sports’ pre-game coverage, the man dubbed “the Rolls Royce” did all he could to will his team over the line, finishing with 27 touches and 10 clearances. He began quietly with just the five first-term touches, but got moving in the second, finding himself more goal-side. He was sent forward in the third, but injected himself more into the midfield in the final term, delivering run and carry. 7.5/10 (6) Cooper Hynes: The strong-bodied forward-midfielder was prolific early with 15 disposals and 318 metres gained to half-time. He continued to work hard, and was steady when the contest was there to be won. 6.5/10



(7) Rory Lobb: The veteran defender looked lost up forward against Collingwood last week, and was sent to defence on Riley Thilthorpe, where he was excellent until the final break when the burly Crow got busy. That wasn’t just on him though, for the Crows lifted through the midfield. 7/10 (9) Ryley Sanders: The exciting midfielder won’t want to watch this game again. He was another who struggled to get going early, having just the five touches before half-time, and finished with only 10 disposals. Needed to lift after the main break, but had a nightmare moment early in the third term when he dropped the ball, leading to an Izak Rankine goal. 3/10 View post on X (14) Rhylee West: Typically a goal-kicking forward, the son-of-a-gun was injected into the midfield in a brilliant move by Luke Beveridge. He was arguably best afield in the first half with 12 touches, including five clearances, but faded as the evening progressed. 6.5/10 (18) James O’Donnell: The reliable defender had the job on Taylor Walker, and was at his intercept-marking best early. But “Big Tex” lifted late, as all great forwards do. 6.5/10



(19) Connor Budarick: The versatile small defender worked hard but did not have a major impact. 5/10 (20) Ed Richards: The dashing midfielder snapped the Dogs’ opening goal, the visitors rewarded for multiple inside-50 entries. He kept an eye on Izak Rankine at stoppages, and had 16 touches and 411 metres gained to half-time. He delivered a moment of inspiration with a brilliant running goal in the final term to knot scores, finishing with 27 disposals. 8/10 View post on X (24) Buku Khamis: The rebounding defender had the job on Darcy Fogarty, and broke even, before he was sent forward in the final term as the Bulldogs, with only five goals, desperately sought another avenue. Had a chance to cut the Crows’ lead to five points, but his long set shot drifted wide. 6/10 (26) Josh Dolan: The creative midfielder-forward was quiet in the first half. He battled hard, but did not have an impact when the game was there to be won. 5/10



(27) Joel Freijah: He’s spent more time in the midfield over the past month, and pushed forward in the second term to snap a crucial goal. He could have done better with a snap early in the final term, which would have closed the Crows’ lead to a goal. 6.5/10 (28) Will Lewis: Replaced the concussed Matthew Kennedy in the 23 and had the job of keeping Crows defender Mark Keane honest. Delivered a slick pass to Weightman in the second term, but the latter missed the set shot. Exploded in the final term with two goals, which cut the Crows’ lead to a goal. 6.5/10 (29) Lachlan Bramble: The dashing utility and half-back flanker had a quiet evening but worked hard in the contest. 6/10 (30) Lachie McNeil: He was a late inclusion after Michael Sellwood pulled out on the cusp of the opening ball-up when concussed in the warm-up. He only had five touches to the final break and was a non-factor. 3/10 (31) Bailey Dale: The creative defender kicks the ball “hard and fast”, as Brad Johnson put it, but didn’t have as much of the Sherrin as the Bulldogs would have wanted. He was steady under pressure in the final term but couldn’t generate enough run. 6.5/10



Arthur Jones had an impact in the second quarter in what could yet prove to be his final game for the Bulldogs. AFL Photos (32) Arthur Jones: The exciting forward delivered when needed in the second term with two goals. The first was after a contentious free kick, his celebration not well received by the locals, while another came after a strong lead into space. The Bulldogs needed more from him after the main break. 6/10 (33) Aaron Naughton: The Bulldogs needed their “astronaut” to take flight and build on his stellar performance against the Magpies. He began well, and that continued in the second term with a juggling mark and goal in wet and windy conditions. He hit the post with less than 30 seconds left in the third term, and early in the fourth, diminishing his good work. 6.5/10 (34) Bailey Williams: The rebounding half-back counter-attacked well, having 11 disposals and 248 metres gained before the main break. He was lucky not to let himself down when Darcy Fogarty marked – but missed a set shot – in the third term. 7/10 (35) Luke Kennedy: The speedy midfielder had eight touches, including two clearances, to half-time, but couldn’t lift his side late. 6/10



(42) Sam Davidson: The hard-running wingman would have been disappointed with his unsuccessful snap at goal late in the second term, compounding a poor start with only five touches. Had only 10 touches in the end, but finished with 229 metres gained. 4/10 (43) Ryan Gardner: The former Cat had just the one touch to half-time and three to the final break. 2/10 (44) Tim English: The blue-chip ruckman was a big disappointment, adding to his woes against the Crows this year. He broke even with his opponents to half-time, but needed to be a physical warrior after the break, particularly when sent forward to help Aaron Naughton. He finished with only 10 touches, one mark and 19 hitouts. 3.5/10 Get around our AFL finals coverage

World.title: Crows fans stand for their coach as the Bulldogs’ season ends in an elimination final
World.content:
Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli cut a disappointed figure post-game after his side fell short in their elimination final against the Crows tonight.

Bontempelli praised his side for fighting back into the game early in the last term before the Crows kicked away at the end.

“It definitely does [hurt] mate,” Bontempelli told Seven.

“I thought we really challenged them at certain points. We clearly couldn’t make enough of our entries, and they are a very good intercept marking team – if you allow them to do it, then they can repel off the back of it and, gee, they have some mercurial players who can really hurt you.

“I’m proud of the boys. We weren’t going all that well halfway through the year.

“We found some grit to get in this position and even in that game – I don’t think we looked too far off it despite the margin.”

World.title: The little barrier that couldn’t: This $1.3 million project has taken longer than the Fremantle bridge
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWARoads The little barrier that couldn’t: This $1.3 million project has taken longer than the Fremantle bridge Hamish Hastie September 6, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To the outsider, works happening on the Malcolm Street bridge leading into the western end of St George’s Terrace seem like a simple upgrade to the traffic barriers. But the project has proven so tricky for Main Roads WA that it will have taken longer to complete than the entire $596 million Fremantle traffic bridge replacement. The delayed Malcolm Street Bridge barrier project in West Perth. Hamish Hastie The $1.3 million project started in February 2024, forcing the closure of the right-hand lane on Malcolm Street to traffic. Main Roads is upgrading and lengthening the guardrails on both sides of the bridge but work on the ground has virtually halted for more than a year.



In June 2025, Main Roads assured the public the job would be finished by October that year. During this masthead’s last inquiry in February Main Roads said it would be completed by April, having resolved “site and design complexities, as well as delays with service relocation works.“ Work stalled on the project again last week when more guardrails started being installed further up Malcolm Street. A Main Roads spokeswoman said more unforseen issues had arose with the project but they expected the project would be finished by the end of this month. “Changes needed to be made to the final design to address unforeseen complexities with the site, such as installation of additional posts and railing,” she said.



Related Article Exclusive

Roads The traffic barriers that are taking as long to build as Boorloo Bridge “The changes to the design are now being implemented and Main Roads anticipates the project will be completed by the end of September.” The spokeswoman said the changes were made within the existing project budget. Construction on the Fremantle traffic bridge started in September 2024 with the installation of the bridge pylons. The old traffic bridge was closed and dismantled in February this year. The traffic bridge was expected to be finished early next year, but the state government recently announced it was ahead of schedule and would be open for traffic by the end of the year.

World.title: Midland headspace one of 10 centres in Australia to receive upgrade
World.content:
NationalWAMental health Midland headspace one of 10 centres in Australia to receive upgrade Michael Philipps September 6, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A mental health care facility in Perth’s north-east will be one of the first 10 across the nation to transition to a new model, as the federal government rolls out its headspace Plus centres throughout Australia. Midland will be one of the first mental health centres in the nation to upgrade to the headspace Plus models. headspace Midland The upgrades follow federal government figures released in June that revealed one mental health clinic in Perth’s east had delivered more than 25,000 appointments since it opened. Part of the Commonwealth’s plan to expand access to free mental health care, the existing headspace Midland centre will be upgraded, meaning a larger centre, an expanded workforce of mental health professionals and an increase in the centre’s capacity to support young people and families. The Midland facility has already delivered around 9000 free appointments to local young people in the area.



In June, it was revealed that the Midland Medicare Mental Health Centre - one of five mental health support centres introduced in WA by the federal government - had provided more free sessions than the other four combined. The figures showed that 48,140 sessions were delivered through all five operating centres located in Armadale, Gosnells, Midland, Mirrabooka and Northam. However, the Midland clinic had outstripped them all by responding to particularly high community need - delivering more than 25,000 free appointments since opening. Member for Hasluck Tania Lawrence said expanding the Midland facility to the headspace Plus model will mean services are even easier to access. “I think most of us know a young person who, at some point, has struggled and needed someone to talk to,” she said.



“It’s about making sure a young person who is doing it tough can walk through the door and know someone is here to help.” A new headspace centre will also be established in Wanneroo, bringing free mental health support to one of Perth’s fastest-growing communities. The service will support young people aged 12 to 25 experiencing anxiety, depression, psychological distress and other mental health challenges Member for Pearce Tracey Roberts said the City of Wanneroo is one of Perth’s largest and fastest-growing communities “It’s important our young people have mental health support close to home,” she said.



“For years, families in Pearce have had to travel to headspace Joondalup, one of the busiest centres in WA, just to access this kind of support. “This new centre means young people and families in Pearce will finally have somewhere local to turn to.” Assistant Mental Health Minister Emma McBride said around two in five young Australians experience mental health challenges every year. “The upgrade of headspace Midland and the establishment of a new headspace centre in Wanneroo will help more young people access free mental health care in their local community,” she said. Both headspace Plus Midland and headspace Wanneroo are expected to open in the next financial year.

World.title: US strikes three Iranian oil tankers after it says warships were targeted
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war US strikes three Iranian oil tankers after it says warships were targeted Amir Vahdat , Toqa Ezzidin and Cara Anna September 6, 2026 — 1:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy warships were targeted with missiles, the American military said on Saturday, warning that it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”. The strikes – a day after President Donald Trump sought to minimise the conflict as “small potatoes” – keep up a new tilt back toward fighting after six months of on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks on February 28. Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain, and negotiations have collapsed. View post on X The military’s statement said a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling in the region and no US personnel were hurt. It said two Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled” and the third, unladen one, was destroyed. The US statement said the tankers were part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region. There was no immediate Iranian response.



Earlier, Iranian state TV had said four US missiles struck a tanker about six miles (10 kilometres) from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil. Kharg Island been repeatedly targeted during the war, including US strikes on military sites there in March. US President Donald Trump, pictured boarding Air Force One on Friday, downplayed the conflict with Iran as “small potatoes”. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The US said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman, and the US said its crew had been “directed to abandon ship”. The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes. After the US statement, Iran’s state broadcaster reported the two other tankers attacked, saying their crews had evacuated. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of US Central Command Admiral Brad Cooper said.



The strikes came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm, with the strait and Iranian communities along it again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a US bombardment of southern Iran. One strike hit a wedding. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Iran accuses US of bombing a wedding in first major strikes since July Masoumeh Zarei, 13, was wounded in the attack. She spoke to The Associated Press at a hospital while being treated for injuries to her abdomen. She said that the wedding celebration had already begun when she set out to join it. She never made it there. She was knocked unconscious when a telecommunications tower was struck. Her next memory was of waking up in a hospital. Her friend, 14-year-old Kiana Karimi, was also wounded and in intensive care. She told the AP that she heard five explosions.



US Vice President JD Vance said that strike would be investigated “fully”, while repeating the manta that the US never deliberately attacks civilians. The resumption of fighting came after new US efforts to apply economic pressures on Tehran, whose hard-line new senior leaders have signalled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. The resumption of fighting in the past week came after new US efforts to apply economic pressures on Tehran, whose hard-line new senior leaders have signalled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. The elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, however, has said that it favours a negotiated end to the war. Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions – and now a US blockade of its ports – and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil. Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war – Iran’s nuclear program – was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June. Now diplomats say the US, Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

World.title: ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller Steve Barrett September 6, 2026 — 1:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Adelaide: The Western Bulldogs were brave, they were willing, but just lacked that touch of class that the competition’s top-shelf contenders possess. In a nutshell, the Bulldogs’ 22-point elimination final loss to Adelaide was a microcosm of their 2026 season. Aaron Naughton congratulates Taylor Walker after the former Crows skipper’s final Adelaide Oval game. AFL Photos Their evening couldn’t have begun more horribly when defender Michael Sellwood was concussed by a stray football during the warm-up. Their backline was summarily rejigged, their midfield – piloted brilliantly by Ed Richards and Joel Freijah – had a huge say in proceedings, but it was ultimately their forward efficiency (or lack thereof) that cost them a semi-final berth.



The Dogs chalked up repeat entry after repeat entry, especially early, with the Crows hemmed inside their defensive-50 at the river end. But the visitors just couldn’t make Adelaide pay – not early when they had all the ascendancy, and not at the start of the final term when they looked as though they had discovered a second wind to roll over the Crows. In the end, it was a familiar finish for Luke Beveridge and his Bulldogs. “We unfortunately lacked a bit of polish,” Beveridge said. “We couldn’t convert or complete some of our prime opportunities at different times. “On the flipside, we were giving them their opportunities too close.”



Meanwhile, for the Crows and coach Matthew Nicks – who entered the match with more noise than necessary surrounding his future – the proverbial monkey is well and truly off the back. Adelaide notched their first finals victory since 2018 to lock in a semi-final date with the Brisbane Lions at the Gabba next Saturday night. View post on X “We can’t wait – we actually cannot wait to get up there,” said Nicks, who received a booming ovation from the 51,370-strong crowd every time his broad-smiling face flashed on the big screen in the fourth quarter. “Our goal is to play for a month. We’re one down, and we’ve got three to go.



“I think it comes on the back of, 12 months ago, going through a fair bit of pain.” Izak Rankine, who missed last year’s finals while serving a suspension for directing a homophobic slur at an opponent, was masterful, while Josh Worrell played the game of his life behind the footy – racking up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions. After a topsy-turvy first half, the Dogs looked out of energy and options following a goalless third term, before suddenly bursting to life with three goals in five minutes early in the fourth. View post on X With the scores level and the visitors boasting all the momentum, Aaron Naughton soared for a spectacular mark for a shot at goal straight in front.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it Jon Pierik Sports journalist for The Age A third-straight Crow choke in a final was on the cards. But then Naughton let them off the hook, hitting the post for the third time to give the Bulldogs the lead by just that margin – one point. From that moment, the Crows wouldn’t be denied. Their big three forwards – all of whom had been held in relative check on a night favouring smaller crumbing types – stepped up in the crunch.



Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker – playing at Adelaide Oval for the last time – and Darcy Fogarty went bang-bang-bang in front of goal. And then there was that man Rankine. At long last playing the first final of his burgeoning career, he showed he has the capacity to be “Mr September” – much like a former Crow wearing the iconic No.23 jumper, the incomparable Andrew McLeod. Rankine put an exclamation point on a wonderful night by conjuring an incredible crumbing finish from the south-western pocket, before Josh Rachele added a fifth-straight goal for the fast-finishing Crows, pouring some more icing on a sweet-tasting cake. Despite bowing out at the elimination final stage for the third time in the past five years, Beveridge feels his team is tracking in the right direction.



View post on X “I believe the boys have come a long way, and it’s a good platform for the future,” he said. “It seems like it’s one that got away ... we did a lot right, we were just not good enough tonight. “It’s a bitter pill when you know you can measure up, but you ultimately come away without the chips.” Freijah, one of the Dogs’ best against Adelaide, agrees that the future is rosy at Whitten Oval.



“There’s a really strong bond of characters within this team,” he said. “As a group and club, we’ve had some challenges this year with injuries and guys being out. View post on X “I’m proud of us as a group. Although this was a disappointing night, we’re definitely going in the right direction, and I’m optimistic about what we can do going forward.” That future could include Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, who announced after the home-and-away season his intention to leave the Power and return home to Victoria.



The Bulldogs will in the coming days, and weeks, ramp up their pitch to Butters, who supported the Dogs and idolised Marcus Bontempelli while growing up in Darley. An invitation to have a hit with some of the Bulldogs’ keen golfers could be just the trick in enticing Butters, a regular at Glenelg Golf Club throughout his time in South Australia. “There are a few handy golfers who go pretty well, like Oskar Baker, Bailey Dale and Timmy English,” Freijah said. “Zak’s an awesome player with real integrity in his game. He’s one of the stars of the competition. “We’ll see what happens over the trade period, and we’ll go from there.”

World.title: Sometimes the best part of travel is shutting yourself into a hotel room
World.content:
I often use the hours before a midday checkout to sit and read, as a relaxing contrast to the usual busy travel day. On this occasion, I have a limited choice of onward trains: departing at either 5.30am or 12.30pm. I’ve already sampled everything this city has to offer in my research for a travel guidebook, but I don’t fancy dragging myself to the railway station before dawn. So I choose the later train, linger over the hotel’s lavish breakfast spread (the Poles do a good buffet breakfast, with lots of breads and meats and cheeses and pickles), then read in my room until checkout over a fruit tea (another excellent Polish specialty).

It’s not very rock and roll but not all travel has to be frantic. I sometimes enjoy a period of quiet time in a hotel room, to simply sit and cocoon, appreciating a break between commitments.

Do you have a kettle? My Polish is a bit rusty and I’ve had to look up the word for kettle, but my request is successful and I’m soon back in my hotel room in the mountain town of Jelenia Gora, brewing a herbal tea.

I’ve never been that fussed about hotel rooms as I’m usually travelling to experience a destination, and I don’t spend much time in my room. I don’t care if it’s big or small or luxurious or plain, it’s just a place to lay my head after I’ve been out and about all day.



However, every so often an editor needs a piece filed quickly to meet a deadline, so I carve out half a day from my on-the-road schedule and hole up in my room. The Do Not Disturb sign is hung over the door handle, the kettle and coffee sachets (if available) are put on standby, and I tap away at a portable keyboard and tablet.

Amid a busy travel schedule, there’s something calming about spending a few hours in one place, focused on a creative task. On my Eurail trek across Europe in 2025, for example, I spent a solid writing session in my pleasant single room with a skylight in Bucharest’s gorgeous Hotel La Boheme, writing an article about coping without my phone weeks earlier in London.

A few years before, while in the US, I shut myself up in a room at the Sheraton Grand Seattle to write a story about Australian food and coffee in Los Angeles, which I’d just visited. On another occasion in Wurzburg, Germany, I took on an urgent rewrite of a piece about Hawaii’s Tiki culture. Sitting in bed at 6am I furiously redrafted it via frenzied finger jabs on an iPad, before emailing it off and heading down to breakfast.

And in 2015, arriving on a different trip to Poland aboard a train from Vienna, I shut myself away in a Katowice hotel. My mission? Writing an urgently needed article about a tour of Sound of Music locations which I’d taken earlier in Salzburg, Austria, to mark the 50th anniversary of the popular movie. Unusually for a Polish hotel, the room had an electric kettle, so hot beverages were the go as I typed away. To paraphrase Maria, the hotel room was alive with the sound of typing; and that was one of my favourite things.

World.title: Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Adelaide v Western Bulldogs player ratings: Beveridge’s men were down and out. These guns made a game of it Jon Pierik Sports journalist for The Age September 5, 2026 — 10:45pm

September 5, 2026 — 10:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

After doing it the hard way, through a wildcard final win over Collingwood at the MCG last week, The Bulldogs were right up against it at Adelaide Oval. But no one should ever write-off Luke Beveridge’s men and their never-say-die spirit. The Dogs charged to a one-point lead in the final term. But Adelaide, courtesy of their firepower up forward, responded in style – winning by 22 points in front of more than 51,000 screaming fans. Jon Pierik runs his eye over every player in this elimination final. Taylor Walker leaves the Adelaide Oval surface for the final time as an AFL player. AFL Photos



Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Had a crucial role as a defensive forward on Bailey Dale, but his attacking bent kicked in – literally – with a left-foot snap for the Crows’ second goal of the night. He is an energiser battery, and lifted the locals with a long-snap in the third term. 6.5/10 (3) Sam Berry: He was at his robust best in the midfield, but was prepared to push back defensively. Finished the night with 20 disposals. 6.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: The Brisbane Lions premiership player was recruited for nights like this, and used his left foot to deliver a steadying goal late in the second term. He was always dangerous when near the goal, and even spent time behind the ball late in the game to steady his side. 6.5/10



(6) Daniel Curtin: The big-bodied midfielder ran with Marcus Bontempelli early and did an excellent job, nullifying the Bulldogs great in the first term. Curtin complemented Jordan Dawson and Izak Rankine, finishing with 15 disposals and 340 metres gained. 7/10 Job done: Daniel Curtin and Josh Worrell. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: The bustling forward had a great record against the Bulldogs, booting 13 goals in four games. He was well held here by Rory Lobb until he took a strong mark and converted a set shot on a tight angle in the final term, regaining the lead. He found himself in more key contests, lifting when the game was on the line. 6.5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: The dynamic forward is the Crows’ leading goal-kicker, and loomed large all night. He had a crowd-pleasing moment with an opportunistic snap in the second term to extend his team’s lead. He was fortunate to not be concussed in a tackle in the third term, and finished with three goals. 7.5/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: The inspirational Crows skipper ripped the Bulldogs apart earlier in the season, but had a relatively quiet 13 disposals to half-time. Of concern was that he had failed to have a clearance in that period. He finished with 28 disposals and five tackles, but the Crows will look for a goal or two from him next week. 7/10



View post on X (13) Taylor Walker: In what was his final game at Adelaide Oval, the retiring forward was barely sighted in the first half until a strong mark midway through the second term led to a Brayden Cook goal. But this is a man who is never out of the contest. He lifted after half-time, his mark and long bomb – his 319th career goal at the venue – extending the Crows’ lead to double digits with just over 10 minutes remaining in the game and igniting the crowd. 6.5/10 (14) Jake Soligo: The busy midfielder/forward had 11 disposals and 309 metres gained in the first half. He botched a regulation set shot for goal in the third term which would have extended the Crows’ lead to beyond four goals. 5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The clever wingman held his line late in the first term to mark and goal, giving the Crows the lead. He was busy all night, including a slick pass to Rachele, who snapped a goal. Delivered a fine tackle late when the desperate Dogs were pressing. 6.5/10 (16) Max Michalanney: The young defender had the job on Arthur Jones, and was unlucky to cede a free kick – and goal – in the second term. Remained strong in the contest after the main break. 5.5/10



(23) Izak Rankine: Wow, what a night to remember for the dynamic midfielder, who banished memories of a controversial end to his 2025 campaign. In his maiden final, Rankine, the top-ranked player in the league since round 17, put on a show. He had the first clearance out of the middle, the Dogs opting not to tag him. He had 17 touches and 300 metres gained to half-time, finishing with 34 touches, seven clearances and two goals. 9/10 After missing last year’s finals series, Izak Rankine was superb in this elimination final. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: The robust defender was here, there and everywhere in what was arguably a best-afield effort with a whopping 19 intercept possessions. He not only silenced creative small forward Cody Weightman, but had 10 touches of his own in the first term. By half-time, he had nine interceptions and a game-high 19 touches, rising to 32 to three quarter-time. Why the Bulldogs did not do more to avoid him was baffling. 9/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: The hard-running utility was busy with 10 disposals to half-time. He continued to work hard after the break. 6/10 (28) Alex Neal-Bullen: The former Melbourne premiership star worked hard but did not have a great impact before half-time. His tackling pressure is elite, and that was reinforced in the third term. 6.5/10



(29) Rory Laird: The veteran midfielder had 13 disposals to half-time, and sent his team forward early in the second half. He was a solid contributor. 6.5/10 (30) Wayne Milera: Despite the inclement weather, the dashing All-Australian half-back was at his creative best. He finished with 27 disposals and 402 metres gained, and was a prime mover when the game was there to be won. 7.5/10 View post on X (32) Darcy Fogarty: Gave the Crows’ faithful what they wanted by delivering the game’s opening goal with a clever bunt in traffic. He worked hard all night, and was rewarded with a strong mark and long goal late in the final term that put the contest beyond the Bulldogs’ reach. 6.5/10 (35) James Borlase: The intercept-marking defender had only the four touches to half-time but played the role the Crows needed. 5/10



(40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The mid-season draftee has impressed at half-back since joining the club. That continued with 10 touches to half-time. He had the job on Buku Khamis in the final term. 6/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: The young ruckman was determined to flourish against Tim English, and had a solid evening. While he had only nine disposals, 30 hitouts and four clearances got the job done. 6.5/10 Marcus Bontempelli leads the Bulldogs off the field for the final time in 2026. AFL Photos (44) Isaac Cumming: The former Giant had eight disposals to half-time, but finished the night with a workmanlike 206 metres gained. He was a calm presence. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: The reliable defender delivered his typical run and rebound, and had 201 metres gained just in the first term. Had 22 touches and 426m gained by night’s end, and will be a man the Lions will need to curb next week. 6.5/10



Western Bulldogs (3) Cody Weightman: The flashy small forward had an early set shot snap from the boundary, but went to ground too often in the first term. While his endeavour could not be questioned, he needed to do better to negate opponent Josh Worrell, who was arguably best afield. 3/10 Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘It’s a bitter pill’: The key fourth-quarter moment that cost the Dogs dearly in knockout final thriller (4) Marcus Bontempelli: Branded “the best Bulldog ever” by club great Brad Johnson during Kayo Sports’ pre-game coverage, the man dubbed “the Rolls Royce” did all he could to will his team over the line, finishing with 27 touches and 10 clearances. He began quietly with just the five first-term touches, but got moving in the second, finding himself more goal-side. He was sent forward in the third, but injected himself more into the midfield in the final term, delivering run and carry. 7.5/10 (6) Cooper Hynes: The strong-bodied forward-midfielder was prolific early with 15 disposals and 318 metres gained to half-time. He continued to work hard, and was steady when the contest was there to be won. 6.5/10



(7) Rory Lobb: The veteran defender looked lost up forward against Collingwood last week, and was sent to defence on Riley Thilthorpe, where he was excellent until the final break when the burly Crow got busy. That wasn’t just on him though, for the Crows lifted through the midfield. 7/10 (9) Ryley Sanders: The exciting midfielder won’t want to watch this game again. He was another who struggled to get going early, having just the five touches before half-time, and finished with only 10 disposals. Needed to lift after the main break, but had a nightmare moment early in the third term when he dropped the ball, leading to an Izak Rankine goal. 3/10 View post on X (14) Rhylee West: Typically a goal-kicking forward, the son-of-a-gun was injected into the midfield in a brilliant move by Luke Beveridge. He was arguably best afield in the first half with 12 touches, including five clearances, but faded as the evening progressed. 6.5/10 (18) James O’Donnell: The reliable defender had the job on Taylor Walker, and was at his intercept-marking best early. But “Big Tex” lifted late, as all great forwards do. 6.5/10



(19) Connor Budarick: The versatile small defender worked hard but did not have a major impact. 5/10 (20) Ed Richards: The dashing midfielder snapped the Dogs’ opening goal, the visitors rewarded for multiple inside-50 entries. He kept an eye on Izak Rankine at stoppages, and had 16 touches and 411 metres gained to half-time. He delivered a moment of inspiration with a brilliant running goal in the final term to knot scores, finishing with 27 disposals. 8/10 View post on X (24) Buku Khamis: The rebounding defender had the job on Darcy Fogarty, and broke even, before he was sent forward in the final term as the Bulldogs, with only five goals, desperately sought another avenue. Had a chance to cut the Crows’ lead to five points, but his long set shot drifted wide. 6/10 (26) Josh Dolan: The creative midfielder-forward was quiet in the first half. He battled hard, but did not have an impact when the game was there to be won. 5/10



(27) Joel Freijah: He’s spent more time in the midfield over the past month, and pushed forward in the second term to snap a crucial goal. He could have done better with a snap early in the final term, which would have closed the Crows’ lead to a goal. 6.5/10 (28) Will Lewis: Replaced the concussed Matthew Kennedy in the 23 and had the job of keeping Crows defender Mark Keane honest. Delivered a slick pass to Weightman in the second term, but the latter missed the set shot. Exploded in the final term with two goals, which cut the Crows’ lead to a goal. 6.5/10 (29) Lachlan Bramble: The dashing utility and half-back flanker had a quiet evening but worked hard in the contest. 6/10 (30) Lachie McNeil: He was a late inclusion after Michael Sellwood pulled out on the cusp of the opening ball-up when concussed in the warm-up. He only had five touches to the final break and was a non-factor. 3/10 (31) Bailey Dale: The creative defender kicks the ball “hard and fast”, as Brad Johnson put it, but didn’t have as much of the Sherrin as the Bulldogs would have wanted. He was steady under pressure in the final term but couldn’t generate enough run. 6.5/10



Arthur Jones had an impact in the second quarter in what could yet prove to be his final game for the Bulldogs. AFL Photos (32) Arthur Jones: The exciting forward delivered when needed in the second term with two goals. The first was after a contentious free kick, his celebration not well received by the locals, while another came after a strong lead into space. The Bulldogs needed more from him after the main break. 6/10 (33) Aaron Naughton: The Bulldogs needed their “astronaut” to take flight and build on his stellar performance against the Magpies. He began well, and that continued in the second term with a juggling mark and goal in wet and windy conditions. He hit the post with less than 30 seconds left in the third term, and early in the fourth, diminishing his good work. 6.5/10 (34) Bailey Williams: The rebounding half-back counter-attacked well, having 11 disposals and 248 metres gained before the main break. He was lucky not to let himself down when Darcy Fogarty marked – but missed a set shot – in the third term. 7/10 (35) Luke Kennedy: The speedy midfielder had eight touches, including two clearances, to half-time, but couldn’t lift his side late. 6/10



(42) Sam Davidson: The hard-running wingman would have been disappointed with his unsuccessful snap at goal late in the second term, compounding a poor start with only five touches. Had only 10 touches in the end, but finished with 229 metres gained. 4/10 (43) Ryan Gardner: The former Cat had just the one touch to half-time and three to the final break. 2/10 (44) Tim English: The blue-chip ruckman was a big disappointment, adding to his woes against the Crows this year. He broke even with his opponents to half-time, but needed to be a physical warrior after the break, particularly when sent forward to help Aaron Naughton. He finished with only 10 touches, one mark and 19 hitouts. 3.5/10 Get around our AFL finals coverage

World.title: Crows fans stand for their coach as the Bulldogs’ season ends in an elimination final
World.content:
Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli cut a disappointed figure post-game after his side fell short in their elimination final against the Crows tonight.

Bontempelli praised his side for fighting back into the game early in the last term before the Crows kicked away at the end.

“It definitely does [hurt] mate,” Bontempelli told Seven.

“I thought we really challenged them at certain points. We clearly couldn’t make enough of our entries, and they are a very good intercept marking team – if you allow them to do it, then they can repel off the back of it and, gee, they have some mercurial players who can really hurt you.

“I’m proud of the boys. We weren’t going all that well halfway through the year.

“We found some grit to get in this position and even in that game – I don’t think we looked too far off it despite the margin.”

World.title: Qantas flight diverted to Christchurch after 'engine issue'
World.content:
A Qantas flight from Queenstown had to be diverted to Christchurch on Saturday afternoon, after it experienced an "engine issue" after takeoff.

The Boeing 737-800 aircraft had just become airborne when the incident occurred.

Witnesses reported hearing banging noises. Video footage on social media appeared to show flames coming from an engine.

Nic Chamberlain was among those in Queenstown who saw flames and heard a series of loud noises.

"It was like just shoots of orange flames shooting out the back.

"You can tell it was coming out of the left engine," he told RNZ.

There was a delay before the loud noises followed, he said.

"This was kind of like rapid succession boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. And then it was loud enough that everyone kind of turned their heads and looked to see what the noise was," he said.

Flight QF122 touched down safely at Christchurch Airport at about 5pm on Saturday. There were no reports of injuries.

RNZ understands about 160 passengers were on board.

A Qantas spokesperson said the incident was under investigation.

"One of our flights to Sydney experienced a suspected engine issue after take-off from Queenstown this afternoon and the aircraft diverted to Christchurch.

"Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely.

"We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support," they said.

Earlier, the Civil Aviation Authority said bird strike caused the incident. It has since amended that statement, saying that it was unable to confirm the cause at this stage.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of a flight diversion at 4.25pm and multiple ambulance resources responded to Christchurch Airport as a standard procedure.

A spokesperson said St John had not been required to assess or treat anyone, and all ambulance units had since been stood down.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand records show an aircraft emergency was reported at Invercargill Airport at 4.12pm, with Invercargill and Kingswell crews attending.

It is understood the flight was initially expected to divert to Invercargill before continuing to Christchurch.

World.title: Fullback Taine Tuaupiki saves Warriors with hattrick of tries over Sea Eagles
World.content:
Fullback Taine Tuaupiki - who wasn't originally named to play - has saved NZ Warriors' bacon with a hattrick of tries in a desperate 31-30 win over Manly Sea Eagles to keep their NRL minor premiership hopes alive.

The home side needed a late field goal from Chanel Harris-Tavita to snatch victory from their dogged opponents and now await the result between Penrith Panthers and Wests Tigers on Sunday, which will determine the winners of the regular-season crown.

Off to a slow start, the Warriors trailled 12-4 after 20 minutes, but rattled on the next four tries - two to Tuaupiki - to lead 24-12 just after halftime.

Tuaupiki was initially named on the interchange bench as backline cover, but entered the starting line-up when centre Leka Halasima withdrew with an ankle injury 24 hours out.

His inclusion saw Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad shifted to the wing, where he also had a try double in that 20-point run before the Sea Eagles came charging back.

As the match continued, star fullback Tom Trbojevic started to stamp his class on the game, creating chances for those around him.

Manly scored the next three tries and almost had a fourth, which was disallowed for a penalty back on halfway, to grab a 30-24 advantage late in the second half.

Tuaupiki brought the Warriors back on level terms, slicing against the grain to score next to the posts and then converting from in front.

The Warriors had two tries ruled out in the closing minutes, with Harris-Tavita and prop Tanner Stowers-Smith both crossing, and Harris-Tavita also had a field goal attempt charged down.

With the final seconds ticking down, halfback Te Maire Martin received the ball in front of the posts, but was run off his kick. On the next play, Harris-Tavita had more room to operate and duly slotted in the gamewinner.

Victory sees the Warriors set a club record of 18-6 for the season and puts them two points clear at the top of the NRL table.

Penrith can still secure the minor premiership with a three-point win over the 15th-placed Tigers.

World.title: Grain sector 'disappointed' farmers are choosing cheap palm kernel feed over local grain
World.content:
Disappointment is deepening in New Zealand's struggling arable sector over farmers continuing to opt for imported animal feeds over local grain.

New Zealand was one of the largest importers of palm kernel expeller (PKE) in the world, using the byproduct of the palm oil industry as a feed supplement for dairy cattle, largely when pasture was scarce.

Midday rural news for 4 September 2026 Rural News Download MP3 3m

Arable farmers growing feed grain had long fought for greater uptake of their product domestically, but struggled to be competitive against similar imported products on price.

The issue was raised at the industry association Seed and Grain New Zealand (SGNZ) conference in Christchurch this week, where some of the country's top arable and seed companies and government officials explored challenges and opportunities for the legacy sectors.

At the conference, SGNZ vice president Jo Townshend of Midlands Seed in Mid Canterbury raised concerns about the challenges for arable to compete against the usually cheaper imports.

Townshend said New Zealand's arable domestic manufacturing sector lacked government support to help it remain viable and cost competitive.

"It's a huge amount of importing coming into this country, possibly due to free trade agreements or other agreements, that are really putting a ceiling on the ability of arable farmers to support our own domestic economy, including process growers," she said.

"I mean, for $2 billion worth of animal feed coming into the country, for a country that's pretty good at producing it itself, is pretty disappointing."

Aotearoa imported more than 2 million tonnes of the PKE feed product from countries like Indonesia and Malaysia each year, a mostly dry matter product from the fruit of the palm.

When pastures are dry, farmers have a choice of supplementary feeds for dairy herds. Susan Murray RNZ

Environmentalists opposed importing PKE, due to its environmental effects and links to deforesting tropical rainforests.

SGNZ president Edward Luisetti of Canterbury's Luisetti Seeds said arable farmers with irrigation were looking forward to a warmer summer, particularly on the East Coast, if El Niño arrived as forecast.

However, he also expected the drier conditions to drive up farmers' PKE imports this year.

Competitive price point

Farming leader Nathan Guy was a former Horowhenua dairy farmer and agriculture minister, and now is the country's special agricultural trade envoy, flying the flag with government officials to grow New Zealand agriculture exports.

In response to questions from Jo Townshend at the event, Guy said he fed his cattle PKE and found it was an easy supplement to switch on and off.

"A benefit with PK is you can start the cows on it tomorrow. There's no rumen digestion change as there is with some other feeds."

But he said the costs for PKE had increased, and local grain was less price competitive.

"PK's very expensive right now, very expensive with shipping costs," he said.

"But I think right now there's a price point.

"Is there a way of potentially the arable over time becomes more cost competitive?"

He said many farmers, including himself, would get to a point where they would look to grow maize themselves in the face of rising costs.

One farmer who contacted RNZ said PKE was $300 per tonne, versus $500 for grain, and dairy was a business not a national charity.

Fonterra said its cows were 96 percent grass-fed (including silage, hay and forage crops like legumes and brassicas).

The dairy co-op and world's largest exporter of dairy previously told RNZ that PKE made up less than 2 percent on average of its farmer-shareholders' cows' overall diet

Meanwhile, Greenpeace activists staged a protest at an Agrifeeds PKE storage shed at Port Taranaki last year.

Greenpeace activists occupied part of Taranaki's port in April last year, to protest Fonterra's use of palm kernel. Supplied / Greenpeace

Its global project lead for agriculture, Amanda Larsson, said the palm kernel supply chain was "incredibly murky" and made it difficult to guarantee that no rainforests were destroyed in the process.

"We're pretty aligned with the arable farmers on this one," Larsson said.

"I think most New Zealanders would be pretty horrified to hear the dairy industry is connected to rainforest destruction, when there is a homegrown alternative that would actually support New Zealand's own farmers."

Larsson said farmers may need support in transitioning to more diverse and less monocultural farming systems, in the face of climate change.

Delegates at the 2024 Fonterra AGM were greeted by a Greenpeace protest about the use of palm kernel as a stock feed. RNZ / Robin Martin

The Foundation for Arable Research (FAR) [

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/country/575244/arable-sector-launches-new-trademark-to-champion-nz-grain-over-imports launched a landmark NZ Grown Grains certification last year], to help consumers identify products made with local grain and promote local uptake among farmers.

More than 34 producers were now certified, with more being assessed, including grain for animal feed.

World.title: More than half of KiwiSaver hardship applicants directed to other options
World.content:
More than half of would-be applicants for KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals to Simplicity, Milford, SuperLife and NZ Funds are being directed to other ways to deal with their problems instead.

KiwiSaver hardship withdrawal numbers have increased rapidly in recent years. In July 2026, $45.2 million was withdrawn for hardship reasons, up from $43.2m in July 2025.

Some providers have engaged third-party providers to help manage the workload that comes with the applications, such as Debtfix.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

In a new report, Debtfix said in the year to March 2026, it received 5964 referrals to it from the KiwiSaver schemes it works with, of people who were seeking money from their KiwiSaver accounts for hardship reasons.

Of those, 2516 went on to be approved for a hardship withdrawal. Another 3450, or 57.9 percent, were supported through other solutions to the problem.

Debtfix said accessing KiwiSaver was not always the most appropriate or sustainable solution.

Alternatives could include applying to creditors for hardship arrangements, negotiating debt repayment plans, no asset procedures or budget and cash flow planning.

Applicants for KiwiSaver withdrawal are meant to have exhausted their other options.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people had sometimes not considered the alternatives before putting in an application.

The country's biggest KiwiSaver provider, ANZ, said it saw supporting KiwiSaver members through difficult economic times as part of its role.

"When people reach out to us because they're under financial pressure, our focus is on understanding their circumstances, helping them explore the options available, and providing support through what can often be a very stressful time. We also support members through the hardship withdrawal process itself and can assist them with their application.

"Between December 2025 and July 2026, our KiwiSaver Contact Centre received almost double the number of contacts relating to financial hardship as actual hardship withdrawals. These included enquiries about existing applications, the hardship withdrawal process, and eligibility requirements.

"We would note that because many of our KiwiSaver customers contact us more than once and enquiries cover a wide range of topics, these figures can't be viewed as indicating the proportion of customers who ultimately make a withdrawal."

ANZ's spokesperson said the bank shared the view that KiwiSaver hardship applications should only be made after all reasonable alternatives had been exhausted.

"Applicants need to demonstrate they have explored other reasonable avenues of support, which may include using available savings, cashing in investments or shares, seeking assistance from their bank, or approaching WINZ for support."

Debtfix said people were increasing seeking assistance not because of their own financial decisions, but because they had run out of resources to help them cope with increasing costs.

Loss of employment or reduced work hours were some of the most common reasons people wanted help.

It said there were more people experiencing sustained periods of hardship, rather than isolated financial events.

World.title: Blaze at cafe next to New Zealand's oldest building 'suspicious', FENZ says
World.content:
A café situated just metres from New Zealand's oldest surviving building has been damaged in an overnight blaze, but volunteer firefighters managed to stop the flames spreading to 204-year-old Kemp House at Kerikeri Basin.

Police are investigating the blaze, which started in a storage shed next to Honey House Café around 11.30pm on Friday.

The shed was destroyed while one wall of the café was burned and its water pipes and electric cables were badly damaged.

The two-storey Honey House has the café on the ground level and offices for Heritage New Zealand upstairs.

The business is next to Kemp House, which was built between 1821 and 1822 by missionaries, and was an important focus for early relationships between Māori and Pākehā.

Another heritage building, the Stone Store, which was built not much later - from 1832 to 1836 - is also next door to the cafe.

The fire had been small, and "both Kemp House and Stone Store were thankfully unaffected by the blaze," a Honey House Café spokesperson said.

The Stone Store and Kemp House, seen from Kororipo Pā in 2025. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger said the nation owed a debt of gratitude to a Kerikeri man whose vigilance may have saved New Zealand's oldest building.

Hamberger said a man on his way to work about 11.30pm on Friday called 111 when he spotted smoke near Kerikeri Basin.

The first fire truck at the scene found a storage shed next to the Honey House Café - which was immediately behind the 204-year-old Kemp House - was burning fiercely.

The crew called for a second truck as well as backup from Ōkaihau and Paihia.

Hamberger said the shed was razed and the café's exterior, water pipes and electrical cabling were badly damaged.

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger during an exercise at the Stone Store in February this year. PETER DE GRAAF / RNZ

If firefighters had arrived a few minutes later the flames could have taken hold of the two-storey Honey House and spread from there to nearby Kemp House, which was currently wrapped in plastic for re-roofing.

"It was called in by a chap who was going to work, he spotted the fire," Hamberger said.

"Without him the potential for spread to Kemp House was actually quite scary, to be honest, because they've got it surrounded with plastic sheeting to protect it. Potentially we could have had a fire in that Kemp House as well," he said.

"I don't know him but a big shout out to that guy, because without him being pretty vigilant on his way to work, we could be looking at a major building fire, or a heritage building being lost, or certainly significantly damaged."

John O'Hare, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga spokesman for Northland, said the entire Kerikeri Mission Station site was closed while police and FENZ carried out their investigations.

It was too early to say with certainty what had caused the fire but initial indications were that it had been deliberately lit.

Fortunately, neither Kemp House nor the Stone Store had been damaged.

"But it was too close for comfort. It was very, very close, and we're just very thankful that that Kemp House didn't catch alight, and incredibly disappointed that somebody would do this. The indicators are that this was a deliberate act, which is appalling," O'Hare said.

The café was likely to be closed for the foreseeable future.

The cause had yet to be confirmed but if police found it had been deliberately lit, as was suspected, that would be "appalling" and "deeply disappointing", he said.

Despite its historic appearance, the Honey House - a former curator's cottage - was only built in 1976.

It was built on the site of a historic barn and took its name from James Kemp Jr's storage shed for beehives, which once stood nearby.

The café opened in 2012 with some of its recipes sourced from historic archives, or made with fruit grown in Kerikeri Mission Station's heritage orchard.

Kemp House was erected in 1821-22 by the London-based Church Missionary Society for the Reverend John Butler, the only ordained minister in the settlement at the time.

It was built by missionary carpenters and Māori sawyers, and later became the home of the Kemp family.

Kemp House is currently wrapped in plastic while it is roof shingles are being replaced, which could have made a fire even more catastrophic.

World.title: The psychiatrist who can now prescribe MDMA
World.content:
Dr Gary Wynn is one of two psychiatrists who have just been approved to administer and prescribe MDMA in New Zealand, to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

In legal terms, MDMA is a Class B high risk drug. It is also known as ecstasy, E, or molly, and is a stimulant and hallucinogen.

It is the first time MDMA assisted treatment has been allowed in Aotearoa.

Dr Wynn talked with Saturday Morning about the research his team will be doing, who could be treated, and what their sessions might look like.

The Psychiatrist Who Can Now Prescribe MDMA Saturday Morning Download MP3 22m

In the 1970s, MDMA's first use was as a medicine known as 'empathy', used by therapists," Wynn says.

"It creates an openness, a connection. An empathy-enhancing compound that sort of reduces the fear centres in the brain, and puts people in this really open space to do some deep work, particularly around traumas that they've experienced in their life."

In the early 1980s MDMA became better known as a party drug, and by the mid-1980s it was made illegal in the United States - which soon became the norm around the world. "And we spent 40-ish years with it being illegal, until Australia in 2023."

Australia's medicines regulator granted permission in 2023 for psychedelics to be used in therapy nationally there, including psilocybin for depression, and MDMA for PTSD.

What could MDMA do clinically?

MDMA's potential "is pretty amazing," Wynn says.

He has done training in Canada and Australia on providing MDMA treatment, and will be working with Dr Tom Paterson for the New Zealand trials.

"It's one of those drugs that when it works it feels almost magical, people get better sometimes so quickly and so intensely that you're like 'wow', it's almost unbelievable given the typical history of psychiatric treatments where medications take months to work, therapies sometimes years to work.

"In one study, about 80 percent of people were significantly better from treatment from three rounds of MDMA treatment, and at least 50 percent had full remission of their PTSD. And I don't know anything else that even comes close to those numbers in terms of treatment efficacy for PTSD."

Who could receive the treatments?

"There's a lot of reasons people can be severely traumatised," Wynn says.

"Military and veteran PTSD had got a lot of attention - I think deservedly so - but the truth of the matter is people get traumatised and severely traumatised from a whole host of reasons." Among them, sexual assault, prolonged childhood abuse and domestic violence, he says.

The test patients will be people who have PTSD, and who have not had success with an earlier treatment, such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor medicines) or talk therapy.

"Typically we're looking at more severe cases upfront.

"That's the other really unique thing about MDMA, most treatments for PTSD as you get more severe the treatments work less and less, so they work the best in sort of mild to moderate PTSD. And then gosh, really severe PTSD, nothing seems to work."

But so far, MDMA trials seem to show pretty even benefit across the different severities of PTSD, he says.

What will the work involve?

MDMA affects a number of neurotransmitters in the brain, including serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine and oxytocin - a brain chemical involved with feelings of connection. It also quietens down the fearful side of the brain, Wynn says.
