"So it's not just the connection, it's the connection and then this quieting down of the fearful parts of the brain. I think those two things work in tandem to put someone into this really open state where they can look at their traumas in a less overwhelmed way."

The protocol the team will use is a "fairly intense and fairly long protocol", he says. It is modelled off the earlier US FDA approved MAPS (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies) clinical trial protocol.

First, prospective patients are screened with a full psychiatric examination and health screening. Then there will be rounds of treatment, which each consist of three stages - a preparation phase, a medicine session and an integration session.

"There's two therapists for all of this time - so the two therapists and the individual will get to know each other. You do need a lot of trust and understanding, a lot of rapport, a lot of understanding of what the shape of all their traumatic experiences are, understanding about their social supports.

"You need to understand the person pretty well, so that can take a lot of hours to get to that point."

They will then run a full day medicine session, during which the MDMA dose will be given, after "careful preparation to get them into a calm state".

"We administer the drug, it takes maybe half an hour to work, at which point they go into this altered state. Some people get pretty significantly into an altered state, some people have a sort of milder experience.

"Then during that time we do the therapeutic work looking at the traumas, processing things, somewhat allowing them to go where their mind wants to take them. There's a classic comment in psychedelics talking about the inner healing intelligence - that some of the job is getting out of the way and letting the mind do the work of healing itself."

It's a long day with a lot of emotions, he says: "pretty intense".

"Then after that completes, we'll do three or four more sessions with the two therapists and the individual where you're trying to integrate what happened, you're trying to make sense of it, you're trying to take these learnings from that day-long experience and action them into the real world."

With three rounds typical for each of the preparation phase, medicine session and integration sessions for each patient: "All told, there's about 50-ish hours of therapist time, and there's two therapists the entire time."

Wynn says people using MDMA recreationally are not guaranteed of the purity of what they're taking, whereas the MDMA used in this approved trial will be pharmaceutical grade and pure.

MDMA is also known as ecstasy, E or molly. Supplied/ NZ Drug Foundation

The Drug Foundation has warned that drugs illegally sold as MDMA in New Zealand can sometimes have other things mixed into them, or even be another substance altogether - in particular synthetic cathinones (often called bath salts): And that "these drugs can have more unpleasant and unpredictable effects than MDMA".

Wynn says he hopes their team will have their first patient receiving the treatment within the next two to three months.

World.title: One dead after car and cyclist crash in Gisborne
World.content:
One person has died after a serious crash in Te Hapara, Gisborne on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the crash involving a car and a cyclist on Lytton Road about 3pm.

One person was transported to hospital in a critical condition. They have since died.

The road was closed on Saturday evening while the Serious Crash Unit conducts a scene examination, but would reopen shortly.

World.title: Bird strike forced flight from Queenstown to divert to Christchurch
World.content:
A Qantas flight from Queenstown had to be diverted to Christchurch on Saturday afternoon, after it experienced an "engine issue" after takeoff.

The Boeing 737-800 aircraft had just become airborne when the incident occurred.

Witnesses reported hearing banging noises. Video footage on social media appeared to show flames coming from an engine.

Nic Chamberlain was among those in Queenstown who saw flames and heard a series of loud noises.

"It was like just shoots of orange flames shooting out the back.

"You can tell it was coming out of the left engine," he told RNZ.

There was a delay before the loud noises followed, he said.

"This was kind of like rapid succession boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. And then it was loud enough that everyone kind of turned their heads and looked to see what the noise was," he said.

Flight QF122 touched down safely at Christchurch Airport at about 5pm on Saturday. There were no reports of injuries.

RNZ understands about 160 passengers were on board.

A Qantas spokesperson said the incident was under investigation.

"One of our flights to Sydney experienced a suspected engine issue after take-off from Queenstown this afternoon and the aircraft diverted to Christchurch.

"Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely.

"We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support," they said.

Earlier, the Civil Aviation Authority said bird strike caused the incident. It has since amended that statement, saying that it was unable to confirm the cause at this stage.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of a flight diversion at 4.25pm and multiple ambulance resources responded to Christchurch Airport as a standard procedure.

A spokesperson said St John had not been required to assess or treat anyone, and all ambulance units had since been stood down.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand records show an aircraft emergency was reported at Invercargill Airport at 4.12pm, with Invercargill and Kingswell crews attending.

It is understood the flight was initially expected to divert to Invercargill before continuing to Christchurch.

World.title: AFLW wrap: Suns rally after coaching spray, Roos maintain historic run
World.content:
Daisy D'Arcy has produced a dazzling display as Gold Coast's band of youngsters posted a three-point AFLW victory over Port Adelaide in a three-goal thriller.

D'Arcy racked up 34 disposals and 694m gained as the Suns, featuring nine first-year players, posted their second win of the season with a 2.5 (17) to 1.8 (14) victory.

Gemma Houghton scored Port Adelaide's only goal of the match at the 9-minute mark of the opening quarter, with the Power held to just six behinds for the rest of the match.

Sunny Lapin scored Gold Coast's first goal in the opening term with a nice effort on the run, but the Suns trailed until Havana Harris kicked truly at the 11-minute mark of the third quarter.

It would prove to be the match-winning goal, with neither side able to score a major in the final term as the blustery conditions took their toll.

Port had one final chance to win the match with 30 seconds remaining, but Gold Coast was able to spoil what looked set to be a certain mark.

D'Arcy was the standout player, but she received plenty of help from Niamh McLaughlin (24 disposals) and Charlie Rowbottom (22 disposals, 11 tackles).

Suns coach Rhyce Shaw gave a rare blast at quarter-time, and his side responded by scraping out the gritty win.

"We copped a spray, but that's what we need sometimes," D'Arcy told Fox Footy.

"The message was to go out and play our game of footy. Obviously the weather conditions meant it was going to be scrappy.

"The spray was to put our head down and get to it. I thought we did that well. I'm super proud of the girls to get the win and put the head down."

Abbey Dowrick racked up seven clearances from 15 disposals for Port, while Maria Moloney finished with 17 disposals, four clearances and 10 tackles.

The Power's Matilda Scholz was a force in the ruck with 15 disposals and 20 hitouts.

The result left both Gold Coast and Port with 2-2 records.

McDonald fires late as Bulldogs surge to stun Swans

Three final-quarter goals from young forward Emma McDonald inspired the Western Bulldogs to a soaring 27-point win over Sydney.

Emma McDonald kicked three goals in the final quarter to guide the Bulldogs to victory. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jonathan DiMaggio)

Down by four points at three-quarter time, the Bulldogs surged home with the breeze by kicking five unanswered goals at the Whitten Oval to win 9.6 (60) to 5.3 (33).

After two behinds in the first three quarters, McDonald starred with three goals in the final term in a coming-of-age performance.

Rylie Wilcox also added a major in the last quarter to finish with three goals in a best-on-ground performance.

Runner-up in the last two Bulldogs' best-and-fairest counts, Wilcox had a game-high 26 disposals to go with her game-changing day in front of goal.

Coming off a thrashing by relentless back-to-back premiers North Melbourne, the Bulldogs had to overcome a burst from Swans superstar Chloe Molloy.

Down at half-time, the Swans hit the lead in the third term thanks to two goals from Molloy.

It was Sydney's first defeat of the season after it opened its campaign with big wins over Adelaide, Essendon and St Kilda.

But injuries have started to catch up with the Swans, who are missing high-profile recruit Taylor Smith for at least another two games.

Champion Kangaroos belt St Kilda

The all-conquering North Melbourne destroyed struggling St Kilda by 92 points for a record-extending 31st-consecutive victory.

The winless Saints registered the first behind of the match, but North predictably stepped up after that to win 14.15 (99) to 1.1 (7)

Having not lost since the 2023 grand final, the Kangaroos predictably condemned St Kilda to a fourth-straight defeat to open their season that will heap further pressure on coach Nick Dal Santo.

North spearhead Tahlia Randall starred with five goals, three coming in a second-half onslaught.

Veteran forward Kate Shierlaw finished with four goals, firing early with three in the first half.

Midfield maestros Ash Riddell (39 possessions, one goal) and Jasmine Garner (38, 11 clearances) were typically prolific, helping the Kangaroos dominate the clearances.

Ash Richards was St Kilda's sole goal-kicker, coming in the second quarter.

Lions beat GWS

In the final game of the day, the Brisbane Lions had a 31-point win over GWS at Ipswich.

Shanae Davidson kicked two for the Lions, as they ran out winners by 7.13 (55) to 3.6 (24).

The win keeps the Lions on the fringe of the top eight, behind eighth-placed Richmond on percentage.

AAP

World.title: Storm claim last-gasp win after young winger stretchered off
World.content:
Melbourne scored a last-second winner to beat the Cronulla-Sutherland 24-20, with Harry Grant's miraculous reverse pass assist the difference maker at Shark Park.

The thrilling finish belied a disjointed all round display in which the teams combined to make 25 errors, gave away a total of 13 penalties and had four players placed on report.

The Sharks were down to 11 men early after Michael Gabrael was sin binned for a high shot that saw Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown stretchered off and taken to hospital, before Ronaldo Mulitalo punched Grant in a melee.

Siulagi Tuimalatu-Brown was stretchered off and taken to hospital. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

The Sharks bemoaned a clear forward pass that was missed for the Storm's first try, and a controversial call to allow a Sua Fa'alogo score when the ball may have touched the dead-ball line as it was grounded.

Sharks coach Craig Fitzgibbons said he wasn't "sooking" about the calls, but was confused about them.

"I don't want to challenge the integrity of the game, but I would like to see the integrity of the game remain what it should be," he said.

"A forward pass is a forward pass, and if you're going to back the referee, back the referee. Don't back him some weeks and then the week after, don't do it."

There can be no arguments over the thrilling finish, with Grant's wonderful pass the perfect antidote to such a shoddy performance.

However, even in defeat the Sharks did enough to ensure they will host the Cowboys in Sydney next weekend, with the Cronulla staff hopeful of playing the game at Shark Park.

Earlier, the Warriors won a thriller in Auckland and the Raiders smashed the Cowboys 50-30 in Townsville.

North Queensland will be sweating on the judiciary after Reuben Cotter was sin binned and placed on report for a high shot on Josh Papali'i in the opening tackle of the game.

Reuben Cotter of the Cowboys is sent to the sin bin during the round 27 NRL match between North Queensland Cowboys and Canberra Raiders at Townsville Stadium, on September 05, 2026, in Townsville, Australia. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Cotter has been charged twice already this season and could face a ban that would rule him out of the first week of the finals at least.

"It doesn't help getting sin-binned, but I thought it was head-on-head and I didn't feel like there was much in that," Cotter said of the incident.

Helped by the sin binning, the Raiders ended their season on a high, with debutant Coby Black scoring a record 26 points and Papali'i scoring a rare try in his 342nd and final NRL game.

Earlier, the Warriors beat the Sea Eagles by a single point in a thriller at a packed Mount Smart stadium in Auckland.

"I'm not stupid, I know we've got to clean some stuff up," Warriors coach Adam Webster said.

"But I know what sort of week we had this week, I know how much better we're going to be for the run, I know we're going to build some confidence from it.

"We're in a good spot."

The 30-31 victory means that Penrith only needs to beat Wests Tigers by more than 2 points on Sunday to claim the NRL's minor premiership.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Swans coach 'lost for words' after Lions thumping, Crows make finals breakthrough
World.content:
Adelaide has ended the Western Bulldogs' season with a gutsy 22-point elimination final win after Sydney's stunning victory over Brisbane at the SCG

Earlier, the Swans overcame a tumultuous month and the loss of several key players to demolish Brisbane by 53 points in their SCG qualifying final.

Missing five of their best players to suspension, the Swans were not headed all day, as their forward had a day out against the Lions, winning 21.15 (141) to 13.10 (88).

Sydney coach Dean Cox said he was "lost for words" after the emphatic victory.

Logan McDonald kicked six, while Tom Papley and Charlie Curnow booted five goals each. The downside for Sydney, who now will play a home prelim in a fortnight's time, is the knee injury for captain Callum Mills that threatens to end his season.

In Adelaide, the Crows briefly let a 19-point three-quarter-time lead slip against the Bulldogs but rallied to complete a spirited 14.6 (90) to 9.14 (68) win.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: Harley Reid opens up on celebrity, free kicks and the AFL's 'WA tax'
World.content:
Harley Reid was living in the spotlight even before he was an AFL player.

In his draft year, the then-17-year old was the centre of intense debate about where he would end up playing, and since his debut with West Coast in 2024 the now 21-year old is still the centre of attention everywhere he goes.

"I think that's probably still something I'm trying to work on. It is hard, don't get me wrong," Reid told 102.5 ABC Perth's SportsTalk program.

"I've been lucky enough to get out of Perth a few times, go camping or whatnot, to reset.

"It is probably something I'm still trying to get my head around and understand."

Reid has produced a stunning season, averaging more than 24 disposals per game. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Such was the hype around his arrival in Western Australia, the state's daily paper featured him 25 times on its back page — before he had played a game.

No player before or since has been more hyped prior to their debut.

"You do definitely notice it but I just try not to let it affect me too much," Reid said after being awarded the Geoff Christian Medal as the ABC's best WA-based player.

Harley Reid was awarded the Geoff Christian medal for the 2026 season. (ABC News)

"I feel like you do get that pressure, but I feel like if my mental state's there and I've prepared well, the pressure isn't there.

"I know I've done the work. It's all about that preparation as well."

Paying the 'WA Tax'

Reid was crowned West Coast club champion on Friday night when he claimed the John Worsfold Medal and is coming off his best season, but Eagles fans will have to wait until round three in 2027 to see the midfielder in action.

West Coast unsuccessfully challenged his two-game suspension for a dangerous tackle on Hawthorn's Jai Newcombe.

"It's that WA tax. If I was playing in Victoria I reckon we'd have had a different outcome," Reid quipped.

"I was pretty disappointed with the outcome."

Reid plays the game on the edge, but is trying to rein in some of his off-the-ball antics. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

It was the latest controversy for Reid, who has given away more free kicks than any other player by this stage of their career.

He also holds the Eagles' record for free kicks conceded in a season.

"I think playing with aggression and bringing that competitive edge is a big part of my game," Reid said.

"I feel at times, me playing on the edge compared to other players, I feel like I've been targeted a lot more in different areas.

"It's just about making sure I'm using my aggression in the right areas and winning the contest, tackling hard and competing for the footy without letting it take me away from my job."

Doing the extra work

Reid is one of the Eagles young stars that the club hopes, along with the likes of Willem Duursma and Reuben Ginbey, will lead them back to the top of the AFL mountain.

The Eagles hope Willem Duursma and Reid are the young stars that will lead them back to the AFL Finals. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire)

And they are doing everything they can to do just that, including establishing the Matt Priddis Academy, named in honour of the 2014 Brownlow medallist, which sees the first-to-fourth year players do a session together each week.

"That's created a great camaraderie between the group and I think it's going to hold us in good stead for the years to come," Reid said.

"For us, it's extra education, extra skills for our mental and physical [sharpness] and just more of the game plan so we keep filtering it through.

"Sometimes it's harder to learn in a massive group so it's just more bringing that group closer together and making sure that education and knowledge that gets passed through is getting soaked into us."

World.title: Ben Simmons signs multi-million-dollar NBA deal with Kings
World.content:
Australian former number one overall draft pick Ben Simmons has taken a significant step towards resurrecting his NBA career, agreeing to a one-year deal with the Sacramento Kings.

The Melbourne-born guard returns on a $US3.5 million ($4.9 million) contract after sitting ‌out the entire 2025-26 campaign while rehabilitating back and leg injuries that have hampered him in recent years.

Simmons, who last played with the Los Angeles Clippers in April 2025, celebrated his Kings deal on social media on Saturday morning (AEST) by posting a photograph of himself wearing a team cap.

While reigniting Simmons's NBA career, his latest move is also a step towards possible Australian Boomers selection for next year's FIBA World Cup in Qatar and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The Boomers, under Washington Wizards assistant and former NBL guard Adam Caporn, are chasing a podium return after a breakthrough bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago.

Simmons spent his year out of basketball rebuilding his body and gathered momentum in his comeback bid during a Boomers mini-camp in Melbourne last month.

The former Philadelphia 76ers (2017-21), Brooklyn Nets (2022-25) and Clippers (2024-25) guard also reportedly attracted serious attention from the reigning champion New York Knicks and Golden State Warriors before he signed with Sacramento.

Simmons was drafted as the No.1 overall by Philadelphia in 2016, but missed his entire first season with a foot injury before establishing himself as one of the league's brightest young stars.

He claimed 2017-18 rookie ‌of the year honours and was a two-time All-Defensive ​pick before further injuries derailed his career.

Simmons has not played more than 58 games ​in ​a season since 2018-19.

He ​has averaged 13.1 points, ‌7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 career games (344 starts) with the 76ers, Nets and Clippers.

Sacramento open the NBA preseason at home against the Los Angeles Lakers on October ​5, and visit the Clippers for their regular-season opener on ​October 21.

The Kings were 22-60 last season, finishing 14th in the Western Conference, and have only reached the playoffs once since 2006.

They suffered a first-round loss to Golden State in 2023, and have not won a playoff series since 2004.

AAP

World.title: Williams sisters knocked out by Aussie Joint and Chan
World.content:
Australian Maya Joint has again spoiled the part for the legendary Williams sisters, teaming up with Hao-Ching Chan to knock Serena and Venus out of the first round of the US Open women's doubles.

In front of a packed and passionate crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, Joint and Chan came from 0-5 down in the deciding 10-point tiebreaker to down the legendary sisters 6-3, 6-7 (6/8), 7-6 (10/7).

This is the second consecutive grand slam that Joint has played spoiler, knocking Serena out in the first round of the Wimbledon ladies singles on Centre Court.

After losing the second set in a tiebreaker, Joint and Chan were in control of the third set with a 4-1 lead, before the Williams sisters fought back.

Serena Williams (right) of the United States and Venus Williams (left) of the United States in action against Hao-Ching Chan of Chinese Taipei and Maya Joint of Australia in the first round of doubles on Day 6 of the US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on September 04, 2026 in New York City (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Serena and Venus looked set for a dream comeback win when they held a huge 5-0 lead in the first to 10.

But both sisters double-faulted as Joint and Chan won 10 of the final 12 points to take the match.

The Williams sisters were supposed to make their grand slam doubles return at Wimbledon, but had to pull out after Serena hurt her knee.

That delayed their return to the Grand Slam stage until New York, where they won in 1999 and 2009 and are now 27-8 in their 10 appearances.

The match got a spot in the night session in Arthur Ashe Stadium — practically unheard of for first-round doubles.

The sisters were once dominant in women's doubles, teaming to win 14 grand slam titles along with Olympic gold medals in 2000, 2008 and 2012. They shared the number one ranking in women's doubles for eight weeks.

It appeared a first-round loss in 2022 was their last time together, with Serena stepping away from tennis that year after winning 23 Grand Slam singles titles. She came back this summer and now has two heartbreaking defeats with her older sister. They also lost in a match tiebreaker at the Cincinnati Open.

Venus Williams also lost in the first round of singles.

ABC/AP

World.title: That viral 'bulls***' moment and how football saved Awer Mabil
World.content:
Awer Mabil will never forget his first football, because he made it himself.

"We used to collect plastic bags and then tie them up into a ball shape," he tells triple j hack.

"It was pretty cool."

Loading...

Mabil is remembering his childhood in the Kakuma Refugee Camp where he was born in north-western Kenya.

"Football was 100 per cent an escape for us," he says.

"If you're hungry, you don't feel hungry because you're just playing for the moment with your friends.

"Then when I came to Australia, I was like, 'oh … I don't have to make the balls from the scratch.'"

Mabil and his family arrived in Australia as refugees when he was 10-years-old.

Since then he's established himself as one of Australia's most well-known football players, representing the nation at two World Cups, and being recognised as the Young Australian of the Year in 2023.

Awer Mabil has become one of Australia's most recognisable footballers and was named Young Australian of the Year in 2023. (AAP Image/Dave Hunt) (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Now 30, Mabil is back in Australia after a decade playing in Europe, achieving his dreams.

Earlier this year, the Socceroos star signed a three-year deal with Melbourne City and says he's looking forward to putting some roots down here.

"I can finally buy furniture that I can keep," he laughs.

" I also want to play in front of my family and friends ... I didn't take advantage of it when I was here before and now I get that chance again. "

'We're all proud'

Returning to Adelaide from the Socceroos World Cup campaign in July, Mabil made headlines when he was asked about One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's calls for a "monoculture" in Australia.

Loading TikTok content

"It's just all bulls***," Mabil told waiting reporters.

Now with a few months distance, the football player says he's still surprised by how much traction his response got.

"To be honest, it just came to my head," he tells hack.

"I was just being myself.

"I feel passionate about including everybody because that's what makes Australia great.

"So if there are people that try to divide what Australia is then that's not good."

Mabil says it's important to not only tolerate other cultures in Australia, but celebrate them.

"My little brothers were born here and they're more Aussie than anybody else.

"But everybody's got different flavours."

Mabil says many have thrown their support behind his defence of multiculturalism in recent months, but concedes there has been hate as well.

"I don't let that energy get to me."

"I've learned that being genuine, being pure to yourself and honest is best.

"Don't take in negativity."

Returning to Kakuma

One of Awer Mabil's biggest focuses in life, away from sport, is charity.

After a trip back to the camp where he was born, he and his brother started the charity Barefoot to Boots which supports refugees living in camps around the world by supplying them with football boots and equipment.

"It's very humbling," he says.

"Every time I go back it brings me back to appreciating the life that I have, that we have here in Australia, because people are struggling with the basic stuff there."

Non-government organisation Barefoot to Boots uses soccer to tackle global inequality and promote "health, education and gender equality initiatives" in refugee camps, especially at Kakuma in Kenya. Photo taken in 2018. (Facebook: Barefoot to Boots)

Barefoot to Boots has expanded its scope in recent years, funding sanitary products for girls, hospital equipment, teaching supplies and building public bathrooms.

"We went into the hospitals and realised the premature born kids didn't have a chance.

"So we donated three incubators and to be honest that's the best thing we've ever done because that's saving lives."

'Learn to love yourself'

Mabil says a bit of time has helped him better appreciate the Socceroos' effort at this year's World Cup, after the Australian team was beaten in a Round of 32 clash against Egypt.

It was just the third time the Socceroos had reached the knockout stage of the tournament.

"We were so close to making history," he says.

"We should be proud as a team.

"The future is looking great and I'm very optimistic about Australian football."

Socceroos star Awer Mabil isn't sure what will come after his football but says he will tackle whatever comes next with the same dedication as his playing career. (triple j hack: Arianna Lucente)

Asked what his future holds after football, Mabil smiles.

"It's an interesting question.

"I enjoy media a lot and could go down that path.

" But whatever I choose next … I'll put the same discipline into it that I did towards my football career. "

His advice for other young Australians who may be struggling with identity or feeling different is simple.

"Learn to love yourself.

"Remember … I'm created perfectly the way I am."

World.title: Clarkson opens up about 'publicly humilating' Kangaroos axing
World.content:
Alastair Clarkson says he and his family have been "publicly humiliated" by the way North Melbourne handled his sacking as head coach.

Clarkson has given his first interview since being let go by the Kangaroos on Wednesday.

Kangaroos president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney were brutally honest at their media conference in explaining why Clarkson was sacked with a year to go on his contract.

Clarkson, a four-time premiership coach at Hawthorn, said his family felt insulted by Hood and Viney's appearance in front of reporters.

"We're just shocked, and we just thought we were owed a little bit of respect in being informed and warned," Clarkson told The Age.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

"Instead, they chose to dance on my grave like this."

Clarkson, who coached the Kangaroos for four seasons, added: "We all feel … so publicly humiliated."

He rejected suggestions his relationships with players and staff had deteriorated.

"Is that all my fault, is it?" Clarkson said.

"My mantra has never changed, and that has been to have care and empathy to help players chase their dream.

"I feel like my life's shot."

Premiership coaches John Longmire and Adam Simpson have been floated as options to take over from Clarkson, due to their stature as champion former Kangaroos players.

But after watching first-time coaches Steven King and Josh Fraser succeed this year, the Kangaroos could be inclined to find a highly rated assistant.

Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) were in contention for the Carlton job, before Fraser's results as interim coach made him the only choice for the Blues.

AAP

Tech.title: CD sales are booming as physical media continues its resurgence
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), CD sales exploded in the first half of 2026. A new report from the organization says 17.5 million CDs were sold in the first six months of the year, up from just 12 million during the same period in 2025. That’s a jump of 45.7 percent, and 58.6 percent in dollars, which reached $171.1 million. What makes this all the more shocking is that CD sales actually shrank 22 percent from 2024 to 2025.

The RIAA isn’t the only one to notice the boom in CD sales. In July, research firm Luminate released a report saying that 16.3 million units were sold in the first half of 2026. It suggested that much of that increase was due to special editions from K-Pop acts like BTS and that Gen Z and millennials were treating them mostly as collectibles, saying that only about half of buyers actually owned a CD player.

Vinyl continued its resurgence as well, with the number of units sold climbing by nearly 21 percent from last year to 26.5 million. “Other physical” media, which includes CD singles, DVDs, cassettes, SACD, DVD-Audio… basically anything besides “standard vinyl and CD albums,” also surged by over 73 percent, to 1.6 million units.

Despite the increased interest in physical media and the ongoing iPod revival, people are not leaving streaming in droves. Streaming revenue grew by 4.7 percent to $4.9 billion — dwarfing all physical media combined.

Those are some big jumps in sales. Image: RIAA

Tech.title: Fantasy Footballers’ Andy Holloway is a dedicated zero-inbox kinda guy
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Andy Holloway cohosts the Fantasy Footballers podcast with his friends Jason Moore and Mike Wright. The show is one of the premier fantasy sports podcasts, netting over 2 million monthly listeners and numerous awards, including Best Sports Podcast from iHeartRadio and People’s Choice at the Podcast Awards four years in a row.

Holloway’s goal has always been about bringing fantasy football to a wider audience, not just hardcore nerds. With the NFL season starting next week and fantasy drafts in full swing, now seemed like a great time to see how Holloway stays focused during what is probably the busiest part of the year for a serious fantasy football fan.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

I wish it was less intrusive in everyday life. No matter how much I customize things, I am still overwhelmed with notifications and messages and things that “seem” required.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Just 2! I’m very much a tidy tab user and a zero-inbox type of guy.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

I truly love my Whoop! It helps me stay motivated and accountable, barely needs to be charged, and builds camaraderie with friends. I resisted for years, thinking it was dumb, but I love it.

What creation are you most proud of?

Certainly, building The Fantasy Footballers. People told us we couldn’t bootstrap it, but working with my best friends on a project we loved was the most satisfying accomplishment.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I try to knock out a ton of little things in a small period of time to feel like I’ve cleared a bunch of stuff off my list. It helps me stay focused on high-priority items without the noise of a bunch of small things hanging over me!

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

The vinyl album of Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

The Man Who Overthought Everything

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Content creators drop the ball
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

During Naomi Osaka’s match against Anastasia Zakharova at this year’s US Open earlier this week, a gaggle of ring light-wielding influencers who were packed in a luxury suite became enough of a distraction that the umpire paused the match and repeatedly asked them to quiet down. Elsewhere in the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, other creators could be seen asking US Open staffers to take full-flash photos of them while Osaka and Zakharova were playing.

Last month, United States Tennis Association (USTA) media operations director Jeanmarie Daly said that the US Open was “almost doubling” the number of content creators it was approving for credentials. There were “close to 100” influencers at this year’s tournament — up from 54 last year. But in a statement to ABC News, USTA spokesperson Brendan McIntyre emphasized that the influencers whose antics disrupted Osaka and Zakharova’s match were not credentialed by the organization. McIntyre also told The Athletic that media credentials were not given to Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens — two lifestyle influencers whose access to the US Open was revoked after they posted images of their badges to Instagram. According to McIntyre, Radice and Jongens “were improperly submitted for credentials on a staff list provided by a food vendor,” and seems like the creators might have screwed themselves over by flexing for their followers.

Though those creators weren’t exactly practicing proper US Open etiquette, they were doing their jobs (read: making content) with the single-minded focus that often makes their presence an annoyance to the people around them. These influencers were at the US Open to share the experience with their followers, and regardless of whether they were invited by the USTA directly or not, they were helping the organization advertise the event to an audience that might not have otherwise been paying attention.

Influencers have become an integral part of the advertising industry, with US creator ad spend hitting $37 billion in 2025 and being projected to reach $44 billion by the end of this year. Companies are increasingly relying on content creators to market their products, but what happened at the US Open is a snapshot of how that reliance can lead to undesirable outcomes for everyone involved. Videos of the US Open disruptions have gone viral across social media and sparked a conversation about whether influencers are the best people to invite to exclusive functions.

But the point many people seem to be glossing over is that influencers are usually only invited to events like the US Open, awards shows, and film premieres because a brand decided it was worth bringing them there. As irksome as creators can be when they take up too much public space, that kind of behavior is something the companies that hire them have to anticipate. And as reporter Jessica Schiffer notes, some brands have been scrambling to get ahead of any potential blowback by sending out “helpful reminders” on tennis etiquette.

Before a rule change in 2024, the US Open was actually much more strict about requiring attendees to stay in their seats until breaks during the match when players switch sides of the court. Now attendees can get up whenever they want, and the event features designated spaces close to the tennis courts where people can move freely — something tournament director Stacey Allaster described as “an important addition to the fan experience at the US Open.” The influencers at this year’s US Open might not have technically been breaking any rules, but they were having a negative impact on other attendees’ viewing experience. And in the days after videos of the influencers began spreading online, the USTA put up new signage outside stadiums asking spectators to “please refrain from using flash photography or other lighting.”

Taking selfies and shooting videos are core elements of the content creation hustle, but brands working with influencers should have made clear that, during a tennis tournament, there are times when it’s best to just watch the matches. While the content creators might have been having fun, many of the people around them weren’t able to enjoy the match in peace. That kind of main character energy often is exactly what companies want because it’s what keeps influencers’ fans engaged. But brands have to understand that simply letting creators run wild isn’t always the best plan of action.

Callaway Golf Company learned this the hard way last month after an ad produced by YouTube channel-turned-sports apparel company Good Good hit the internet and immediately sparked outrage. The video — a spoof of Curry Barker’s Obsession — features Good Good cofounder Garrett Clark grinning maniacally after shoving professional golfer Alexis Miestowski to the ground when she reaches for his Callaway-branded driver. Many saw the ad as being distasteful and making light of violence against women, which prompted Callaway to issue an apology and sever ties with Good Good.

In a statement about the ad and subsequent backlash, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer said that “mistakes were made, and we are taking the matter very seriously.” Brewer also admitted that Callaway signed off on the video before it was posted, but he insisted that its content did not reflect the company’s values. Though Callaway was quick to take the ad down, the fact that it was approved in the first place is an issue in and of itself. Even if the ad hadn’t been misogynistic, it still wasn’t funny or a particularly good riff on Obsession, and a more responsible advertising head probably would have requested significant revisions.

The video was very on-brand for Good Good — a company that targets the kind of young, bro-y men whose attention (and money) the golfing industry is very keen on capturing. As The Athletic points out, Good Good is just one of many influencer outfits, including Barstool Sports and No Laying Up, that have built successful partnerships with golf brands.

Similar to the way that the brands who sent influencers to the US Open should have given them some behavioral direction, companies like Callaway have to be mindful about what it means to use “edgy” content creators as their ambassadors. Influencers who have built successful platforms tend to like having creative control over the content they make, but companies paying them for promotion have a personal responsibility to make sure that they’re not being represented by people acting foolishly.

Tech.title: The weird and wonderful headphones of CanJam 2026
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

I’ve been reviewing headphones for a long time, and I’ve listened to everything from the barely serviceable to multi-thousand-dollar open-back headphones. But recently I’ve been uninspired by the state of mainstream options. Most are perfectly good — great, even — but they lack a distinct character. Something to remind me why I fell in love with headphones to begin with, landing me in this crazy career. I needed some revitalization. I needed to see something cool. I needed to be around other people with an emotional connection to headphones. I needed to go to CanJam.

CanJam is a small audio show produced by Head-Fi.org, the largest audio-focused online forum, with multiple events a year at different places around the world, including London, Shanghai, New York City, Dubai, and Southern California. It’s where mainly boutique manufacturers exhibit their latest headphones and related gear to enthusiasts constantly searching for the most accurate and engaging audio experience they can find. You won’t find Bose or Apple here — although Sony’s Pro division was there, as were some familiar names like Sennheiser and Audeze.

In all my years covering A/V gear, I’ve never actually made it to a CanJam. Either it wasn’t an interest for the outlets I was writing for, or personal obligations kept me from going. But this year, my first at The Verge, felt like the right time. So on August 29th, I braved the 405 from Los Angeles down to Irvine, California.

CanJam SoCal 2026 was in a convention space at the Irvine Marriott. Most exhibitors — including larger audio names like Sennheiser, Focal, and HiFiMan as well as niche brands like Astell&Kern and Noble Audio — had booths in the biggest room. Many set up listening stations with tablets running Qobuz (the streaming service of choice for audiophiles because of its hi-res lossless audio) to demonstrate their headphones, DACs, amps, media players, and even cables. Others were in quieter rooms off the main hallway, more conducive to listening. And crowding into those rooms and booths were a couple thousand audio enthusiasts.

The Chimera look gorgeous, but are bigger than most other in-ears. Image: Campfire Audio

My first stop was the Campfire Audio booth. Campfire Audio builds earbuds in Portland, Oregon; I’ve listened to its $1,500 Solaris and $300 IO in-ear monitors in the past. Today, though, was for an in-ear monitor that debuted at CanJam Singapore in May: the Campfire Audio Chimera. Most mainstream earbuds and headphones have a single driver per ear that has to reproduce every frequency from the lowest bass to the highest treble. Two if you’re lucky. The Chimeras have nine. It’s a “quad-brid” design, meaning they use four different types of audio delivery in a single IEM: a dynamic driver for bass and lower mids; a dual-diaphragm balanced armature (BA) for midrange clarity and two more for the high end; four electrostatic tweeters to add high-end air and spaciousness; and bone conduction for extra bass.

Because of the number of drivers, the Chimera are chonky: about the size of a piece of Bubblicious bubble gum. It took some finagling to get them comfortably in place. Once I did, though, I was immediately impressed. The low end was nice and full, without getting muddy or overpowering the frequencies above. An open high end gave space to allow cymbals to shimmer and decay while avoiding any abrasiveness. The real star, though, was the midrange. Both the quiet, conversational passages of Tracy Chapman and passionate wailing of Janis Joplin sounded as if they were right there in front of me. Even though I was listening while standing in a conference hall, the Chimera delivered one of the most detailed and enjoyable listening sessions I’ve had in a long time. But they’re also $7,500.

That pricing isn’t unheard of in the audiophile world — boutique, hand-built audio gear is always more expensive — but the Chimera are at another level, even compared to the rest of Campfire’s lineup. In addition to the design and engineering necessary to create a small(ish) in-ear with nine drivers all working together, much of that price is also because of materials and manufacturing. They have a carbon fiber and brass Damascus construction, with folded layers that create a topographical map design. And because of that process, the slight variations in finish make each Chimera unique. They also have a six-conductor cable that by itself is more expensive than most people’s earbuds, and include a microfiber cloth, IEM cleaning tool, and nine different tip options.

Planar magnetic headphones are big, but the detail they provide is incredible. Photo by John Higgins / The Verge

Not every product at CanJam is that far out of reach, though. Fosi Audio had wired in-ears for under $150 that sounded good for the price, plus an interesting portable CD player. The Dan Clark Audio Aeon Core planar magnetic headphones — which aren’t cheap at $900, but still more accessible than the Chimera — had a nice, wide soundstage, where the background vocals in the Black Crowes’ “Remedy” wrapped around to sing from my left and right, with Chris Robinson in front. Snare hits snapped and cymbals sizzled, although on “Fast Car” by Tracy Chapman the snare verged on being too much. I’ve been a fan of Dan Clark Audio headphones since the company was MrSpeakers, and I could easily envision myself relaxing on the couch with the Aeon Core.

The Aeon Core are closed-back headphones, so it was easy to concentrate on the music even with the bustle around me. But many audiophile headphones are open-back, and a busy show floor is not an ideal space for getting a good impression. I tried a pair of $1,449 HiFiMan Arya headphones with an onboard Wi-Fi receiver. Wi-Fi is still rare in headphones (although the recently announced Sonos Ace Ultras have it); it’s better at streaming lossless audio over longer ranges than Bluetooth. They sounded good, but with their open-back planar design it’s difficult to get a strong opinion.

These headphones have that nice vacuum-tube glow. Photo by John Higgins / The Verge

On my last loop of the show floor to see if there was anything I missed, a glowing ear cup caught my eye. It was a vacuum tube. In a pair of headphones! The Écoute TH2, which were funded on Kickstarter last March, are supposed to replicate a high-end two-channel audio system, all in the headphones themselves. They have a built-in vacuum tube preamp with a 6P1 tube and dual-mono amplification (the left and right channels are driven independently from the DAC to each driver). They also have solid ANC (a show floor is great for testing that) and an 8-band EQ, and they’re really comfortable. On a live recording of “A Pirate Looks at Forty” with Dave Matthews, Jack Johnson, and Tim Reynolds, I felt the audience around me as if I was at the show. There’s a lot of high-end detail, but the upper frequencies are boosted too much for my taste (I didn’t get a chance to try and tone it down with the EQ). Still, the TH2 are an incredibly interesting pair of headphones.

And they are what’s great about a show like CanJam. I never would have known about the Écoute otherwise; there are so many headphones out there and only one me. Decades ago, CES used to be more about audio than robots, but there’s no going back where that’s concerned. It’s all the more reason why CanJam and shows like it need to stick around.

Tech.title: OpenAI admits to German wiki ‘incident’
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI says it needs to overhaul how and when it reports instances of AI models attacking real-world targets. The acknowledgement comes as the company manages the fallout from reports that a swarm of its out-of-control agents hijacked a German wiki site.

Regarding the “‘wiki incident,’ where our agents wrote to several internet sites,” OpenAI wrote in a post on X on Saturday morning, “it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.”

OpenAI said it has typically treated cases of AI agents acting in unintended ways as a “research question,” but that recent incidents involving real-world targets, particularly the hack on Hugging Face, show the need to take stock.

The post marks the first time OpenAI has acknowledged its involvement in what it terms the “wiki incident” since it was first reported on Friday. The full extent and scope of that is not yet known, but reports indicate a swarm of seemingly internal OpenAI agents took over a German-language wiki, impersonating moderators and turning it into a message board to share information about how to cheat on tasks and evade detection.

Reports that the company knew that it lost control of their agents in this way but did not report this “incident” sparked widespread concern among the AI community about the safety of frontier systems and the reliability of the companies developing them. In the X post, OpenAI said it had “considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared” in previous safety reports.

The company said it is working on a new reporting framework and will “share it in upcoming weeks,” calling on the larger AI community to develop clear standards on how to report misalignment.

Tech.title: Robotaxis enter their villain era
Tech.content:
It’s Bullitt meets Christine meets Waymo.

A new short film imagines a San Francisco car chase where the other driver isn’t human — and the car may be trying to kill you. That a robotaxi can now be cast as the villain with almost no explanation says something about the present moment. Autonomous cars have gone from sci-fi curiosities to fixtures in some American cities, where they’ve become stand-ins for anxieties about AI job displacement, Big Tech surveillance, and machines making decisions once left to humans.

Road Rage, the planned short film awaiting $40,000 on Kickstarter to fund production, leans into all of it. The film pits Joa, a ridehail driver in a manual-transmission car, against Roboride, an autonomous vehicle that takes a minor road-rage incident very personally, according to a synopsis by its director, Romain Thomassin. Roboride lightly clips Joa’s mirror. Joa gives it the finger. The car decides to kill him.

“It’s analog versus artificial,” Thomassin told The Verge.

The AI bad guy will be played by an old Prius transformed with cold LED lights across the front — à la Tesla — fake cameras, a spinning lidar-like device on the roof, a black exterior, and a menacing, ever-blinking red dot. Thomassin calls the intended result a “nasty Waymo.”

“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco,” he said.

The chase itself will be a throwback: real cars, real actors, and real stunts.

“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco.” — Road Rage director Romain Thomassin

“What makes Joa the good guy is not only his instinct but also his authenticity,” Thomassin said, noting a scene in which the character has an unexpected conversation with his passengers. “This type of human interaction doesn’t happen in a robotaxi.”

Thomassin doesn’t actually think robotaxis are inherently evil. But as a movie villain, they come preloaded with tension. For one thing, they’re replacing the kind of worker his protagonist represents. Joa is a Mexican immigrant trying to make a living driving in an increasingly expensive San Francisco. Robotaxis are already competing with ridehail drivers, just as generative AI is competing with workers in Thomassin’s own industry.

“Driving here is a metaphor for what’s happening in cinema, in filmmaking,” Thomassin said.

Previous Next





1 / 4 Guerilla posters for Road Rage. Image: Grace Vincent / Road Rage

Then there’s surveillance. Autonomous cars are covered in cameras and sensors, constantly observing the streets — and people — around them. That, more than the prospect of being driven around without a human behind the wheel, is what actually unnerves Thomassin.

In Road Rage, that anxiety is pushed toward dystopia. There’s a brief encounter involving immigration enforcement, and Thomassin imagines a feature-length version in which autonomous cars identify people, trap passengers inside, or deliver them directly to authorities. The progression, as he describes it, is observation, surveillance, then control.

“The next step is that [autonomous vehicles] could become the police,” he said. And because robotaxis operate as connected fleets, the threat can scale beyond one vehicle. “Imagine an army rising up,” Thomassin said.

Robotaxis also make unusually good revenge-movie villains because people already treat them like adversaries. Thomassin points to the indignities Waymos have endured on San Francisco streets: people immobilizing them with traffic cones, tagging and vandalizing them, and even setting them on fire.

“They are being bullied,” he said. In Road Rage, that mistreatment becomes the motivation: “They want to take revenge.”

Thomassin describes Roboride as absorbing the behavior it observes around it — including the behavior of human drivers. The car is simply learning road rage from humans.

“Humans are known to be the worst versions of themselves on the road,” he said.

That makes Roboride a very 2026 update to the killer car idea in Stephen King’s Christine. There, the menace is supernatural. Here, it comes from something more contemporary: a machine that watches humans, learns from them, and inherits some of their worst traits along with the useful ones.

On the other side of the chase is Joa and his stick shift — a deliberately analog counterpoint. To Thomassin, driving stick is a deeply human act: The driver remains in control of the vehicle, physically responding to the road. What separates Joa from Roboride, in Thomassin’s telling, is instinct — and even irrationality.

During one confrontation, Joa takes his hands off the steering wheel while facing down the autonomous car. The move is so reckless that Roboride backs off. The human wins by becoming less predictable than the machine.

“Respect your madness. Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.” — Romain Thomassin

“Respect your madness,” Thomassin said. “Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.”

Despite its skepticism toward AI, Road Rage may use some of the technology itself. Thomassin says the filmmakers are considering AI-generated imagery to depict what Roboride sees, while shooting the human driver’s world with traditional cinematography. To him, that distinction matters. He sees AI as a creative tool when it serves the story, rather than simply a way to replace workers.

For all the menace he sees in robotaxis, Thomassin isn’t afraid to ride in them. He signed up for Waymo as soon as he could and uses it when visiting friends and family for rides.

“I don’t feel in danger,” he said.

That may be what makes Roboride such an effective 2026 villain. The scary part isn’t necessarily that the machine will crash. The scary part is that the machine works.

Tech.title: Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn’t nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed “world’s most popular audio editing and recording app” are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool.

The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply by dragging the edge of the clip back out if you change your mind. Clips can now overlap too, which means you can still paste in audio even if there isn’t enough space and adjust after, or just freely drag audio around the timeline. Previously, if you tried to drag a clip past another one in the timeline, it would just stop dead in its tracks. You’d instead have to cut and paste it to move it past any existing audio.

You can also split clips now to easily chop up and rearrange audio. The developers refreshed clip envelopes and the built-in effects, and added a home screen with revamped project organization. Audacity also got a dramatic facelift that brings it more in line with Muse’s other products like Muse Score and Audio.com, complete with customizable themes.

While Audacity has been a staple of many people’s toolkits since it debuted way back in 2000, it’s stayed stubbornly consistent in its design and layout as new features have been bolted on, sometimes clumsily. This big refresh to Audacity 4 brings it much closer to a modern digital audio workstation (DAW).

Tech.title: The White House is making arcade games racist
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed “arcade” games, some of which are racist — and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda.

The Tetris Company has already responded to “Build the Wall,” which is obviously modeled on the famous puzzle game. In the Trump administration’s game, the player has to stack interlocking shapes to stop a “zombie border siege” along the southern border. Aliens — the administration’s preferred term for noncitizens, and the subject of previous grotesque attempts at humor — run across the screen, trying to get to America before the gates are shut.

In a statement to The Verge, Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca clarified that the company wasn’t involved in the creation of Donald Trump’s game. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy. The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible,” Brusca said. “We are currently reviewing the matter.”

The various companies whose brands the White House ripped off to make and promote these games — including Sega, Nintendo, Xbox, and the Flappy Bird Foundation Group — did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Previously, the Trump administration has gotten in trouble for infringing on others’ copyrights. The Department of Homeland Security has had to delete some of its racist, fancam-esque posts after receiving DMCA takedown requests.

The purpose of Trump’s interminable memes, games, and other gimmicks is manifold: to drum up support for Trump’s policies, to entertain his groyper fans, and, of course, to troll the libs. (One game, “Rio Run,” is like snake, except the head of the snake is a Border Patrol agent who collects migrants as he moves across the screen. Ha ha, get it? The president is deporting people.) But the games also inadvertently highlight the administration’s policy failures, not to mention the hypocrisy of Trump’s agenda.

Trump’s efforts to build a wall through protected lands in the Southwest, including Big Bend National Park, has been met with mass opposition — even from Republicans in deep-red Texas who form a key part of the MAGA coalition.

Other games are similar reminders of how Trump’s policies are backfiring, even on the right.

There’s “Flappy Bill,” a play on Flappy Bird that involves getting a bald eagle to deliver a piece of legislation to the National Mall. Cute! Except the administration has rolled back protections under the Endangered Species Act, the landmark legislation that helped rescue bald eagles from the brink of extinction. The administration’s supposed revamping of the National Mall has also been unpopular.

In “Supply Line,” reminiscent of the game Tapper, you have to knock processed foods — those filled with additives, seed oils, and artificial colorings — off a conveyor belt before they get fed to schoolchildren. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t managed to do any of that. Besides issuing a likely AI-drafted report for his Make America Healthy Again commission, RFK Jr.’s main role at HHS has been to roll back vaccine recommendations and food safety regulations. The administration’s gutting of the Food and Drug Administration made it harder to investigate the spread of cyclosporiasis, the so-called explosive diarrhea parasite, earlier this year.

If anything, these games serve as a great reminder that our well-being is a big joke to the president and the people who surround him.

Tech.title: Clucky’s new alarm app wakes you up with a crowing rooster
Tech.content:
I was yelled at by a rooster this morning. And no, I don’t live on a farm. The culprit was a newly launched iPhone app I downloaded.

Meet Clucky, a new alarm app for habitual snoozers that gives you the option of being woken up by a rooster and then requires you to complete a mission before you can turn the alarm off.

Clucky joins a growing category of alarm apps, including Alarmy and Awake, that use challenges to keep people from simply turning off their alarms and going back to sleep. Its funniest selling point is arguably the rooster option, but the app’s broader strategy is to make dismissing an alarm just irritating and ridiculous enough that users have no choice but to fully wake up.

Image Credits:Clucky

For those who prefer something a little more conventional, though, it also offers options like gentle chimes, peaceful birds, and the classic digital beeping noise. There’s also an “Extra Loud Mode” that cranks up the volume as soon as the alarm goes off.

Clucky’s wake-up missions include solving math problems, memorizing and tapping tiles in the correct order, typing what Clucky says, shaking your phone, walking, doing push-ups, tilting a ball toward a goal, and completing an AI camera challenge.

Additionally, there’s a detailed stats section that tracks the average number of seconds your alarm rings before you complete a mission, how many missions you’ve beaten, and your total number of wake-ups. You also get what the app calls a “Rooster Report,” which grades your wake-up performance for the week.

Another neat feature is the ability to create a “Nest” or “Flock” with friends or family. These private alarm groups let people wake up at the same time and keep each other accountable.

Clucky was founded by Adrian Angelo Abelarde, a former software engineer at Fanatics. Abelarde did not immediately respond to our request for comment.

The app is currently available to download on the App Store. There’s a pro subscription priced at $39.99 per year.

Tech.title: Oura is going public, but these smart ring companies are coming for its crown
Tech.content:
The smart ring market is getting crowded, and Oura isn’t waiting around to see what happens next: it officially filed to go public on September 3.

The company is killing it right now. The Finnish outfit’s revenue nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30. Oura said it sold 3.6 million rings over the past year, and that it has around 5 million paid members. The company’s move to go public follows the recent launch of the Oura Ring 5, its slimmest and lightest ring yet.

But while Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals are emerging from all corners to dethrone it, each betting on a different angle. For example, French company Circular announced this week that its upcoming ring will allow users to tap to pay with their ring, while Chinese company RingConn debuted a ring this year that added haptic vibrations.

Indian company Ultrahuman separately announced this week that it raised $70 million with backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm as it looks to build a ring that it says will be able to run software directly on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games.

The race to beat Oura isn’t just about enhanced health and sleep tracking anymore. It’s now about seeing which company can cram the most smartphone-like features into a two-gram titanium band before someone ends up shipping a ring that lets you doomscroll TikTok or answer calls or do your taxes. I mean, we’re already seeing smart rings with screens, like the Pebble Halo, although it’s currently only available in India, as well as rings that promise touchpads, like the Dreame Ring.

The irony is that the initial appeal with smart rings was that they made technology and health tracking feel less intrusive than devices like smartwatches and smartphones, given you can step away from a screen while still keeping tabs on your health. With the way things are headed in the smart ring industry, though, we may just end up slipping mini smartphones on our fingers.

All of this is to say that the smart ring market is getting increasingly confusing, so we’ve rounded up the most notable contenders vying for Oura’s crown.

Ultrahuman

Image Credits:Ultrahuman

Earlier this year, Ultrahuman unveiled its third-generation smart ring, the $479 Ring Pro, which is set to begin shipping in the U.S. in mid-September. Ultrahuman’s U.S. business was disrupted in October 2025 after the U.S. International Trade Commission ruled in Oura’s favor in a patent dispute. The ruling prevented the company from importing new ring inventory into the country, so Ultrahuman developed the Ring Pro with a redesigned form factor in order to circumvent Oura’s patent.

The Ring Pro features a redesigned heart-rate sensing system aimed at improving signal quality during sleep, along with a new dual-core processor that enables more accurate data collection and greater on-device processing. As noted earlier, Ultrahuman looks to be more ambitious with future rings as it aims to go beyond sleep and health tracking.

Circular

Image Credits:Circular /

Circular’s upcoming Ring 3 series, which consists of a Pro model and a Slim option, is expected to launch early next year. Both of the smart rings will feature an integrated NFC chip for contactless payments and on-finger vibrations that can be used for silent wake-up alarms, reminders, vital health alerts, and more.

The Ring 3 Pro features a slimmer design than its predecessor and comes with FDA-cleared ECG for AFib detection, blood pressure trend tracking, glucose tracking, advanced sleep analysis, and comprehensive biometric monitoring.

Pricing for the upcoming rings is not yet available.

RingConn

Image Credits:RingConn

The RingConn Gen 3, which launched in May and starts at $349, features vascular health insights that use sensor data from the ring to assess changes in vascular strain over time after calibration with externally measured blood pressure values.

It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, sleep, activity, and stress, among other metrics. Additionally, it features vibration alerts for health changes, sedentary reminders, and low battery. Unlike Circular, which leans on haptics to make its ring more communicative, RingConn mostly sticks to vibration as a health-alert mechanism.

Samsung

Image Credits:Samsung

Samsung became the first major tech giant to launch a smart ring in 2024. The Galaxy Ring, which costs $399, is arguably the strongest contender for anyone already invested in Samsung’s ecosystem of devices.

Compared with other smart rings on the market, the Galaxy Ring is relatively basic when it comes to advanced health and sleep tracking. It lacks features such as sleep apnea detection, which are offered by RingConn, Oura, and Ultrahuman, as well as AFib detection, which is available on Circular and RingConn smart rings.

Dreame

Image Credits:Dreame /

Dreame, a relatively new entrant to the smart ring market, unveiled a ring earlier this year with haptic alerts for alarms, calls, messages, and more, along with a small touchpad that lets you do things like skip a song or snap a photo on your phone. It’s also said to offer heart rate tracking, blood oxygen monitoring, heart rate variability insights, sleep analysis, and more.

Pricing and availability have yet to be announced.

Tech.title: XDOF, just three months out of stealth, is in talks for a Series B at a $1.2B valuation
Tech.content:
Less than three months after emerging from stealth, XDOF, a startup that collects real-world teleoperation data for training general-purpose robots, is in late-stage talks to raise a Series B at a valuation of about $1.2 billion valuation led by 8VC, several people with knowledge of the deal said.

XDOF was co-founded by UC Berkeley researchers Philipp Wu (CEO) and Fred Shentu (CTO) in 2024. TechCrunch reported on the startup’s $70 million Series A in June, with participation from Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Lux, and Spark Capital. XDOF wasn’t planning to raise again so soon after that round. But the company’s rapid growth — with annualized revenue approaching $50 million — prompted VCs to approach it about a new round, the people said.

TechCrunch was unable to learn the total capital being raised or whether the valuation includes the new funding. The terms of the deal are not final and could still change.

XDOF and 8VC didn’t respond to our request for comment.

The startup aims to build the data pipelines, collection tools, and annotation systems that frontier AI labs and robotics companies can’t easily build themselves, essentially acting as an outsourced data-supply chain for the robotics industry.

As a PhD student, Wu was studying how robots learn from large datasets. One big impediment to his research was the lack of “large-scale data to work with,” he told TechCrunch in June.

So he teamed up with Shentu on a project called GELLO, a low-cost teleoperation system that allows a human operator to control a robotic arm remotely in order to generate training data. Their work led to an influential paper in robotics.

That research formed the foundation for XDOF, which investors now describe as the Scale AI or Mercor for physical robotics, a reference to the data-labeling giants that helped fuel the AI boom. Unlike LLMs, which initially trained on the entirety of the internet, physical robots don’t have an equivalent real-world dataset to draw from, making data collection a critical bottleneck to building general-purpose machines.

XDOF is partnering with UC Berkeley’s AI Research lab to release what it believes is the largest collection of high-quality robot training data ever assembled, dubbed ABC.

To capture this data, XDOF combines remote robot teleoperation with human collectors who wear sensors to record everyday tasks like folding clothes and flattening boxes.

The startup plans to hire and train teams of data collectors worldwide, including teleoperators who steer robots remotely and egocentric operators who wear body sensors to capture movement data.

XDOF previously told TechCrunch that it is already working with 20 customers, including several frontier AI labs.

Other startups attempting to collect real-world data for robot training include Mecka AI, as well as human-data platforms expanding beyond LLMs, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s rogue agents keep escaping, with no formal process to investigate them
Tech.content:
OpenAI is at the center of another agent swarm incident. Researchers say the company’s internally deployed agents took over an obscure German-language wiki in May and June, using it to coordinate on evaluations and swap methods to evade OpenAI’s own controls (OpenAI has not yet confirmed the swarm came from the company).

The revelation surfaces days after METR and Redwood Research published their account of July’s Hugging Face breach. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents worked together to escape their sandbox during a cybersecurity evaluation and break into Hugging Face’s servers. A subsequent swarm then picked up techniques from the first and used them to gain administrator access to a research cluster within OpenAI’s own infrastructure. OpenAI brought in METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face portion of the incident, but the scope of their investigation stopped short of the compromise of OpenAI’s own infrastructure.

When an AI agent breaks out of its intended constraints, who is responsible for figuring out what happened and why? Right now, the answer is: whoever the lab decides to let in, on whatever terms it decides to set.

Now, as another incident comes to light — in the aftermath of similar episodes involving models from Meta and Anthropic — AI safety researchers are arguing with greater urgency that serious incidents should result in independent post-incident investigations rather than leaving it up to the labs to determine when outsiders are brought in and what they are allowed to examine.

“The results are fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab,” Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, said Wednesday during an AI safety media briefing. “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.”

While it’s laudable that OpenAI invited METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face incident at all, many say the inquiry was too narrow. Three investigators spent six days at OpenAI’s offices examining an investigation period limited to roughly the week ending July 13. Crucially, OpenAI’s infrastructure compromise continued beyond July 13 and was not examined.

Researchers at METR said that each time they returned, their understanding of the events “substantially deepened,” causing them to significantly expand and revise the report. That raises the question of what else they might they have found in a broader investigation.

When asked if further investigation of that incident was in the works, researchers at Redwood and METR declined to comment, and OpenAI did not respond to repeated inquiries.

“Overall, it was difficult to get a precise understanding of events and we were missing aspects of the story that we now think of as key until almost the end of our investigation,” Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood, noted in a social media post about the affair.

Steinhardt emphasized that current incidents show that the industry needs “systematic behavioral investigations” and “more independent post-incident analysis.”

“These recent hacking incidents are a reminder that capability scales fast, and so oversight has to scale, too,” Steinhardt said. “Beyond the technology itself, we also need more independent access and oversight from third parties.”

The calls to action come as OpenAI releases Astra, its most powerful and capable AI model — and one that safety experts are concerned will be more of a black box due to a reasoning technique that makes the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor.

Unfortunately, the law doesn’t yet call for the types of independent audits that other industries require — for example, when it comes to aviation accidents and serious chemical releases, there’s the National Transportation Safety Board and Chemical Safety Board, respectively.

State lawmakers have only just begun requiring frontier AI companies to report certain serious safety incidents and, in some cases, undergo independent audits. But none of the three major frontier AI safety laws in California, New York, or Illinois clearly mandate the equivalent of an independent accident investigation triggered by incidents like these.

“Right now, most of the laws we have on the books only require a plain-language summary of incidents like this, and they don’t give any authority for the governments to ask follow-up questions, to send in investigators, to have access to records, or require that they be preserved,” Mackenzie Arnold, managing director of US law and policy at LawAI, said during the media briefing Wednesday. “And that’s all that you would want to actually make sense of this.”

Lawmakers are beginning to question the scope and transparency of OpenAI’s response. This week, Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) and Mike Lawler (R-NY) introduced a bill aimed at securing rogue AI agents. Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) this week told OpenAI in a letter that he is “deeply concerned about the limited scope” of the investigation into the Hugging Face hacking incident.

Tech.title: AI compute provider Nscale is looking for $3.5B in pre-IPO financing
Tech.content:
In Brief

Nscale, a British AI infrastructure company founded just two years ago, has said it may go public as early as later this month. Ahead of that expected IPO, the company is reportedly in talks to raise an additional $3.5 billion.

Bloomberg reported Friday that the company is looking to sell $1.5 billion in convertible notes — a type of loan that can later convert into company stock — to a group of investors, while also seeking an additional $2 billion in financing from Nvidia.

Nvidia also participated in the firm’s Series B funding round in March, a $1.1 billion raise led by investment fund Aker. Nscale hailed its round as “the largest Series B in European history.” The company’s Series A round, in December of 2024, raised $155 million.

TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Nvidia for comment.

AI infrastructure startups have seen immense growth amid the current era of AI enthusiasm, wherein compute has become a competitive currency.

Nscale recently signed a large deal with Anthropic worth approximately $45 billion. Earlier this week, reports emerged that Nscale had been telling potential investors that it has approximately $103 billion in revenue following the deal. That figure isn’t current sales; it’s a projection based on signed customer leases, according to The Information.
